Let \(A=F^r|_{V_0}\in\operatorname{GL}_K(V_0)\). Then, as polynomials in \(K[T]\), \(\det(T\operatorname{id}_V-F)=\det(T^r\operatorname{id}_{V_0}-A)\).
proof:
We prove the statement by a purely linear-algebraic computation. Throughout, matrices act on column vectors, and for a basis $\mathcal B=(b_1,\dots,b_N)$ of a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space $W$ and $G\in\operatorname{End}_K(W)$, the matrix $[G]_{\mathcal B}$ is defined by $G b_\beta=\sum_\alpha ([G]_{\mathcal B})_{\alpha\beta} b_\alpha$ (columns are images of basis vectors). For such $G$ we write $\chi_G(T):=\det(TI_N-[G]_{\mathcal B})\in K[T]$; this is independent of $\mathcal B$, because changing $\mathcal B$ conjugates $[G]_{\mathcal B}$ by an invertible matrix $P$, and $\det(TI-P^{-1}[G]P)=\det(P^{-1}(TI-[G])P)=\det(TI-[G])$. All determinants below are taken over the commutative ring $K[T]$, where the usual rules (multiplicativity, invariance under elementary row/column operations of the type "add a multiple of one row/column to another", determinant of a triangular matrix = product of diagonal entries) hold.

STEP 1 (Consequences of the cyclic hypothesis; the case $n=0$).
For $0\le j\le r-2$ the restriction $F_j:=F|_{V_j}:V_j\to V_{j+1}$ is $K$-linear, injective (because $F$ is), and surjective (because $F(V_j)=V_{j+1}$ means exactly that the image is $V_{j+1}$). Hence each $F_j$ is an isomorphism, and all $V_0,\dots,V_{r-1}$ have the same dimension; write $n:=\dim_K V_0$. Also $F^{-1}(V_{j+1})=V_j$ for $0\le j\le r-2$ and $F^{-1}(V_0)=V_{r-1}$, so $F^{-1}$ also permutes the summands cyclically; consequently $F^r(V_0)=V_0$ and $F^{-r}(V_0)=V_0$, and $A=F^r|_{V_0}\in\operatorname{GL}_K(V_0)$ (its inverse on $V_0$ is $F^{-r}|_{V_0}$).
If $n=0$ then $V_0=0$, hence $V_j=F^j(V_0)=0$ for every $j$, so $V=\bigoplus_j V_j=0$. Both sides of the claimed identity are then the determinant of the unique endomorphism of the $0$-dimensional space, namely $1\in K[T]$, and the identity holds. From now on assume $n\ge1$.
If $r=1$, the hypotheses give $F(V_0)=V_0$ and $A=F^r|_{V_0}=F$, so both sides are literally $\det(T\operatorname{id}_V-F)$. From now on assume $r\ge2$ (the computation below also covers $r=1$ formally, but we keep the two cases apart for clarity).

STEP 2 (Adapted bases and the block-cyclic matrix).
Choose a $K$-basis $e_1,\dots,e_n$ of $V_0$. For $0\le j\le r-1$ and $1\le\alpha\le n$ put $e^{(j)}_\alpha:=F^{j}e_\alpha\in V_j$. Since $F^{j}|_{V_0}=F_{j-1}\circ\cdots\circ F_0:V_0\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }V_j$ is an isomorphism, $\mathcal B_j:=(e^{(j)}_1,\dots,e^{(j)}_n)$ is a basis of $V_j$. Because $V=V_0\oplus\cdots\oplus V_{r-1}$, the concatenated family $\mathcal B:=(\mathcal B_0,\dots,\mathcal B_{r-1})$ is a basis of $V$, of length $rn$; we use it to identify $V$ with $K^{rn}$ written as $r$ block columns of length $n$, block $j$ carrying the coordinates in $V_j$.
Let $M\in M_n(K)$ be the matrix of $A$ in the basis $\mathcal B_0$, i.e. $Ae_\alpha=\sum_\beta M_{\beta\alpha}e_\beta$.
We compute the matrix of $F$ in the basis $\mathcal B$, block by block.
\quad For $0\le j\le r-2$: $Fe^{(j)}_\alpha=F^{j+1}e_\alpha=e^{(j+1)}_\alpha$, so the block $(j+1,j)$ of $[F]_{\mathcal B}$ is $I_n$ and all other blocks in block column $j$ are $0$.
\quad For $j=r-1$: $Fe^{(r-1)}_\alpha=F^{r}e_\alpha=Ae_\alpha=\sum_\beta M_{\beta\alpha}e_\beta=\sum_\beta M_{\beta\alpha}e^{(0)}_\beta$, so the block $(0,r-1)$ of $[F]_{\mathcal B}$ is $M$ and all other blocks in block column $r-1$ are $0$.
Thus, with block rows and columns indexed by $0,\dots,r-1$,
$$[F]_{\mathcal B}=M_r(M):=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&\cdots&0&M\\ I_n&0& & &0\\ 0&I_n&\ddots& &\vdots\\ &\ddots&\ddots&0&\\ 0& &I_n&0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\text{i.e. } (M_r(M))_{ij}=\begin{cases}I_n,&i=j+1,\\ M,&(i,j)=(0,r-1),\\ 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
Consequently
$$\chi_F(T)=\det\bigl(TI_{rn}-M_r(M)\bigr),\qquad\text{and}\qquad \chi_A(S)=\det(SI_n-M)\ \ (S=T^r),$$
the second identity being the definition of $\chi_A$ applied to $S=T^r$ (equivalently, $T^rI_n-M$ is the matrix of the $K(T)$-linear endomorphism $T^r\operatorname{id}_{V_0}-A$ of $V_0\otimes_K K(T)$, so its determinant is $\det(T^r\operatorname{id}_{V_0}-A)$). It remains to prove
$$\det\bigl(TI_{rn}-M_r(M)\bigr)=\det(T^rI_n-M).\tag{$*$}$$

STEP 3 (Block elimination over $K[T]$).
Put $B:=TI_{rn}-M_r(M)\in M_{rn}(K[T])$. Its blocks are
$$B_{ii}=TI_n\ (0\le i\le r-1),\qquad B_{j+1,j}=-I_n\ (0\le j\le r-2),\qquad B_{0,r-1}=-M,$$
all other blocks being $0$. Write $C_j$ for the $j$-th block column of $B$; thus $C_j$ has $TI_n$ in block row $j$, has $-I_n$ in block row $j+1$ when $j\le r-2$, has $-M$ in block row $0$ when $j=r-1$, and is $0$ elsewhere.

3a. Column operations. Let $Q\in M_{rn}(K[T])$ be the block matrix with blocks
$$Q_{mj}=\begin{cases}T^{\,j-m}I_n,&m\le j,\\ 0,&m>j.\end{cases}$$
$Q$ is block upper triangular with all diagonal blocks equal to $I_n$, so $\det Q=1$. The $j$-th block column of $BQ$ is $C'_j:=\sum_{k=0}^{j}T^{\,k}C_{j-k}$ (indeed the block $(m,j)$ of $Q$ is $T^{j-m}I_n$ for $m\le j$, contributing $T^{j-m}C_m$, and setting $m=j-k$ gives the weight $T^k$). We compute the blocks of $C'_j$.
\quad Fix $j$ with $0\le j\le r-1$ and a block row $i$.
\quad\textbullet\ If $1\le i\le j$: the term $m=i$ (weight $T^{j-i}$) contributes $T^{j-i}\cdot TI_n=T^{j-i+1}I_n$, and the term $m=i-1$ (weight $T^{j-i+1}$) contributes $T^{j-i+1}\cdot(-I_n)=-T^{j-i+1}I_n$; no other $m\in\{0,\dots,j\}$ has a nonzero entry in block row $i$. Total: $0$.
\quad\textbullet\ If $i=j+1$ (possible only for $j\le r-2$): only $m=j$ (weight $1$) contributes, giving $-I_n$.
\quad\textbullet\ If $i>j+1$: no contribution, so $0$.
\quad\textbullet\ If $i=0$: the term $m=0$ (weight $T^{j}$) contributes $T^{j}\cdot TI_n=T^{j+1}I_n$; there is no term with $m=-1$; and the term $m=r-1$ (whose column has $-M$ in block row $0$) occurs only when $r-1\le j$, i.e. only for $j=r-1$ (weight $1$), contributing $-M$.
Hence, writing $B':=BQ$ (so $\det B'=\det B\cdot\det Q=\det B$),
$$C'_j=\begin{cases}\text{$T^{j+1}I_n$ in block row $0$, $-I_n$ in block row $j+1$, $0$ elsewhere},&0\le j\le r-2,\\[2pt] \text{$T^{r}I_n-M$ in block row $0$, $0$ elsewhere},&j=r-1.\end{cases}$$

3b. Row operations. Let $E:=I_{rn}+\sum_{j=0}^{r-2}T^{\,j+1}\,\mathcal E_{0,j+1}$, where $\mathcal E_{0,j+1}$ is the block matrix unit with $I_n$ in block position $(0,j+1)$ and $0$ elsewhere. Since the $\mathcal E_{0,j+1}$ multiply to $0$ pairwise ($\mathcal E_{0,a}\mathcal E_{0,b}=\delta_{a0}\mathcal E_{0,b}=0$ as $a=j+1\ge1$), $E$ is $I$ plus a strictly block-upper-triangular matrix, hence $\det E=1$ (equivalently: left multiplication by $E$ is the composition, for each $j$, of the $n$ elementary row operations "add a $K[T]$-multiple of a row of block row $j+1$ to a row of block row $0$", each of determinant $1$).
Set $B'':=EB'$. For $1\le i\le r-1$ the block row $i$ of $B''$ equals that of $B'$, namely $-I_n$ in block column $i-1$ and $0$ elsewhere. The block row $0$ of $B''$ is the block row $0$ of $B'$ plus $\sum_{j=0}^{r-2}T^{j+1}\cdot$(block row $j+1$ of $B'$). Since block row $j+1$ of $B'$ is supported in block column $j$ with value $-I_n$, this adds $-T^{j+1}I_n$ to the block $(0,j)$, cancelling the entry $T^{j+1}I_n$ there; and since block rows $1,\dots,r-1$ of $B'$ vanish in block column $r-1$, the block $(0,r-1)$ is unchanged. Thus
$$B''=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&\cdots&0&T^{r}I_n-M\\ -I_n&0& & &0\\ 0&-I_n&\ddots& &\vdots\\ &\ddots&\ddots&0&\\ 0& &-I_n&0&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
By multiplicativity of the determinant, $\det B''=\det E\cdot\det B'=\det B=\det\bigl(TI_{rn}-M_r(M)\bigr)$.

3c. Determinant of the block-monomial matrix. Define $\sigma\in S_{\{0,\dots,r-1\}}$ by $\sigma(j)=j+1$ for $0\le j\le r-2$ and $\sigma(r-1)=0$; $\sigma$ is the $r$-cycle $(0\ 1\ \cdots\ r-1)$, so $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)=(-1)^{r-1}$. Let $P$ be the block permutation matrix with $I_n$ in block position $(\sigma(j),j)$ and $0$ elsewhere, and let $D=\operatorname{diag}(D_0,\dots,D_{r-1})$ with $D_j=-I_n$ for $0\le j\le r-2$ and $D_{r-1}=T^{r}I_n-M$. Then $(PD)_{ij}=(P)_{ij}D_j=\delta_{i,\sigma(j)}D_j$, which is exactly $B''$; hence $B''=PD$.
The matrix $P$ permutes $r$ blocks of $n$ standard basis vectors. An adjacent transposition of two blocks of $n$ vectors is, as a permutation of $rn$ letters, a product of $n^2$ transpositions, hence has sign $(-1)^{n^2}=(-1)^n$; since $\sigma$ is a product of $r-1$ transpositions, $\det P=\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)^{n}=(-1)^{n(r-1)}$. Also $\det D=\det(T^{r}I_n-M)\cdot\bigl(\det(-I_n)\bigr)^{r-1}=\det(T^{r}I_n-M)\cdot(-1)^{n(r-1)}$. Therefore
$$\det B''=\det P\cdot\det D=(-1)^{n(r-1)}\cdot(-1)^{n(r-1)}\cdot\det(T^{r}I_n-M)=\det(T^{r}I_n-M),$$
because $(-1)^{2n(r-1)}=1$. This is exactly $(*)$.

STEP 4 (Conclusion).
Combining Step 2 and Step 3,
$$\det(T\operatorname{id}_V-F)=\det\bigl(TI_{rn}-M_r(M)\bigr)=\det B''=\det(T^{r}I_n-M)=\det(T^{r}\operatorname{id}_{V_0}-A)$$
as elements of $K[T]$. The case $n=0$ (both sides $=1$) and the case $r=1$ (both sides identical) were settled in Step 1, and no other case exists. This completes the proof. $\blacksquare$

(Remark on the shape of the result, for later use: the identity says that the characteristic polynomial of $F$ is obtained from that of $A=F^r|_{V_0}$ by the substitution $S=T^r$; in particular $\chi_F$ has degree $rn=\dim_KV$, is monic, and its constant term is $(-1)^{rn}\det A$, consistent with $\det F=(-1)^{rn}\chi_F(0)=\prod_j\det(F_j)\cdot(-1)^{...}$, and it is the characteristic-polynomial analogue of the semisimplicity statement for a Frobenius-permuted family of geometrically connected components.)

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge2\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and let \(Y\subset X\) be an effective very ample Cartier divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) that is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\), with closed immersion \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the cycle class of \(Y\) and let \(L\) denote cup product with \(\xi\). Then \(\ker\bigl(L:H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)=\ker\bigl(i^*:H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)\).
proof:
We write K = \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) and \(Q:=q^m=p^{am}\), so \(K=\mathbb F_Q\) is a finite field and \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\) is an algebraic closure of \(K\): indeed \(\mathbb F_q\subset K\subset \overline{\mathbb F}_q\), every element of \(\overline{\mathbb F}_q\) is algebraic over \(\mathbb F_q\), hence over \(K\), and \(\overline{\mathbb F}_q\) is algebraically closed, so \(\overline{\mathbb F}_q=\overline K\).

**Step 0: Conventions, traces, and the Gysin map.** Fix once and for all a nonzero element \(u\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and use it to identify \(\mathbb Q_\ell(r)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell\) by \(u^r\mapsto 1\); this is the identification appearing in the statement, and it is used uniformly for both \(X\) and \(Y\) below. For \(Z\in\{X,Y\}\) let
\[
\operatorname{tr}_Z:H^{2\dim Z}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Q_\ell
\]
be the Poincar\'e duality trace of \(eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77\)(a) (normalised by \(\operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}_Z(z))=[\kappa(z):K]\) for closed points \(z\)) composed with the above identification \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-\dim Z)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell\). For \(Y\) the trace of \(eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_439\_gysin\_projection\_formula\_divisor\) is the sum of the traces over the geometrically connected components of \(Y\); since \(Y\) is geometrically connected over \(K\), \(Y_k\) is connected, so that sum is exactly the single trace \(\operatorname{tr}_Y\) just defined. Thus our \(\operatorname{tr}_X,\operatorname{tr}_Y\) are precisely the traces occurring in the two lemmas we cite.

We record two elementary consequences of the hypotheses. (i) \(Y\neq\varnothing\): \(Y\) has pure dimension \(d-1\ge 1\), so it has at least one point (and it is geometrically connected). (ii) \(Y\neq X\) and \(Y\) is an **ample** effective Cartier divisor: \(Y\) being a very ample effective Cartier divisor means there are a very ample invertible sheaf \(\mathcal A\) on \(X\) and a section with divisor \(Y\), so \(\mathcal O_X(Y)\simeq\mathcal A\); very ampleness gives a closed immersion \(j:X\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^r_K\) with \(\mathcal A\simeq j^*\mathcal O(1)\); \(\mathcal O(1)\) is ample on \(\mathbb P^r_K\) and the pullback of an ample invertible sheaf by a closed (hence finite) morphism is ample, so \(\mathcal O_X(Y)\) is ample, i.e. \(Y\) is an ample effective Cartier divisor. Hence \(X,Y\) satisfy the hypotheses of both \(Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_438\) and \(eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_439\_gysin\_projection\_formula\_divisor\) with the ground field \(\mathbb F_q\) replaced by the prime power \(Q=q^m\) (both lemmas are stated for an arbitrary prime power, and \(\overline{\mathbb F}_Q=k\)).

For \(n\ge 0\) let \(i_!:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{n+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) denote the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear map characterised by
\[
\operatorname{tr}_X(i_!a\cup b)=\operatorname{tr}_Y(a\cup i^*b)\qquad\text{for all }a\in H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\ b\in H^{2d-2-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).\tag{$\ast$}
\]
This is exactly the map of \(eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_439\_gysin\_projection\_formula\_divisor\). In the only degree we use, \(n=d\), existence and uniqueness of \((\ast)\) follow from Poincar\'e duality: since \(d\ge2\), both \(d+2\) and \(d-2\) lie in \([0,2d]\) with \((d+2)+(d-2)=2d\), so \(eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77\)(b) applied to \(X\) (dimension \(d\ge1\)) says that \((\alpha,\beta)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_X(\alpha\cup\beta)\) is a perfect pairing \(H^{d+2}(X_k)\times H^{d-2}(X_k)\to\mathbb Q_\ell\); hence for each \(a\in H^d(Y_k)\) the linear form \(b\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_Y(a\cup i^*b)\) on \(H^{d-2}(X_k)\) is represented by a unique \(\alpha\in H^{d+2}(X_k)\), and we set \(i_!a:=\alpha\).

**Step A (projection formula with the cycle class).** Apply \(eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_439\_gysin\_projection\_formula\_divisor\) over \(K=\mathbb F_{q^m}\): its hypotheses hold (\(X\) smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(K\), \(Y\subset X\) a smooth effective divisor of pure dimension \(d-1\) defined over \(K\), the same fixed \(u\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\), the traces as in Step 0, \(i_!\) as above, and \(\xi\) the cycle class of \(Y\)). Its conclusion is
\[
i_!(i^*x)=x\cup\xi\qquad\text{for every }n\ge0\text{ and every }x\in H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).
\]
Restricting to \(n=d\) and writing \(L(x)=x\cup\xi\), this says
\[
L(x)=i_!(i^*x)\qquad\text{for all }x\in H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).\tag{1}
\]

**Step B (injectivity of \(i_!\) on \(H^d(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\)).** Let \(a\in H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) with \(i_!a=0\). Take any \(b\in H^{d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\); note \(d-2\ge0\) because \(d\ge2\). By \((\ast)\) with \(n=d\) (so that \(2d-2-n=d-2\)),
\[
\operatorname{tr}_Y(a\cup i^*b)=\operatorname{tr}_X(i_!a\cup b)=\operatorname{tr}_X(0\cup b)=\operatorname{tr}_X(0)=0,
\]
the last equality because \(\operatorname{tr}_X\) is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear. Now apply \(Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_438\) to \(X/K\) and \(Y\) (its hypotheses were verified in Step 0): with \(j=d-2\) we have \(j<d-1\), so
\[
i^*:H^{d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^{d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)
\]
is an isomorphism. Hence \(i^*b\) ranges over all of \(H^{d-2}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) as \(b\) does, and we obtain
\[
\operatorname{tr}_Y(a\cup c)=0\qquad\text{for every }c\in H^{d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).\tag{2}
\]
Since \(Y\) is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\ge1\) over \(K\), \(eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77\)(b) applied to \(Y\) (with \(d\) there equal to \(\dim Y=d-1\), \(\ell\neq p\), and the same \(m\)) says that for every \(0\le n\le 2(d-1)\) the pairing \(H^n(Y_k)\times H^{2(d-1)-n}(Y_k)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-(d-1))\), \((x,y)\mapsto\operatorname{tr}^{\mathrm{PD}}_Y(x\cup y)\), is perfect. Taking \(n=d\) is legitimate because \(d\ge2\) gives \(0\le d\le 2d-2=2(d-1)\), and \(2(d-1)-d=d-2\). Composing this perfect pairing with the isomorphism \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-(d-1))\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell\) induced by \(u\) (which is the definition of \(\operatorname{tr}_Y\)) yields a perfect \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-valued pairing
\[
H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\times H^{d-2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow\mathbb Q_\ell,\qquad (x,y)\longmapsto\operatorname{tr}_Y(x\cup y).
\]
By definition of perfectness, the left map \(H^d(Y_k)\to \bigl(H^{d-2}(Y_k)\bigr)^{\vee}\) is injective; (2) says that \(a\) maps to the zero functional, hence \(a=0\). This proves
\[
i_!:H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\hookrightarrow H^{d+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\ \text{ is injective.}\tag{3}
\]

**Step C (the two inclusions).**

*Inclusion \(\ker(i^*)\subseteq\ker(L)\).* Let \(x\in H^d(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) with \(i^*x=0\). By (1), \(L(x)=i_!(i^*x)=i_!(0)=0\) since \(i_!\) is \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear. Hence \(x\in\ker(L)\).

*Inclusion \(\ker(L)\subseteq\ker(i^*)\).* Let \(x\in H^d(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) with \(L(x)=0\). By (1), \(i_!(i^*x)=0\); the element \(i^*x\) lies in \(H^d(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), so by the injectivity (3) we get \(i^*x=0\). Hence \(x\in\ker(i^*)\).

Combining the two inclusions gives
\[
\ker\bigl(L:H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)=\ker\bigl(i^*:H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr),
\]
which is the desired equality. \(
\square\)

(Remarks on the conventions, as required: the whole argument uses one and the same identification \(\mathbb Q_\ell(r)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell\) coming from the fixed nonzero \(u\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\), so that the cycle class \(\xi\) of the statement, the traces \(\operatorname{tr}_X,\operatorname{tr}_Y\) of \(eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77\)(a), and the Gysin map of \(eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_439\_gysin\_projection\_formula\_divisor\) are all computed in the same normalisation; no Frobenius-equivariance statement is used anywhere, and no localisation/affineness argument is invoked.)

statement: Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic \(0\), let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(K\)-vector space, let \(\beta:V\times V\to K\) be a \(K\)-bilinear form such that \(\beta(x,x)\neq 0\) for every nonzero \(x\in V\), let \(c\in K^{\times}\), and let \(F\in\mathrm{GL}_K(V)\) satisfy \(\beta(Fx,Fy)=c\,\beta(x,y)\) for all \(x,y\in V\). Then \(F\) is semisimple on \(V\), i.e. its base change to \(V\otimes_K\overline K\) is diagonalizable.
proof:
We prove the statement in five steps. No symmetry (or skew-symmetry) of \(\beta\) is assumed or used anywhere, and no embedding of \(\overline K\) into \(\mathbb C\) plays any role.

**Step 1: \(\beta\) is a perfect pairing.**
Consider the left radical \(\mathrm{Rad}_\ell=\{x\in V:\beta(x,y)=0\ \text{for all }y\in V\}\). If \(x\in\mathrm{Rad}_\ell\), then in particular \(\beta(x,x)=0\), and the hypothesis on \(\beta\) forces \(x=0\). Hence \(\mathrm{Rad}_\ell=0\). Equivalently, the \(K\)-linear map
\[
\varphi_L:V\longrightarrow V^{*},\qquad \varphi_L(x)=\beta(x,\cdot),
\]\nis injective. Since \(V\) is finite dimensional, \(\dim_K V^{*}=\dim_K V<\infty\), so an injective endo-\(K\)-linear map \(V\to V^{*}\) (after choosing any identification, or simply by rank–nullity) is an isomorphism; thus \(\varphi_L\) is bijective. It remains to check the right radical vanishes, which is the same statement for the map \(\varphi_R:V\to V^{*}\), \(\varphi_R(y)=\beta(\cdot,y)\). Indeed, if \(y\in V\) satisfies \(\beta(x,y)=0\) for all \(x\), and if \(y\neq 0\), then since \(\varphi_L\) is surjective there is \(x\in V\) with \(\varphi_L(x)(y)=\beta(x,y)\neq 0\) (choose any linear functional not vanishing at \(y\), possible because \(y\neq 0\)); contradiction. Hence \(y=0\), \(\varphi_R\) is injective and hence an isomorphism by the same dimension count. So \(\beta\) is perfect.

**Step 2: Jordan–Chevalley decomposition of \(F\).**
Because \(\operatorname{char}K=0\) and \(V\) is finite dimensional, \(F\) admits a (multiplicative) Jordan–Chevalley decomposition
\[
F=F_sF_u=F_uF_s,
\]\nwith \(F_s\in\operatorname{GL}_K(V)\) semisimple, \(F_u\in\operatorname{GL}_K(V)\) unipotent, and with \(F_s\in K[F]\), \(F_u\in K[F]\) polynomials in \(F\) (so in particular both are \(K\)-linear automorphisms of \(V\) commuting with \(F\), and with each other). Recall the two standard facts we use: (a) an operator \(A\in\operatorname{GL}_K(V)\) is semisimple if and only if its minimal polynomial \(m_A\in K[t]\) is squarefree; (b) the decomposition is unique among decompositions \(A=A_sA_u=A_uA_s\) with \(A_s\) semisimple and \(A_u\) unipotent. From (b) it follows that \(F_u=\mathrm{id}_V\) if and only if \(F\) is semisimple: if \(F_u=\mathrm{id}\) then \(F=F_s\) is semisimple; conversely if \(F\) is semisimple then \(F=F\cdot\mathrm{id}\) is such a decomposition, so uniqueness gives \(F_u=\mathrm{id}\).

**Step 3: the unipotent part is an isometry of \(\beta\).**
We apply the proved lemma Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/753e2a to the data \(K\) (characteristic \(0\)), \(V\) (finite dimensional), the perfect bilinear pairing \(\beta\) (Step 1), the scalar \(c\in K^{\times}\), and \(T=F\in\operatorname{GL}_K(V)\), which satisfies \(\beta(Fx,Fy)=c\,\beta(x,y)\) for all \(x,y\in V\) by hypothesis. Writing \(T=T_sT_u\) for its Jordan–Chevalley decomposition — which is exactly \(F_sF_u\) from Step 2, the Jordan–Chevalley decomposition being unique — the lemma yields
\[
\beta(F_ux,F_uy)=\beta(x,y)\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in V.
\]

**Step 4: the unipotent part is the identity.**
We now apply the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_585 to \(K\), \(V\), the same bilinear form \(\beta\) (which satisfies \(\beta(x,x)\neq 0\) for every nonzero \(x\in V\) by hypothesis), and \(U=F_u\). Its hypotheses are all satisfied: \(\operatorname{char}K=0\), \(V\) is finite dimensional, \(U=F_u\in\operatorname{GL}_K(V)\) is unipotent, and Step 3 gives \(\beta(Ux,Uy)=\beta(x,y)\) for all \(x,y\in V\). Its conclusion is that \(U\) is the identity on \(V\), i.e.
\[
F_u=\mathrm{id}_V.
\]

**Step 5: conclusion.**
By Step 2(a)/(b) with \(A=F\), \(F_u=\mathrm{id}_V\) implies \(F=F_s\) is semisimple. It remains only to unpack this in the form demanded by the statement. Since \(F\) is semisimple, its minimal polynomial \(m_F\in K[t]\) is a product of pairwise distinct monic irreducible polynomials \(m_F=\prod_{j=1}^{r}p_j\) with \(p_j\) distinct and irreducible. As \(\operatorname{char}K=0\), every irreducible polynomial in \(K[t]\) is separable, so each \(p_j\) has \(\deg p_j\) distinct roots in \(\overline K\), and the \(p_j\) being pairwise coprime in \(K[t]\) implies they remain pairwise coprime in \(\overline K[t]\) (their gcd divides the resultant \(\prod_{j<k}\operatorname{Res}(p_j,p_k)\in K^{\times}\), which is unchanged by extension of scalars). Hence
\[\nm_F=\prod_{j=1}^{r}\ \prod_{\alpha:\,p_j(\alpha)=0}(t-\alpha)
\]\nis a product of distinct linear factors in \(\overline K[t]\). An operator over a field is diagonalizable if and only if its minimal polynomial splits into distinct linear factors over that field; applied to the base-changed operator \(F\otimes\mathrm{id}\) on \(V\otimes_K\overline K\), whose minimal polynomial divides \(m_F\) and in fact equals it (minimal polynomials are unchanged by faithfully flat base change \(K\to\overline K\), e.g. because \(1,\dots,F^{n-1}\) are \(K\)-linearly independent iff they are \(\overline K\)-linearly independent, as \(\overline K\) is free, hence faithfully flat, over \(K\)), we conclude that \(F\otimes\mathrm{id}\) is diagonalizable on \(V\otimes_K\overline K\).

This is exactly the required conclusion: \(F\) is semisimple on \(V\). \(\blacksquare\)

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be prime, let m >= 1, and put k = overline(F_q). Let r >= 1 and let C_1,...,C_r be smooth projective geometrically connected curves over F_{q^m}. Then the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (id x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_et((C_1 x ... x C_r)_k,Q_ell) for every integer n >= 0.
proof:
We prove the statement by a change of notation that reduces it verbatim to the already-proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_382_product_of_curves_semisimplicity, which is stated for an arbitrary prime power base field.

Step 1 (re-indexing the base field). By hypothesis q = p^a with a >= 1 and m >= 1. Put
    Q := q^m = p^{am}.
Since a >= 1 and m >= 1, the exponent am is an integer >= 1, so Q is again a prime power, of the same prime p. The prime ell satisfies ell != p by hypothesis, exactly as required in the cited lemma.

Step 2 (identification of the base fields inside a fixed algebraic closure). We work inside the fixed algebraic closure k = overline{F}_q of F_q. Since F_q is algebraically closed in no sense relevant here but overline{F}_q is algebraic over F_q, and F_q \subset F_{q^m} \subset overline{F}_q, the field overline{F}_q is algebraic over F_{q^m} as well (a tower of algebraic extensions is algebraic) and is algebraically closed; hence overline{F}_q is an algebraic closure of F_{q^m}. Moreover F_{q^m} is precisely the unique subfield of overline{F}_q with Q = q^m elements, i.e. F_{q^m} = F_Q. Consequently:
  (i) each C_i, being by hypothesis a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over F_{q^m}, is a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over F_Q (the properties "smooth", "projective", "geometrically connected" are properties of the structural morphism to Spec F_{q^m} = Spec F_Q, which is literally the same morphism of schemes);
  (ii) the fibre product C_1 x ... x C_r in the statement is taken over F_{q^m} = F_Q, so it is exactly the fibre product C_1 x_{F_Q} ... x_{F_Q} C_r over F_Q;
  (iii) k = overline{F}_q is an algebraic closure of F_Q, so (C_1 x ... x C_r)_k is the base change of C_1 x_{F_Q} ... x_{F_Q} C_r to an algebraic closure of F_Q.

Step 3 (identification of the Frobenius operator). The automorphism of k occurring in the target statement is sigma: c |-> c^{q^m}. By the definition Q = q^m this is literally the map c |-> c^{Q}. Hence the operator appearing in the target,
    F := (id_{(C_1 x ... x C_r)_k} x Spec sigma)^*  on  H^n_et((C_1 x ... x C_r)_k, Q_ell),
is exactly the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius (id x Spec sigma_Q)^*, sigma_Q(c) = c^Q, on the etale cohomology of the base change to k of C_1 x_{F_Q} ... x_{F_Q} C_r. No further comparison or conjugacy argument is needed: the two operators are the same automorphism of the same Q_ell-vector space.

Step 4 (application of the proved lemma). The lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_382_product_of_curves_semisimplicity asserts: for every prime power, say p_0^{a_0}, every integer r >= 1, every r-tuple of smooth projective geometrically connected curves over the corresponding finite field, every prime different from p_0, and every n >= 0, the p_0^{a_0}-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on the n-th etale cohomology Q_ell-vector space of the base change to an algebraic closure of the finite field. This lemma is universally quantified over the prime power; we instantiate it with p_0 := p, a_0 := am (so p_0^{a_0} = Q), with the same r and the same curves C_1,...,C_r (which are smooth projective geometrically connected over F_Q by Step 2(i)), with the same prime ell (ell != p = p_0), and with the same algebraic closure k (Step 2(iii)). Its conclusion is then precisely: for every integer n >= 0, the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^n_et((C_1 x ... x C_r)_k, Q_ell).

Step 5 (matching the conclusion). By Step 3 the operator just obtained is exactly the operator (id x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(c) = c^{q^m}, of the target statement, and "semisimple" is used in both statements in the same sense for a Q_ell-linear automorphism of a finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector space (namely: its base change to H^n tensor_{Q_ell} overline{Q}_ell is diagonalizable). Hence the target conclusion holds for every n >= 0.

Since n >= 0 was arbitrary and no case distinction was needed (the cited lemma already covers all degrees n >= 0, including n = 0, where H^0 of a geometrically connected smooth projective variety is Q_ell with trivial Frobenius action, and n > 2r, where the group vanishes by the projective top-degree vanishing, so that the zero operator is trivially semisimple), the proof is complete.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let l != p be prime, let m>=1, and put k=overline(F_q). Let A be an abelian variety over F_{q^m}. Then the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (id_{A_k} x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_et(A_k,Q_l) for every n>=0.
proof: Let Q = q^m. Since q = p^a, Q = p^{am} is a prime power and l != p. Also k = overline(F_q) = overline(F_Q). If dim A = 0, then A is the trivial abelian variety Spec F_Q. Indeed, a zero-dimensional abelian variety is a finite connected group scheme over F_Q; hence A = Spec L for a finite field extension L/F_Q. The identity section Spec F_Q -> A gives an F_Q-algebra map L -> F_Q, forcing L = F_Q. Thus A_k = Spec k. Since k is algebraically closed (hence separably closed), H^0_et(Spec k,Q_l) = Q_l and H^n_et(Spec k,Q_l) = 0 for n > 0. The Q-power arithmetic Frobenius on Spec k is Spec sigma_Q with sigma_Q(c) = c^Q; its pullback on H^0 is the identity on Q_l, which is semisimple. Hence the assertion holds in dimension 0. Assume now dim A = g >= 1. By lemma_463_abelian_variety_covered_by_product_of_curves applied over F_Q, there exist smooth projective geometrically connected curves C_1,...,C_g over F_Q and a proper surjective generically finite morphism f: C_1 x_{F_Q} ... x_{F_Q} C_g -> A. The product is smooth projective geometrically connected, and A is smooth projective geometrically connected by definition of an abelian variety. Apply lemma_584 with the prime power q replaced by Q and X = A. Its hypotheses are satisfied: A is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension g over F_Q, and it is dominated over F_Q by a product of g smooth projective geometrically connected curves over F_Q via a proper surjective generically finite morphism. Lemma_584 therefore implies that the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius (id_{A_k} x Spec sigma_Q)^*, sigma_Q(c)=c^Q, is semisimple on H^n_et(A_k,Q_l) for every n >= 0. Since Q = q^m, this is exactly the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius required in the statement. QED.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let \beta:V\times V\to K be a perfect bilinear form, let \varepsilon\in\{1,-1\} satisfy \beta(y,x)=\varepsilon\beta(x,y), let c\in K^{\times}, and let T\in\operatorname{GL}_K(V) satisfy \beta(Tx,Ty)=c\beta(x,y) for all x,y\in V. Define G:V\times V\to K by G(x,y)=\beta(x,Ty)+\varepsilon c\beta(x,T^{-1}y). If G(x,x)\neq 0 for every nonzero x\in V, then T is semisimple on V.
proof:
We keep the notation of the statement: char K = 0, V finite dimensional over K, β:V×V→K a perfect bilinear form, ε∈{1,−1} with β(y,x)=εβ(x,y), c∈K^×, T∈GL_K(V) with β(Tx,Ty)=cβ(x,y), and G(x,y)=β(x,Ty)+εc·β(x,T^{-1}y), with the hypothesis G(x,x)≠0 for all x≠0. We prove T is semisimple, i.e. that T⊗_K 1 on V⊗_K K̄ is diagonalisable (K̄ an algebraic closure of K).

The proof has two parts: (I) we construct the additive/multiplicative Jordan–Chevalley decomposition of T in full (this is the step that was defective before; we use the Hensel/Newton lift so that p_j(T_s)E_j = 0 is an honest equality, not a nilpotence statement); (II) we apply the two supplied lemmas.

===================================================================== PART I. Jordan–Chevalley decomposition of T.

1.1. Minimal polynomial and its factorisation. Let μ(t)∈K[t] be the monic minimal polynomial of T. Since T is invertible, t∤μ: indeed if μ=tν then 0=μ(T)=Tν(T), and multiplying by T^{-1} gives ν(T)=0, contradicting minimality of μ (as deg ν<deg μ=deg t+deg ν≥1). Factor μ=∏_{j=1}^{s} p_j^{e_j} with the p_j distinct monic irreducible polynomials and e_j≥1. By 1.1, p_1,…,p_s are all different from t.

1.2. Separability of the p_j. Since char K=0 and deg p_j≥1, p_j'≠0 and deg p_j'<deg p_j. As p_j is irreducible, gcd(p_j,p_j') divides p_j and has degree <deg p_j, hence gcd(p_j,p_j')=1. Thus there exist u_j,v_j∈K[t] with
   (∗)  u_j p_j + v_j p_j' = 1.

1.3. Primary idempotents. Put M_j:=μ/p_j^{e_j}=∏_{i≠j}p_i^{e_i}. The polynomials p_j^{e_j} and M_j are coprime, so there are α_j,β_j∈K[t] with α_j p_j^{e_j}+β_j M_j=1. Define e_j(t):=β_j(t)M_j(t) and E_j:=e_j(T)∈End_K(V). Then, by construction,
   e_j ≡ 1 (mod p_j^{e_j}),   e_j ≡ 0 (mod p_i^{e_i}) for i≠j.        (1.3.1)
Hence for all j,k the polynomial e_j e_k−δ_{jk}e_j is divisible by p_i^{e_i} for every i (for i=j both terms are ≡1·1−1=0 mod p_j^{e_j}; for i≠j both are ≡0), hence divisible by μ; likewise Σ_j e_j−1 is divisible by μ. Evaluating at T (μ(T)=0) gives
   E_j E_k=δ_{jk}E_j  and  Σ_{j=1}^{s} E_j = id_V.                       (1.3.2)
Each E_j is a polynomial in T, hence commutes with T and with every polynomial in T. Set V_j:=E_j V; by (1.3.2) the V_j are T-stable, V=⊕_j V_j, and
   p_j(T)^{e_j}E_j = 0   for every j,                                      (1.3.3)
since p_j^{e_j}e_j is divisible by p_i^{e_i} for all i (by (1.3.1) for i≠j, trivially for i=j), hence by μ.

1.4. The Newton (Hensel) lift in A_j:=K[t]/(p_j^{e_j}). Fix j, write θ_j for the class of t in A_j, f:=p_j, and let m_j:=(f(θ_j))⊂A_j be the ideal generated by the class of p_j. Then m_j^{e_j}=0, because f(θ_j)^{e_j} is the class of p_j^{e_j}=0. Note f(θ_j)≠0 is not needed; what is needed is f(θ_j)∈m_j, which is immediate.

(a) f'(θ_j) is a unit of A_j: evaluating (∗) at θ_j gives u_j(θ_j)f(θ_j)+v_j(θ_j)f'(θ_j)=1, and f(θ_j) is the class of p_j, so u_j(θ_j)f(θ_j)=0 in A_j? — no: u_j(θ_j)f(θ_j) is the class of u_j p_j, which is not 0 in general. We instead argue as follows. In A_j the element f(θ_j) lies in m_j, and m_j is nilpotent (m_j^{e_j}=0), hence every element of 1+m_j is a unit. From (∗) evaluated at θ_j we get 1−v_j(θ_j)f'(θ_j)=u_j(θ_j)f(θ_j)∈m_j, so v_j(θ_j)f'(θ_j)∈1+m_j is a unit; therefore f'(θ_j) is a unit.                                                       (1.4.1)

(b) Taylor expansion in a commutative K-algebra. There is a universal polynomial S∈K[X,Y] such that for every commutative unital K-algebra R and all a,h∈R,
   f(a+h)=f(a)+f'(a)h+h^2 S(a,h).                                          (1.4.2)
Indeed, by linearity in f it suffices to check f=t^n, where (a+h)^n−a^n−n a^{n−1}h=Σ_{k=2}^{n} C(n,k)a^{n−k}h^k=h^2·Σ_{k=2}^{n}C(n,k)a^{n−k}h^{k−2}, using that a and h commute.

(c) One Newton step squares the error. Define Φ:A_j→A_j by Φ(a):=a−f(a)v_j(a). Put h:=−f(a)v_j(a). By (1.4.2),
   f(Φ(a))=f(a)+f'(a)h+h^2S(a,h)=f(a)(1−f'(a)v_j(a))+h^2S(a,h),
using commutativity of A_j to write f'(a)v_j(a)=v_j(a)f'(a). Evaluating (∗) at a gives u_j(a)f(a)+v_j(a)f'(a)=1, i.e. 1−f'(a)v_j(a)=u_j(a)f(a). Hence
   f(Φ(a))=u_j(a)f(a)^2+h^2S(a,h)=f(a)^2·(u_j(a)+v_j(a)^2 S(a,h))∈(f(a))^2,   (1.4.3)
because h^2=f(a)^2v_j(a)^2.

(d) Iteration. Set a_0:=θ_j and a_{n+1}:=Φ(a_n). Then f(a_0)=f(θ_j)∈m_j, and by (1.4.3) and induction f(a_n)∈m_j^{2^n} for all n≥0. Choose n with 2^n≥e_j; then f(a_n)∈m_j^{e_j}=0. Each a_n lies in K[θ_j] (clear by induction, since a_{n+1}=a_n−f(a_n)v_j(a_n)), so a_n=r̃_j(θ_j) for some r̃_j∈K[t]. Moreover a_{i+1}−a_i=−f(a_i)v_j(a_i)∈m_j, hence ρ_j:=a_n satisfies ρ_j−θ_j∈m_j=(f(θ_j)); so there is w_j∈K[t] with ρ_j=θ_j+f(θ_j)w_j(θ_j). Define
   r_j(t):=t+p_j(t)w_j(t) ∈ K[t].
Then r_j(θ_j)=ρ_j, and we have the two crucial properties
   r_j ≡ t (mod p_j),                                                       (1.4.4)
   p_j(r_j) ≡ 0 (mod p_j^{e_j})   (equivalently (p_j∘r_j)(θ_j)=f(ρ_j)=0).  (1.4.5)
Note that (1.4.5) is a genuine congruence modulo p_j^{e_j}, not merely modulo p_j; this is exactly the point where the earlier argument broke, and it holds because the Newton iteration drove f(a_n) into m_j^{e_j}=0.

1.5. Definition of T_s and N. Define
   T_s := Σ_{j=1}^{s} r_j(T)E_j ∈ K[T],      N := T − T_s.
Using (1.4.4), t−r_j=−p_j w_j, and Σ E_j=id, we get
   N = Σ_j (T−r_j(T))E_j = −Σ_j p_j(T)w_j(T)E_j.                            (1.5.1)

(a) T_s is semisimple. For each j, since E_kE_j=δ_{kj}E_j and all factors commute,
   p_j(T_s)E_j = p_j(r_j(T))E_j = (p_j∘r_j)(T)E_j = 0,
the last equality by (1.4.5) together with (1.3.3) (write p_j∘r_j=p_j^{e_j}·σ_j; then (p_j∘r_j)(T)E_j=σ_j(T)p_j(T)^{e_j}E_j=0). Now put P:=∏_{k=1}^{s}p_k, a squarefree polynomial. Then
   P(T_s) = Σ_j P(T_s)E_j = Σ_j (∏_{k≠j}p_k(T_s))·p_j(T_s)E_j = 0.
So the minimal polynomial μ_s of T_s divides P, hence μ_s=∏_{j∈J}p_j for some J⊂{1,…,s}. By the Chinese remainder theorem K[t]/(μ_s)≅∏_{j∈J}L_j with L_j:=K[t]/(p_j) a finite separable field extension of K (1.2). Via t↦T_s, V is a K[t]-module annihilated by μ_s, i.e. a module over ∏_J L_j; the standard idempotents of this product give V=⊕_{j∈J}W_j with W_j={x: p_j(T_s)x=0} a vector space over the field L_j. Base-changing to K̄: since p_j is separable of degree d_j and splits in K̄ with d_j distinct roots ρ_{j,1},…,ρ_{j,d_j},
   L_j⊗_K K̄ ≅ K̄[t]/(p_j) ≅ ∏_{σ=1}^{d_j} K̄,
and under this isomorphism multiplication by the class of t (which is the action of T_s) acts on the σ-th factor as the scalar ρ_{j,σ}. Hence T_s⊗1 acts on W_j⊗_K K̄≅(L_j⊗K̄)^{n_j} (n_j=dim_{L_j}W_j) as a diagonal operator. Summing over j, T_s⊗1 on V⊗_K K̄ is diagonalisable, i.e. T_s is semisimple.

(b) T_s is invertible. If p_j divided r_j then (1.4.4) would give p_j|t, hence p_j=t (both monic irreducible), contradicting 1.1. Thus gcd(r_j,p_j^{e_j})=1 and there are a_j,b_j∈K[t] with a_j r_j+b_j p_j^{e_j}=1. Then
   a_j(T)T_sE_j = (a_jr_j)(T)E_j = (1−b_jp_j^{e_j})(T)E_j = E_j − b_j(T)p_j(T)^{e_j}E_j = E_j
by (1.3.3). Hence T_s|_{V_j} is invertible with inverse a_j(T)|_{V_j}, and T_s^{-1}:=Σ_j a_j(T)E_j ∈ K[T] is the inverse of T_s.

(c) N is nilpotent. By (1.5.1), N E_j = −p_j(T)w_j(T)E_j, and since all these operators lie in the commutative algebra K[T] and E_j is an idempotent commuting with them, N^mE_j=(NE_j)^m=(−1)^m p_j(T)^m w_j(T)^m E_j=0 for m≥e_j by (1.3.3). With e:=max_j e_j and (1.3.2), N^m=Σ_j(NE_j)^m=0 for m≥e. So N is nilpotent.

(d) The unipotent part. Define T_u:=T_s^{-1}T ∈ K[T] (T_s^{-1}∈K[T] by (b)). Then
   T = T_sT_u  (immediate),   T_u = T_s^{-1}(T_s+N)=id+T_s^{-1}N,
and (T_s^{-1}N)^m=T_s^{-m}N^m=0 for m≥e, so T_u is unipotent. Since T_s,T_u∈K[T], a commutative algebra, T_sT_u=T_uT_s.

1.6. Uniqueness, hence "the" Jordan–Chevalley decomposition. Suppose T=SU=US with S∈GL_K(V) semisimple and U unipotent. Then S and U commute with T: ST=S(SU)=S^2U=(SU)S=TS, and likewise UT=TU. Extend scalars to K̄; write bars for the extended operators on V̄:=V⊗_K K̄. The four operators S̄,Ū,T̄_s,T̄_u form a commuting family. By the standard joint generalised-eigenspace decomposition of a commuting family over an algebraically closed field (proved by induction from the primary decomposition of a single operator, using that an operator commuting with B preserves each generalised eigenspace of B), V̄=⊕_α V̄_α where each V̄_α is stable under all four operators and, on V̄_α, each of them acts as (its scalar eigenvalue) times a unipotent operator.
Fix α with V̄_α≠0. Since S̄ is diagonalisable (base change of a diagonalisable operator) and V̄_α is contained in the generalised λ_α-eigenspace of S̄ (λ_α the eigenvalue of S̄ on V̄_α), we get S̄|_{V̄_α}=λ_α·id; likewise T̄_s|_{V̄_α}=λ'_α·id. Now on V̄_α, T̄ = S̄Ū = λ_αŪ|_{V̄_α} = λ_α·id + λ_α n with n:=Ū|_{V̄_α}−id nilpotent; hence T̄|_{V̄_α}−λ_α id is nilpotent and λ_α is the only eigenvalue of T̄|_{V̄_α}. But V̄_α is contained in the generalised eigenspace of T̄ for the eigenvalue λ_{α,T}, so λ_α=λ_{α,T}. Repeating the same argument with T=T_sT_u gives λ'_α=λ_{α,T}. Hence λ_α=λ'_α and S̄|_{V̄_α}=T̄_s|_{V̄_α} for every α, so S̄=T̄_s, i.e. S=T_s; then U=S^{-1}T=T_s^{-1}T=T_u.

Conclusion of Part I: T=T_sT_u=T_uT_s with T_s semisimple and T_u unipotent, and by 1.6 this is the unique such decomposition, i.e. the Jordan–Chevalley decomposition of T. In particular T_s and T_u are polynomials in T and commute with T.

===================================================================== PART II. Conclusion.

2.1. G is K-bilinear. For fixed y, x↦β(x,Ty)+εc·β(x,T^{-1}y) is K-linear because β is linear in the first slot and εc∈K. For fixed x, y↦β(x,Ty)+εc·β(x,T^{-1}y) is K-linear because β is linear in the second slot and T,T^{-1} are K-linear.

2.2. T_u ∈ GL_K(V). T_u=id+n with n:=T_s^{-1}N nilpotent of index ≤e, and (id+n)^{-1}=Σ_{i=0}^{e-1}(−n)^i.

2.3. Invariance of G under T_u. All hypotheses of Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/4e641a are satisfied verbatim (char K=0; V finite dimensional; β perfect; β(y,x)=εβ(x,y); c∈K^×; T∈GL_K(V) with β(Tx,Ty)=cβ(x,y); and T=T_sT_u its Jordan–Chevalley decomposition, established in Part I). Its conclusion, with G defined exactly as in the present statement, is
   G(T_u x, T_u y) = G(x,y)  for all x,y∈V.                                (2.3.1)

2.4. Semisimplicity of T_u. Apply Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/781973 with the bilinear form G:V×V→K, the scalar c'=1∈K^×, and F:=T_u. Its hypotheses are: char K=0 (✓); V finite dimensional (✓); G K-bilinear (2.1); G(x,x)≠0 for every nonzero x (hypothesis of the present lemma); F∈GL_K(V) (2.2); and G(Fx,Fy)=1·G(x,y) for all x,y (2.3.1). The conclusion is that T_u is semisimple, i.e. T̄_u is diagonalisable on V̄.

2.5. T_u = id. Over K̄, T̄_u is diagonalisable and (T̄_u−id)^e=0. If v≠0 with T̄_u v=αv then (α−1)^e v=0, so α=1; all eigenvalues are 1, and a diagonalisable operator all of whose eigenvalues are 1 is the identity. Hence T̄_u=id, so T_u=id.

2.6. Conclusion. T = T_sT_u = T_s, which is semisimple by 1.5(a). This is exactly the required conclusion. ∎

(Remarks on the fixes demanded by the feedback: the polynomials r_j are no longer chosen merely with r_j≡t mod p_j; they are Newton/Hensel lifts satisfying the stronger congruence p_j(r_j)≡0 mod p_j^{e_j} (1.4.5), which makes p_j(T_s)E_j=0 an honest equality (1.5(a)) and hence gives an honest semisimple operator T_s; the nilpotence of N is then a separate, correct computation (1.5(c)). No reversed divisibility is used anywhere, and the unused symmetry statement for G is not needed since the cited semisimplicity criterion requires only bilinearity and anisotropy on lines.)

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be prime, let m >= 1, and put k = overline(F_q). Let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d >= 1 over F_{q^m}. Suppose there are an integer m' divisible by m, a smooth projective geometrically connected variety Y of pure dimension d over F_{q^{m'}}, and a proper surjective generically finite morphism f:Y -> X_{F_{q^{m'}}}. If the q^{m'}-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^n_et(Y_k,Q_ell) for every n >= 0, then the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) for every n >= 0.
proof:
We prove: under the stated hypotheses, for every n>=0 the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) is semisimple.

=====================================================================
STEP 0 (Notation for Frobenius operators, finite-dimensionality, and identification with the canonical operator).
For a scheme Z of finite type over F_{q^s} (s>=1), for an integer t>=1, and for n>=0, write
    F_{t,Z,n} := (id_{Z_k} x Spec sigma_t)^* : H^n_et(Z_k,Q_ell) -> H^n_et(Z_k,Q_ell),   sigma_t(c) = c^{q^t},
the pullback in etale cohomology. When n is clear from context we write F_{t,Z}.
Note that sigma_t fixes F_{q^s} whenever s | t; in the situations below t will always be a multiple of the degree of definition of Z, so id_Z x Spec sigma_t is a well-defined automorphism of Z_k as a scheme over F_{q^s}.

(a) Finite-dimensionality. X is proper over F_{q^m}; applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob with the finite field F_{q^m} in the role of the ground field, with K = Q_{ell,X_k} and with the natural arithmetic Frobenius structure psi: F_{m,X}^* Q_ell -> Q_ell, gives that H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) is finite-dimensional over Q_ell and carries a canonical Q_ell-linear automorphism. The same applied to Y (proper over F_{q^{m'}}, q^{m'}-power Frobenius) and to X' (defined in Step 2, proper over F_{q^{m'}}) shows all groups occurring below are finite-dimensional.

(b) These pullbacks are automorphisms. eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a (applied over the ground field F_{q^s} in place of F_q) says that F_ar := (id x sigma)^* and F_geo := (id x sigma^{-1})^* are Q_ell-linear automorphisms of H^n_et(Z_k,Q_ell) with F_geo = F_ar^{-1}. Hence F_{s,Z} is invertible. For t = rs a multiple of s, functoriality of pullback, (g o f)^* = f^* o g^*, and (id x Spec tau) o (id x Spec upsilon) = id x Spec(tau o upsilon) give
    (F_{s,Z})^r = (id x Spec sigma_s)^{*r} = (id x Spec sigma_s^r)^* = (id x Spec sigma_{rs})^* = F_{rs,Z},
since sigma_s^r(c) = (c^{q^s})^{q^s}...^{q^s} = c^{q^{rs}} = sigma_{rs}(c). Thus every F_{t,Z} with s | t is an invertible Q_ell-linear operator, being a power of an invertible one.

(c) Identification with the canonical operator of lemma_45_finite_frob. We record this explicitly so that the operators manipulated below are the same as the "arithmetic Frobenius" of the statement. Take Z = X over F_{q^m} and t = m. In eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob, the canonical automorphism on H^n(X_k,K) = Ext^n_{D^b_c}(Q_ell,K) is, under the Ext identification, u |-> phi o F_X^*(u) o psi^{-1}. Taking K = Q_ell and phi = psi (the natural structure), this is u |-> psi o F_X^*(u) o psi^{-1}. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_39 applied with K = L = Q_{ell,X_k} and phi_K = phi_L = psi, this Ext-side operator corresponds, along the canonical isomorphism theta_n: Ext^n(Q_ell,Q_ell[n]) ~-> H^n(X_k, RHom(Q_ell,Q_ell)) = H^n(X_k,Q_ell), to F_coh(v) = phi_Hom[n] o F_X^* v on H^n(X_k,RHom(Q_ell,Q_ell)), where phi_Hom = RHom(psi^{-1},psi) o c_{Q,Q}. Under the canonical identification RHom(Q_ell,Q_ell) = Q_ell, both the comparison c_{Q,Q} and RHom(psi^{-1},psi) are the identity (c_{Q,Q} is the canonical comparison for the constant sheaf, and psi is the standard structure, so pullback of endomorphisms of Q_ell acts trivially on End(Q_ell) = Q_ell). Hence F_coh(v) = F_X^*(v), i.e. the canonical automorphism of lemma_45_finite_frob is exactly the pullback F_{m,X} = (id x Spec sigma_m)^*. The same argument applies verbatim to Y over F_{q^{m'}} (giving F_{m',Y}) and to X' over F_{q^{m'}} (giving F_{m',X'}).

Let r := m'/m, which is an integer >= 1 because m is divisible by m' ... precisely, m' is divisible by m, so r = m'/m >= 1 is an integer, and q^{mr} = q^{m'}.

=====================================================================
STEP 1 (Linear algebra: semisimplicity vs. diagonalizability over Qbar_ell).
(a) Invariance of the minimal polynomial under field extension. Let K be a field of characteristic 0, V a finite-dimensional K-vector space, T in End_K(V) with minimal polynomial m_T in K[t], and L/K any field extension. The evaluation map K[t] -> K[T] subset End_K(V) has kernel (m_T), hence K[t]/(m_T) ~-> K[T]. Tensoring with the flat K-module L gives an isomorphism L tensor_K K[t]/(m_T) = L[t]/(m_T L[t]) ~-> L tensor_K K[T]. Since K[T] injects into End_K(V) and tensoring with the flat module L preserves injectivity, L tensor_K K[T] injects into L tensor_K End_K(V); as V is finite dimensional, the natural map L tensor_K End_K(V) -> End_L(V tensor_K L), (lambda o f) |-> lambda o (f tensor id), is an isomorphism. Composing, the kernel of the evaluation map L[t] -> End_L(V_L), P |-> P(T tensor id), intersects the image of L[t]/(m_T L[t]) trivially; equivalently the L-images of 1, T, ..., T^{deg m_T - 1} are L-linearly independent. Therefore the minimal polynomial m_{T_L} of T_L = T tensor id_L has degree >= deg m_T. Since m_T annihilates T_L we have m_{T_L} | m_T in L[t], so m_{T_L} = m_T. (This is the argument of eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_64(i), reproduced in full.)
(b) Equivalence. Because char K = 0, every irreducible polynomial in K[t] is separable, so m_T is squarefree in K[t] if and only if its image in Kbar[t] splits as a product of distinct linear factors; by (a) applied with L = Kbar the two minimal polynomials agree, and by (a) applied with L = Kbar(T's splitting field) squarefreeness may be checked after any extension. An operator over a field is semisimple iff its minimal polynomial is squarefree, and it is diagonalizable over an algebraically closed field iff its minimal polynomial splits into distinct linear factors. Hence, with K = Q_ell and Kbar = Qbar_ell:
    (star)  T is semisimple on V  <=>  T_{Qbar_ell} is diagonalizable on V tensor_{Q_ell} Qbar_ell.
This is exactly eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5, which we cite; the discussion above is the justification of its content that we need in both directions.

=====================================================================
STEP 2 (Base change of X to F_{q^{m'}}).
Set X' := X x_{Spec F_{q^m}} Spec F_{q^{m'}}; it is a variety over F_{q^{m'}} and the given morphism f factors, by hypothesis, as f: Y -> X_{F_{q^{m'}}} = X'.

(a) Smoothness, projectivity, geometric connectedness. Smoothness and projectivity are preserved under arbitrary base change, so X' -> Spec F_{q^{m'}} is smooth and projective. For geometric connectedness: let kbar = Fbar_{q^m} = Fbar_{q^{m'}}; then
    X' x_{F_{q^{m'}}} kbar  =  (X x_{F_{q^m}} F_{q^{m'}}) x_{F_{q^{m'}}} kbar  =  X x_{F_{q^m}} kbar,
which is connected because X is geometrically connected over F_{q^m}. Hence X' is geometrically connected over F_{q^{m'}}; in particular X' is connected and nonempty.

(b) Integrality and pure dimension d. We do NOT use the Krull dimension of the local ring at a generic point (that local ring is the function field, of dimension 0). Instead:
  (i) Smoothness. Since X -> Spec F_{q^m} is smooth of pure relative dimension d, the base change X' -> Spec F_{q^{m'}} is smooth of constant relative dimension d. For every closed point x' of X', the local ring O_{X',x'} is a regular local ring (a local ring essentially of finite type and smooth over a field is regular; the field F_{q^{m'}} is perfect, so smooth = geometrically regular), and its Krull dimension equals the relative dimension, dim O_{X',x'} = d (dimension formula for smooth morphisms: dim_{x'} X' = dim_{f(x')} Spec F_{q^{m'}} + rel.dim = 0 + d).
  (ii) Jacobson/dimension. X' is of finite type over a field, hence Jacobson; therefore dim X' = sup{dim O_{X',x'} : x' closed} = d.
  (iii) Local integrality. Regular local rings are domains, so X' is locally integral. A locally noetherian locally integral scheme has open irreducible components (each point has an integral open neighbourhood, whose irreducible component is a neighbourhood of the point inside the given component). Since X' is connected by (a), it has exactly one irreducible component; hence X' is irreducible, and being locally integral and irreducible it is integral. Being integral of dimension d, X' is pure of dimension d.
  The same reasoning applies to Y: Y is smooth (hence regular, locally integral) and geometrically connected over F_{q^{m'}}, so Y is integral, irreducible, and of pure dimension d.

(c) Degree of f. Both Y and X' are integral schemes of finite type over F_{q^{m'}}, both of dimension d, and f: Y -> X' is surjective, hence dominant, and generically finite by hypothesis. Thus the induced extension of function fields k(Y)/k(X') is finite; let N := [k(Y):k(X')] >= 1 be the degree of f. So f is a proper surjective generically finite morphism of degree N >= 1 between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension d >= 1 over F_{q^{m'}}.

=====================================================================
STEP 3 (Translate the hypothesis into diagonalizability).
By hypothesis, F_{m',Y} is semisimple on H^n_et(Y_k,Q_ell) for every n>=0. By (star) (eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5), F_{m',Y} is diagonalizable over Qbar_ell on H^n_et(Y_k,Q_ell) tensor Qbar_ell for every n>=0. (Groups with n<0 are zero, so nothing needs to be checked there.)

=====================================================================
STEP 4 (Descent along the generically finite cover, over F_{q^{m'}}).
Apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_555 with the following substitutions: its "q^m" is our q^{m'} (its parameter m is our m'), its "X" is our X', its "Y" is our Y, and its f is our f. All its hypotheses hold: X' and Y are smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d >= 1 over F_{q^{m'}}, and f: Y -> X' is proper, surjective and generically finite of degree N >= 1 (Step 2(c)); and the diagonalizability hypothesis on Y is Step 3. Its conclusion is:
    (D)  for every n >= 0, the q^{m'}-power arithmetic Frobenius F_{m',X'} = (id_{(X')_k} x Spec(c |-> c^{q^{m'}}))^* is diagonalizable over Qbar_ell on H^n_et((X')_k,Q_ell) tensor_{Q_ell} Qbar_ell.

=====================================================================
STEP 5 (Transport of the q^{m'}-power Frobenius from (X')_k to X_k).
Introduce the operator F_{m',X} := (id_{X_k} x Spec(c |-> c^{q^{m'}}))^* on H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell); by Step 0(b) with s = m and t = m' = mr this is the r-th power of the invertible operator F_{m,X}, hence an invertible Q_ell-linear automorphism. Note carefully: F_{m,X} always denotes the q^m-power operator and F_{m',X} the q^{m'}-power operator; they are distinct operators in general.

Let alpha: (X')_k -> X_k be the canonical k-scheme isomorphism coming from associativity of the tensor product,
    (A tensor_{F_{q^m}} F_{q^{m'}}) tensor_{F_{q^{m'}}} k  ~->  A tensor_{F_{q^m}} k,
    (a tensor b) tensor c  |->  a tensor bc,
for an affine open Spec A of X; these local isomorphisms glue because they are the canonical associativity isomorphisms. On such an affine, alpha^#: A tensor_{F_{q^m}} k -> (A tensor_{F_{q^m}} F_{q^{m'}}) tensor_{F_{q^{m'}}} k is a tensor c |-> a tensor 1 tensor c. The q^{m'}-power arithmetic Frobenius on (X')_k is id_{X'} x Spec sigma_{m'}, which acts on (A tensor F_{q^{m'}}) tensor k by a tensor b tensor c |-> a tensor b tensor c^{q^{m'}} (identity on the X' factor, sigma_{m'} on k). The q^{m'}-power arithmetic Frobenius on X_k is id_X x Spec sigma_{m'}, acting by a tensor c |-> a tensor c^{q^{m'}}. Therefore
    F_{m',X'}^# o alpha^# (a tensor c) = F_{m',X'}^#(a tensor 1 tensor c) = a tensor 1 tensor c^{q^{m'}} = alpha^#(a tensor c^{q^{m'}}) = alpha^# o F_{m,X}'^#(a tensor c),
so F_{m',X'} o alpha = alpha o F_{m',X} as morphisms of k-schemes, and passing to contravariant pullbacks on etale cohomology,
    alpha^* o F_{m',X} = F_{m',X'} o alpha^* .
Thus alpha^*: H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> H^n_et((X')_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism of Q_ell[F]-modules, where F acts as F_{m',X} on the source and as F_{m',X'} on the target (after extending scalars to Qbar_ell, alpha^* tensor id remains an isomorphism with the same intertwining property).

Consequently F_{m',X} is diagonalizable over Qbar_ell on H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) tensor Qbar_ell: indeed, if V := H^n(X_k,Q_ell) tensor Qbar_ell, T := F_{m',X} tensor id, T' := F_{m',X'} tensor id, and A := alpha^* tensor id with A T = T' A, then for each eigenvalue lambda the eigenspace of T for lambda satisfies ker(T - lambda) = A^{-1}(ker(T' - lambda)): if Tv = lambda v then T'(Av) = A(Tv) = lambda Av, and conversely if T'w = lambda w then with v = A^{-1}w, Tv = A^{-1}T'w = lambda v. Since T' is diagonalizable by (D), V is the direct sum of the eigenspaces of T', hence V the direct sum of the eigenspaces of T. So:
    (D')  for every n >= 0, F_{m',X} is diagonalizable over Qbar_ell on H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) tensor_{Q_ell} Qbar_ell.

=====================================================================
STEP 6 (Descent from the q^{m'}-power to the q^m-power operator).
Apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_550 to X viewed over F_{q^m} with its parameter r equal to our r = m'/m >= 1. Its hypothesis is precisely that the q^{mr}-power arithmetic Frobenius (id x Spec sigma_r)^*, sigma_r(c) = c^{q^{mr}}, is diagonalizable over Qbar_ell on H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell); since mr = m', q^{mr} = q^{m'}, and sigma_r(c) = c^{q^{m'}} = sigma_{m'}(c), this operator is exactly F_{m',X}, whose diagonalizability is (D'). Its conclusion is that the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (id x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(c) = c^{q^m}, i.e. F_{m,X}, is diagonalizable over Qbar_ell on H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) tensor Qbar_ell. (Consistency check, not used: by Step 0(b), (F_{m,X})^r = F_{mr,X} = F_{m',X}, so this is the standard fact, Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_548, that diagonalizability of a positive power forces diagonalizability in characteristic 0.)

=====================================================================
STEP 7 (Back to semisimplicity).
By (star) (eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5) applied to V = H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) and T = F_{m,X}, diagonalizability of F_{m,X} over Qbar_ell implies that F_{m,X} is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell). Since n >= 0 was arbitrary, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) for every n >= 0, which is the desired conclusion.

=====================================================================
STEP 8 (Edge cases).
For n < 0 the group H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) is 0 by definition of etale cohomology, so there is nothing to prove. For n > 2d, X_k is a projective scheme over the algebraically closed field k, equidimensional of dimension d (Step 2(b)); by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_projective_cohomology_vanishes_above_twice_dimension, H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) = 0, and the zero operator is semisimple. The case r = 1 (m' = m) is covered without change: lemma_550 with r = 1 has as its hypothesis exactly the diagonalizability of F_{m,X} = F_{m',X} obtained in Step 5. All cases are thus exhausted, and the lemma is proved.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(k\) be an algebraic closure of \(\mathbb F_q\), and fix integers \(d\ge1\) and \(m\ge1\). For \(t\ge1\) let \(F_t\) denote the \(q^t\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \((\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^t}\). Suppose that (i) for every \(t\ge1\) and every smooth projective geometrically connected variety \(Y\) of pure dimension \(<d\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^t}\), \(F_t\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for all \(n\ge0\); and (ii) for every smooth projective geometrically connected variety \(X\) of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) and every \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)-rational very ample divisor \(H\) on \(X\) whose cycle class \(\xi\) makes cup product with \(\xi^{\,d-n}\) an isomorphism \(H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-n}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for all \(0\le n\le d\), \(F_m\) is semisimple on \(\ker(\text{cup product with }\xi:H^d(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+2}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell))\). Then for every smooth projective geometrically connected variety \(X\) of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) admitting such a divisor \(H\), \(F_m\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\).
proof:
Fix once and for all a nonzero element u \in \mathbb Q_\ell(1), and use u^n \mapsto 1 to identify every Tate twist \mathbb Q_\ell(n) with \mathbb Q_\ell. For an \mathbb F_{q^m}-rational divisor D on a smooth variety Z over \mathbb F_{q^m} write \operatorname{cl}(D)\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for its cycle class under this identification. (Changing u multiplies \operatorname{cl}(D) by a fixed nonzero scalar, hence multiplies the Lefschetz operator by a nonzero scalar; neither the kernel of that operator nor the property of being an isomorphism in every degree is changed, so all statements below are independent of the choice of u.)

Let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over \mathbb F_{q^m} admitting an \mathbb F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor H whose class \xi=\operatorname{cl}(H) satisfies Hard Lefschetz, i.e. L^{\,d-n}:H^n\to H^{2d-n} is an isomorphism for every 0\le n\le d, where L denotes cup product with \xi and H^n:=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). We must prove that F_m=(\mathrm{id}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*, \sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n for every n\ge 0.

Preliminaries. X is proper over \mathbb F_{q^m}, so by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob applied to the constant complex \mathbb Q_\ell with its natural Frobenius structure, each H^n is finite-dimensional over \mathbb Q_\ell and F_m is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphism of it; thus "semisimple" (equivalently, diagonalizable after base change to \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell) is a well-defined property of F_m|_{H^n}.

CASE 1: d\ge 2.

Step 1 (all degrees except the middle). We claim that the hypothesis of eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/d0ddec, with its integer d equal to our d, is satisfied. Indeed, that hypothesis asks: for every integer t\ge 1 and every smooth projective geometrically connected variety Y of pure dimension d-1 over \mathbb F_{q^t}, the q^t-power arithmetic Frobenius F_t is semisimple on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every n\ge 0. Since d\ge 2 we have d-1\ge 1 and certainly d-1<d, so any such Y is a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension <d over \mathbb F_{q^t}; hypothesis (i) of the present lemma, applied with this t and this Y, gives exactly the required semisimplicity in every degree. The lemma d0ddec applies (our d\ge 2 is its requirement) and yields: for our m and our X, F_m is semisimple on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every n\ge 0 with n\neq d. (This covers n=0, n=d-2, and all n>2d, where H^n=0 by Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing and the zero operator is semisimple.)

Step 2 (the middle degree). We apply Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/c66177 to X, to the fixed identification \mathbb Q_\ell(1)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell given by u, and to \xi=\operatorname{cl}(H). Its hypotheses are verified as follows: X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d\ge 2 over \mathbb F_{q^m}; \xi is the cycle class of the \mathbb F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor H; and L^{\,d-n}:H^n\to H^{2d-n} is an isomorphism for every 0\le n\le d by the defining property of H. The lemma puts P^d=\ker\bigl(L:H^d\to H^{d+2}\bigr) and requires semisimplicity of F_m on H^{d-2} and on P^d.
- For H^{d-2}: since d\ge 2, d-2\ge 0 is an admissible degree, and d-2\neq d; Step 1 therefore gives semisimplicity of F_m on H^{d-2}.
- For P^d: the operator L is literally "cup product with \xi:H^d(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+2}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)", so P^d is exactly the kernel appearing in hypothesis (ii). Applying hypothesis (ii) to this very X and this very divisor H (which satisfies the Hard Lefschetz requirement by assumption) gives that F_m is semisimple on P^d.
Both inputs being in place, c66177 concludes that F_m is semisimple on H^d, over \mathbb Q_\ell.

Step 3 (assembly). Every integer n\ge 0 satisfies n\neq d or n=d. In the first case semisimplicity is Step 1, in the second it is Step 2. This completes CASE 1.

CASE 2: d=1.
Here neither d0ddec nor c66177 is applicable (both require d\ge 2), so we argue degree by degree; the possible degrees are 0,1,2,3,\dots.

(a) n>2: X_k is a projective scheme over the algebraically closed field k of pure dimension 1 and \ell\neq\operatorname{char}k, so Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing gives H^n=0 for every n>2. In particular H^3=0 and all higher groups vanish; the zero operator is semisimple.

(b) n=0: H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is the group of sections of the constant sheaf \mathbb Q_\ell on X_k, i.e. the \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space of locally constant functions X_k\to\mathbb Q_\ell (\mathbb Q_\ell discrete). The underlying topological space of X_k is quasi-compact (X is noetherian) and connected, because X is geometrically connected over \mathbb F_{q^m}; a locally constant function on a connected space is constant, and conversely every constant function is locally constant. Hence \dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell} H^0=1. Any \mathbb Q_\ell-linear automorphism of a 1-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space is multiplication by a scalar \lambda\in\mathbb Q_\ell^{\times}, whose matrix in any basis is already diagonal; so F_m is semisimple on H^0.

(c) n=2: the Hard Lefschetz property of \xi in degree n=0 says that L^{\,1-0}=L:H^0\to H^2 is an isomorphism. Hence \dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^2=\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^0=1, and as in (b) the automorphism F_m|_{H^2} is scalar, hence semisimple.

(d) n=1: by (a), H^3=0, so the kernel of L:H^1\to H^3 is all of H^1. Hypothesis (ii), applied to X and to the divisor H (whose Hard Lefschetz condition for d=1 consists of the case n=0 used above together with the case n=1, namely L^{\,0}=\mathrm{id}_{H^1}, which is trivially an isomorphism), states precisely that F_m is semisimple on \ker\bigl(\text{cup product with }\xi:H^1\to H^3\bigr)=H^1.

(e) Assembly: degrees 0,1,2 are covered by (b), (d), (c) and all n\ge 3 by (a). This completes CASE 2.

In both cases F_m is semisimple on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every n\ge 0, for every smooth projective geometrically connected X of pure dimension d over \mathbb F_{q^m} admitting a divisor H as above. This is exactly the required conclusion.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let beta:V x V -> K be a perfect bilinear form, let epsilon in {1,-1} satisfy beta(y,x)=epsilon beta(x,y), let c in K^times, and let T in GL_K(V) satisfy beta(Tx,Ty)=c beta(x,y) for all x,y. Define G:V x V -> K by G(x,y)=beta(x,Ty)+epsilon c beta(x,T^{-1}y). Then G(x,x)=2 beta(x,Tx) for every x in V; consequently G(x,x) != 0 for every nonzero x in V if and only if beta(x,Tx) != 0 for every nonzero x in V.
proof:
We work under the stated hypotheses: $K$ has characteristic $0$, $V$ is a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space, $\beta:V\times V\to K$ is a bilinear form (the hypothesis that it is perfect is recorded but will not be needed below), $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ satisfies $\beta(y,x)=\varepsilon\,\beta(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in V$, $c\in K^{\times}$, and $T\in\operatorname{GL}_K(V)$ satisfies $\beta(Tx,Ty)=c\,\beta(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in V$.

Preliminary observations.
(1) Since $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ we have $\varepsilon^2=1$, hence $\varepsilon^{-1}=\varepsilon$.
(2) Since $T\in\operatorname{GL}_K(V)$, the inverse $T^{-1}\in\operatorname{GL}_K(V)$ exists, so $G(x,y)=\beta(x,Ty)+\varepsilon c\,\beta(x,T^{-1}y)$ is a well-defined element of $K$ for all $x,y\in V$.
(3) Since $c\in K^{\times}$, $c^{-1}\in K$ exists.
(4) Since $\operatorname{char}K=0$, the structural map $\mathbb Z\to K$ is injective; in particular $2\cdot 1_K\neq 0$, so $2\in K^{\times}$ and multiplication by $2$ on $K$ is injective (and $a\mapsto 2a$ reflects equality to $0$: $2a=0\iff a=0$).

Step 1: compute $\beta(T^{-1}x,x)$ in terms of $\beta(x,Tx)$. Fix $x\in V$ and apply the similitude relation $\beta(Tu,Tv)=c\,\beta(u,v)$ to $u=T^{-1}x$ and $v=x$. Then $Tu=T(T^{-1}x)=x$ and $Tv=Tx$, so
\[
\beta(x,Tx)=\beta(Tu,Tv)=c\,\beta(u,v)=c\,\beta(T^{-1}x,x).
\]
Multiplying by $c^{-1}$ gives
\[
\beta(T^{-1}x,x)=c^{-1}\beta(x,Tx). \qquad (\ast)
\]

Step 2: compute $\beta(x,T^{-1}x)$. Apply the $\varepsilon$-symmetry relation $\beta(y,x)=\varepsilon\beta(x,y)$ with $y=T^{-1}x$:
\[
\beta(T^{-1}x,x)=\varepsilon\,\beta(x,T^{-1}x).
\]
Multiplying by $\varepsilon^{-1}=\varepsilon$ (using $\varepsilon^2=1$) yields
\[
\beta(x,T^{-1}x)=\varepsilon\,\beta(T^{-1}x,x).
\]
Substituting $(\ast)$ from Step 1,
\[
\beta(x,T^{-1}x)=\varepsilon c^{-1}\beta(x,Tx). \qquad (\ast\ast)
\]

Step 3: evaluate $G$ on the diagonal. By definition, with $y=x$,
\[
G(x,x)=\beta(x,Tx)+\varepsilon c\,\beta(x,T^{-1}x).
\]
Insert $(\ast\ast)$:
\[
G(x,x)=\beta(x,Tx)+\varepsilon c\cdot\bigl(\varepsilon c^{-1}\beta(x,Tx)\bigr)
=\beta(x,Tx)+(\varepsilon\cdot\varepsilon)\,(c\cdot c^{-1})\,\beta(x,Tx)
=\beta(x,Tx)+\varepsilon^{2}\cdot 1\cdot\beta(x,Tx).
\]
Since $\varepsilon^2=1$, this becomes
\[
G(x,x)=\beta(x,Tx)+\beta(x,Tx)=2\,\beta(x,Tx),
\]
which is exactly the claimed identity, valid for every $x\in V$.

Step 4: the consequence for non-vanishing. Because $2\in K^{\times}$ (characteristic $0$, observation (4)), for each fixed $x\in V$ we have
\[
G(x,x)=0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ 2\beta(x,Tx)=0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \beta(x,Tx)=0,
\]
where the second equivalence uses that $2$ is a unit in the field $K$ (multiply by $2^{-1}$). Taking contrapositives,
\[
G(x,x)\neq 0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \beta(x,Tx)\neq 0\qquad\text{for every }x\in V.
\]
We now verify the two implications of the asserted equivalence of universal statements explicitly.

($\Rightarrow$) Assume $G(x,x)\neq 0$ for every nonzero $x\in V$. Let $x\in V$ be nonzero. Then $G(x,x)\neq 0$ by assumption, and the equivalence above gives $\beta(x,Tx)\neq 0$. Since $x$ was an arbitrary nonzero vector, $\beta(x,Tx)\neq 0$ for every nonzero $x$.

($\Leftarrow$) Conversely, assume $\beta(x,Tx)\neq 0$ for every nonzero $x\in V$. Let $x\in V$ be nonzero. Then $\beta(x,Tx)\neq 0$, and since $2\neq 0$ in the field $K$ we have $2\beta(x,Tx)\neq 0$ (a product of two nonzero elements of a field is nonzero). By the identity of Step 3, $G(x,x)=2\beta(x,Tx)\neq 0$. Hence $G(x,x)\neq 0$ for every nonzero $x$.

This completes the proof of both the diagonal identity $G(x,x)=2\beta(x,Tx)$ for all $x\in V$ and the stated equivalence of non-vanishing conditions. (Note that no use was made of the perfection of $\beta$, of finite-dimensionality of $V$, or of any Frobenius-geometric input; the argument is purely formal linear algebra over a characteristic-$0$ field.)

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be prime, let m>=1, and put k=overline(F_q). Let X be smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d>=2 over F_{q^m}, and let i:Y->X be a nonempty effective very ample Cartier divisor defined over F_{q^m}, smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension d-1. Fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1) and identify Tate twists with Q_ell. Let xi be the cycle class of Y in H^2_et(X_k,Q_ell), let L be cup product with xi, and let tr_Y be the Poincare duality trace on Y. Put K=ker(L:H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{d+1}_et(X_k,Q_ell)) and W=im(i^*:H^{d-1}_et(X_k,Q_ell)->H^{d-1}_et(Y_k,Q_ell)). Then i^* induces an isomorphism K -> {w in W | tr_Y(w cup v)=0 for every v in W}.
proof:
PROOF. Throughout, write $H^n(Z):=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ for a variety $Z$ over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$, and write $Q:=q^m=p^{am}$, so that $\mathbb F_{q^m}=\mathbb F_Q$ is itself a prime-power field and $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q=\overline{\mathbb F}_Q$. Fix once and for all a nonzero $u\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ and use it to identify $\mathbb Q_\ell(n)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$, $u^n\mapsto 1$, as the statement requires; all traces below are composed with this identification.

STEP 0 (The traces). Let $\operatorname{tr}_X:H^{2d}(X):\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)$ and $\operatorname{tr}_Y:H^{2d-2}(Y)\to\mathbb Q_\ell(-(d-1))$ be the Poincar\'e duality traces, i.e. the maps induced by the cycle-class/Gysin isomorphisms $\mathbb Q_\ell(d)[2d]\to Rf^!\mathbb Q_\ell$ and $\mathbb Q_\ell(d-1)[2d-2]\to Rg^!\mathbb Q_\ell$ for the structure morphisms $f:X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_Q$, $g:Y\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_Q$, as constructed in part (a) of lemma_77 and normalised there by $\operatorname{tr}(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):\mathbb F_Q]$. These are canonical, hence they are exactly the traces denoted $\operatorname{tr}_X,\operatorname{tr}_Y$ in lemma_439 (there: "the Poincar\'e duality trace composed with this identification"); in particular the $\operatorname{tr}_Y$ of the statement, which is the Poincar\'e duality trace on $Y$, is the same map. Since $Y$ is geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_Q$, $Y_k$ is connected, so the "sum of the traces on the connected components" appearing in lemma_439 is just this single trace. We use the same symbols for the traces after the identification $\mathbb Q_\ell(-\bullet)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell$; composing a perfect pairing with a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism of the target preserves perfectness.

STEP 1 (Geometric setup over $k$). $X$ is nonempty (it has pure dimension $d\ge2$) and $Y$ is nonempty of pure dimension $d-1$, so $Y\neq X$, i.e. $Y\subsetneq X$. Base change to $k$ preserves smoothness, projectivity and pure dimension, so $X_k$ is smooth projective of pure dimension $d$ and $Y_k$ is smooth of pure dimension $d-1$ over $k$, and $Y_k\subsetneq X_k$ is an effective Cartier divisor. Since $X$ (resp. $Y$) is geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_Q$, $X_k$ (resp. $Y_k$) is connected; being proper over the algebraically closed field $k$, $H^0(X_k,\mathcal O)=k$ (resp. $H^0(Y_k,\mathcal O)=k$), and for any field extension $k'/k$ one has $H^0(Z_{k'},\mathcal O)=H^0(Z_k,\mathcal O)\otimes_k k'=k'$, so $Z_{k'}$ is connected; thus $X_k$ and $Y_k$ are geometrically connected over $k$. Finally $\mathcal O_{X_k}(Y_k)$ is the base change of the very ample line bundle $\mathcal O_X(Y)$, hence is very ample, in particular ample. So the hypotheses of lemma_420 are satisfied for $X_k/k/Y_k$.

STEP 2 (Injectivity of $i^*$ in degree $d-1$; weak Lefschetz only). By lemma_420 applied to $X_k\supset Y_k$, the restriction
$$i^*:H^{d-1}(X)\longrightarrow H^{d-1}(Y)$$
is injective (indeed it is an isomorphism in degrees $m<d-1$). No hard Lefschetz statement for $X$ or $Y$ is used. Consequently the restriction of $i^*$ to the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspace $K=\ker(L:H^{d-1}(X)\to H^{d+1}(X))$ is injective, and identifies $K$ $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearly with the subspace $i^*(K)\subseteq W:=\operatorname{im}(i^*)$.

STEP 3 (Gysin projection formula and the fundamental trace identity). Apply lemma_439 over the ground field $\mathbb F_Q$ (the lemma is stated for $\mathbb F_q$ with $q$ an arbitrary prime power; we substitute the prime power $Q=q^m$). It provides the Gysin homomorphisms $i_!:H^n(Y)\to H^{n+2}(X)$ characterised by
$$\operatorname{tr}_X(i_!\alpha\smile\beta)=\operatorname{tr}_Y(\alpha\smile i^*\beta)\qquad\forall\alpha\in H^n(Y),\ \forall\beta\in H^{2d-2-n}(X),$$
and the identity $i_!(i^*x)=x\smile\xi$ for every $x\in H^n(X)$, where $\xi=\mathrm{cl}(Y)$ and $L(x)=x\smile\xi$.

Now take arbitrary $a,b\in H^{d-1}(X)$ and put $\alpha:=i^*a\in H^{d-1}(Y)$ (so $n=d-1$) and $\beta:=b\in H^{d-1}(X)=H^{2d-2-(d-1)}(X)$. The characterising property applies, and then the projection formula gives
$$\operatorname{tr}_Y(i^*a\smile i^*b)=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(i_!(i^*a)\smile b\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl((a\smile\xi)\smile b\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_X(La\smile b).\qquad(\star)$$
All degrees are correct: $i^*a\smile i^*b\in H^{2d-2}(Y)$ is the top degree of $Y$, and $La\smile b\in H^{d+1+d-1}=H^{2d}(X)$ is the top degree of $X$. Note that no commutativity of the cup product is invoked; the order of the factors is preserved throughout.

STEP 4 (Left non-degeneracy of the Poincar\'e pairing of $X$). Apply lemma_77(b) to $X$ (smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $d\ge2$ over $\mathbb F_Q$) with $n=d+1$; this is an admissible degree because $0\le d+1\le 2d$ for $d\ge1$. It says that
$$H^{d+1}(X)\times H^{2d-(d+1)}(X)=H^{d+1}(X)\times H^{d-1}(X)\longrightarrow\mathbb Q_\ell(-d),\qquad (x,y)\longmapsto\operatorname{tr}_X(x\smile y),$$
is a PERFECT pairing of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces. Composing with the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism $\mathbb Q_\ell(-d)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell$ of Step 0, the map $x\mapsto\bigl(y\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_X(x\smile y)\bigr)$ identifies $H^{d+1}(X)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(H^{d-1}(X),\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Hence, for every $x\in H^{d+1}(X)$,
$$\operatorname{tr}_X(x\smile b)=0\ \ \forall b\in H^{d-1}(X)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=0.\qquad(\dagger)$$
(Only perfectness is used; no finite-dimensionality and no semisimplicity hypothesis is needed.)

STEP 5 (The radical of the pairing on $W$ is exactly $i^*(K)$). Write
$$R:=\{\,w\in W\mid \operatorname{tr}_Y(w\smile v)=0\ \text{for every }v\in W\,\}.$$
We prove $R=i^*(K)$.

(a) $i^*(K)\subseteq R$. Let $a\in K$, so $La=0$, and set $w:=i^*a\in W$. For any $v\in W$ there is, by definition of $W$ as the image of $i^*$, some $b\in H^{d-1}(X)$ with $v=i^*b$. Then by $(\star)$,
$$\operatorname{tr}_Y(w\smile v)=\operatorname{tr}_Y(i^*a\smile i^*b)=\operatorname{tr}_X(La\smile b)=\operatorname{tr}_X(0\smile b)=0,$$
using $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linearity of $\operatorname{tr}_X$ and $0\smile b=0$. Thus $w\in R$.

(b) $R\subseteq i^*(K)$. Let $w\in R$ and choose $a\in H^{d-1}(X)$ with $w=i^*a$. For every $b\in H^{d-1}(X)$, the element $i^*b$ lies in $W$, so by $(\star)$
$$0=\operatorname{tr}_Y(i^*a\smile i^*b)=\operatorname{tr}_X(La\smile b).$$
Applying $(\dagger)$ to $x:=La\in H^{d+1}(X)$ yields $La=0$, i.e. $a\in K$, and therefore $w=i^*a\in i^*(K)$.

STEP 6 (Conclusion). The map $i^*$ is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear (functoriality of \'etale cohomology), and Steps 2 and 5 show that
$$i^*|_K:K\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ R=\{\,w\in W\mid \operatorname{tr}_Y(w\smile v)=0\ \forall v\in W\,\}$$
is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear, injective (Step 2) and surjective (Step 5(b)). It is therefore an isomorphism of $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces, which is exactly the required statement.

REMARKS ON WHAT WAS AND WAS NOT USED. (i) The only input on the restriction map is the injectivity in degree $d-1$ supplied by weak Lefschetz (lemma_420); we never asserted that $i^*a=0$ for $a\in K$, nor that $i^*$ is surjective. (ii) No hard Lefschetz isomorphism $L^{d-n}:H^n\xrightarrow{\sim}H^{2d-n}$ was assumed or used for $X$ or for $Y$; in particular nothing was assumed about injectivity of $L_Y$ on $H^{d-1}(Y)$ (which is false when $d=2$). (iii) The passage from "$\operatorname{tr}_X(La\smile b)=0$ for all $b$" to "$La=0$" uses only the perfectness of the Poincar\'e pairing on $X$ from lemma_77(b), applied in the off-middle degrees $d+1$ and $d-1$, which is legitimate without any hard Lefschetz input. This is precisely the isolation of the kernel $K$ that the middle-degree argument requires. $\qquad\blacksquare$

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let m >= 1, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d >= 1 over F_{q^m}. Suppose there exist an integer m' divisible by m, an abelian variety A of dimension d over F_{q^{m'}}, and a proper surjective generically finite morphism A -> X_{F_{q^{m'}}}. Then there exist smooth projective geometrically connected curves C_1, ..., C_d over F_{q^{m'}} and a proper surjective generically finite morphism C_1 x_{F_{q^{m'}}} ... x_{F_{q^{m'}}} C_d -> X_{F_{q^{m']}}.
proof:
We prove the lemma by covering the given abelian variety by a product of curves and composing. No general alteration theorem is used; the only external input is the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_463_abelian_variety_covered_by_product_of_curves.

=== Notation ===
