Write K := F_{q^{m'}} = F_{p^{a m'}}. Since a >= 1 and m' >= 1, am' >= 1, so K is a finite field of characteristic p (and q^{m'} = p^{am'} is a prime power). Write
  X' := X \times_{F_{q^m}} F_{q^{m'}} = X_{F_{q^{m'}}},
and let f: A -> X' denote the given proper surjective generically finite K-morphism (it is a K-morphism by assumption). Note d = dim X = dim A >= 1 by hypothesis, so the case d = 0 (where the empty product would be Spec K) does not arise.

=== Step 1: The schemes involved are integral ===
We need function fields, so we check integrality.

(1a) General fact: if Z is a scheme of finite type over a field and smooth and connected over that field, then Z is integral. Proof. Since Z is of finite type over a field it is noetherian. Smoothness implies that every local ring O_{Z,z} is regular, hence a domain (a regular local ring is a domain). For a noetherian scheme there is a bijection between minimal primes of O_{Z,z} and irreducible components of Z passing through z; since O_{Z,z} is a domain it has exactly one minimal prime, so every point z lies on a unique irreducible component. Let Z_1,...,Z_r (r >= 1) be the irreducible components, which are closed. For each i the set W_i := Z_i \ (union_{j != i} Z_j) is open: its complement is union_{j != i} Z_j, which is closed (every point of Z lies on some component, so the complement of W_i is exactly that union). Each W_i is nonempty, for otherwise Z_i would be contained in the union of the other components, contradicting irreducibility of Z_i and maximality of irreducible components. The W_i are pairwise disjoint and cover Z, so by connectedness r = 1. Thus Z is irreducible. Since all local rings are domains, Z is reduced. Irreducible + reduced = integral.

(1b) X' is integral. Base change of a smooth (resp. projective) morphism is smooth (resp. projective), so X' is smooth and projective over K. Geometric connectedness: (X')_{\bar K} = X_{\bar K}, which is connected because X is geometrically connected over F_{q^m}; the structural map (X')_{\bar K} -> X' is the base change of Spec \bar K -> Spec K, hence faithfully flat and in particular surjective, and the surjective continuous image of a connected space is connected, so X' is connected. By (1a), X' is integral. (In particular X' is irreducible and noetherian, of dimension d.)

(1c) A is integral. An abelian variety over a finite field is smooth: a group scheme of finite type over a perfect field is smooth (and in many conventions smoothness is part of the definition of abelian variety); it is connected by definition. Being of finite type over K, (1a) applies and A is integral.

(1d) Products of the curves we shall obtain are integral. If C_1,...,C_d are smooth projective geometrically connected curves over K, then C := C_1 x_K ... x_K C_d is smooth over K (products of smooth morphisms are smooth) and geometrically connected over K (after base change to \bar K it is a product of connected \bar K-schemes, hence connected, and the same faithfully-flat-surjection argument as in (1b) gives connectedness over K). By (1a), C is integral.

=== Step 2: "Generically finite" — definition and equivalent formulation ===
We use the standard definition for varieties: a morphism h: Z -> Y of finite type between integral noetherian schemes is generically finite if it is dominant and the induced extension of function fields k(Y) -> k(Z) is finite (dominance makes it an inclusion). This is the definition under which the hypothesis on f and the conclusion about the composite are to be read; for completeness we record that it agrees with the "finite over a dense open" formulation.

(=>) Suppose h is dominant and [k(Z):k(Y)] < ∞. Pick a nonempty affine open V = Spec B ⊂ Z and a nonempty affine open U_0 = Spec A ⊂ Y with h(V) ⊂ U_0; then B is a finitely generated A-algebra and a domain with Frac(B) = k(Z) finite over Frac(A) = k(Y). Let c_1,...,c_m generate B as an A-algebra. Each c_i ∈ k(Z) is algebraic, hence integral, over k(Y); choose monic integral equations over k(Y) and clear denominators to obtain 0 != g ∈ A such that each c_i is integral over A_g. Then B_g is generated as an A_g-module by the bounded monomials in the c_i, hence is a finite A_g-module. Next, Z \ V is closed noetherian and h|_{Z\V} is of finite type, so h(Z \ V) is a constructible subset of Y. It does not contain the generic point η_Y of Y: V contains the generic point η_Z of Z (V is a nonempty open of the integral Z) and h(η_Z) = η_Y by dominance. Thus the constructible set U_0 \ h(Z \ V) contains η_Y, hence contains a nonempty open U' = Spec A_{g'} ⊂ U_0 (a constructible subset of an integral noetherian space containing the generic point contains a nonempty open). For this U' we have h^{-1}(U') ⊂ V, so h^{-1}(U') = Spec B_{g'}. Taking U'' = Spec A_{gg'} ≠ ∅ we get h^{-1}(U'') = Spec B_{gg'} with B_{gg'} finite over A_{gg'}, i.e. h^{-1}(U'') -> U'' is finite.

(<=) Conversely, if h is dominant and h^{-1}(U) -> U is finite for some nonempty open U ⊂ Y, then h^{-1}(U) ≠ ∅ (it contains η_Z, as h(η_Z) = η_Y ∈ U), k(h^{-1}(U)) = k(Z) and k(U) = k(Y); writing h^{-1}(U) = Spec B, U = Spec A with B a finite A-module and both domains, Frac(B) is a finite Frac(A)-module, hence a finite field extension. So [k(Z):k(Y)] < ∞.

=== Step 3: Cover the abelian variety by a product of d curves ===
Apply the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_463_abelian_variety_covered_by_product_of_curves with the prime power q^{m'} = p^{am'} in place of q, and with g = dim A = d >= 1. It yields smooth projective geometrically connected curves C_1,...,C_d over F_{q^{m'}} = K and a proper surjective generically finite K-morphism
  g: C := C_1 x_K C_2 x_K ... x_K C_d -> A.
By Step 1(1d), C is integral.

=== Step 4: The composite ===
Define
  h := f ∘ g : C -> X'.
This is a K-morphism, being the composite of the K-morphisms g and f.

(4a) h is proper. Proper = separated + of finite type + universally closed. Finite type is stable under composition (if g is locally of finite type and f is of finite type, so is f∘g; composition of quasi-compact morphisms is quasi-compact). Separatedness is stable under composition. For universal closedness: for any K-scheme T -> X', the base change of f∘g is the composite of the base change of g along T -> X' followed by the base change of f along T -> X'; each is closed (g, f universally closed), and a composite of closed surjective-on-target maps... more precisely, the base change of f∘g to T factors as C_T -> A_T -> X'_T with the first map closed (base change of g) and the second closed (base change of f); the composite of two closed maps is closed, since the image of a closed set under the composite is the image under the second map of a closed set. Hence f∘g is universally closed. Thus h is proper.

(4b) h is surjective. On underlying topological spaces, g and f are surjective by hypothesis, and a composite of surjective maps is surjective.

(4c) h is generically finite. By (4b), h is surjective, hence dominant; likewise f and g are surjective, hence dominant. By Steps 1(1b),(1c),(1d), X', A and C are integral, so their function fields k(X'), k(A), k(C) are defined, and the dominant morphisms f and g induce field extensions
  k(X') ↪ k(A)  (via f^#),   k(A) ↪ k(C)  (via g^#),
whose composite is the map k(X') ↪ k(C) induced by h = f∘g (functoriality of localisation at the nonzero elements: f^# and g^# are the restrictions of the sheaf maps to the stalks at the generic points, and these compose correctly).
The hypothesis on f says (Step 2) that [k(A) : k(X')] < ∞; the conclusion of Step 3 for g says [k(C) : k(A)] < ∞. By the tower law for field extensions,
  [k(C) : k(X')] = [k(C) : k(A)] · [k(A) : k(X')] < ∞.
Together with dominance of h, Step 2 shows that h is generically finite. (Equivalently, by the (=>) direction of Step 2 there is a dense open U ⊂ X' such that h^{-1}(U) -> U is finite: on dense opens both g and f are finite, and the inverse image under f of such a dense open is a dense open of A on which g is finite.)

=== Step 5: Conclusion ===
The curves C_1,...,C_d (exactly d = dim X of them) are smooth, projective and geometrically connected over F_{q^{m'}}, and h: C_1 x_{F_{q^{m'}}} ... x_{F_{q^{m'}}} C_d -> X_{F_{q^{m'}}} is proper by (4a), surjective by (4b), and generically finite by (4c). This is precisely the required conclusion.

Remark on scope. The argument uses only the given domination by an abelian variety of the same dimension, together with the proved covering of an abelian variety by a product of curves; no general alteration-by-a-product-of-curves statement for arbitrary X is invoked, and no surjectivity statement is used to infer generic finiteness — generic finiteness is verified explicitly through the multiplicativity of degrees of function field extensions. The case d = 0 is excluded by the hypothesis d >= 1 (and would be trivial, since a smooth projective geometrically connected 0-dimensional variety over F_{q^m} is Spec F_{q^m}, covered by the empty product).

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let E be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let T in GL_K(E), and let W be a T-stable K-linear subspace of E. Suppose that T restricted to W and the operator induced by T on E/W are semisimple, and that their characteristic polynomials in K[t] are coprime. Then T is semisimple on E.
proof:
We prove the statement by pure linear algebra over the characteristic-0 field $K$; no arithmetic-geometric input is needed, so no external lemma is cited.

SETUP AND NOTATION. Fix an algebraic closure $\overline K$ of $K$; for a $K$-vector space $V$ write $V_{\overline K}:=V\otimes_K\overline K$, and for $A\in\mathrm{End}_K(V)$ write $A_{\overline K}:=A\otimes\mathrm{id}$ for the base-changed endomorphism. By "semisimple on $V$" we mean, as in the statement's own convention elsewhere in this development, that $A_{\overline K}$ is diagonalisable (this is independent of the choice of $\overline K$, and is equivalent to the usual module-theoretic semisimplicity of the $K[t]$-module, but we only need the diagonalisability formulation).

Let $\bar T:E/W\to E/W$ be the endomorphism induced by $T$, let
  $\chi_1(t):=\det(t\,\mathrm{id}_W-T|_W)\in K[t]$, $\chi_2(t):=\det(t\,\mathrm{id}_{E/W}-\bar T)\in K[t]$,
  $\mu_1(t):=$ minimal polynomial of $T|_W$, $\mu_2(t):=$ minimal polynomial of $\bar T$,
with the convention that if $W=0$ we put $\mu_1=\chi_1=1$, and if $W=E$ we put $\mu_2=\chi_2=1$ (the operator on the zero space has minimal polynomial $1$, and its characteristic polynomial is $1$, which is coprime to every polynomial). The hypothesis is that $\chi_1$ and $\chi_2$ are coprime in $K[t]$, that $T|_W$ and $\bar T$ are semisimple, and $W$ is $T$-stable. We must show $T$ is semisimple on $E$. (If $E=0$ there is nothing to prove, so assume $E\ne0$.)

We need three standard facts, each proved in full below.

FACT 1 (Cayley--Hamilton). For every finite-dimensional $K$-vector space $V$ and every $A\in\mathrm{End}_K(V)$, $\chi_A(A)=0$; consequently $\mu_A\mid\chi_A$ in $K[t]$.
Proof. Choose a basis and identify $A$ with a matrix in $M_n(K)$. Over the commutative ring $K[t]$ we have the adjugate identity $\mathrm{adj}(tI-A)\,(tI-A)=\det(tI-A)\,I=\chi_A(t)\,I$. Write $\mathrm{adj}(tI-A)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}t^k C_k$ with $C_k\in M_n(K)$ (the adjugate of $tI-A$ has entries which are polynomials in $t$ of degree $\le n-1$) and write $\chi_A(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\chi_k t^k$ with $\chi_n=1$. Comparing coefficients of $t^k$ in $\bigl(\sum_k t^kC_k\bigr)(tI-A)=\sum_k\chi_k t^k I$ gives
  $t^n:\ C_{n-1}=I$;\qquad $t^k\ (1\le k\le n-1):\ C_{k-1}-C_kA=\chi_k I$;\qquad $t^0:\ -C_0A=\chi_0 I$.
Right-multiply the identity for index $k$ by $A^k$ and sum over $k=1,\dots,n-1$; the left side telescopes:
  $\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}C_{k-1}A^k-\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}C_kA^{k+1}=C_0A-C_{n-1}A^n=C_0A-A^n$,
so $C_0A-A^n=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\chi_kA^k$. Substituting $C_0A=-\chi_0I$ from the constant term gives $-\chi_0I-A^n=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\chi_kA^k$, i.e. $\sum_{k=0}^{n}\chi_kA^k=0$, which is $\chi_A(A)=0$. Since $\mu_A$ generates the ideal $\{f\in K[t]:f(A)=0\}$, we get $\mu_A\mid\chi_A$. $\dashv$

FACT 2 (annihilator ideal is unchanged by scalar extension). For $A\in\mathrm{End}_K(V)$, the ideal $\{f\in\overline K[t]:f(A_{\overline K})=0\}$ equals $\mu_A(t)\,\overline K[t]$; in particular the minimal polynomial of $A_{\overline K}$ is $\mu_A$.
Proof. Let $I=\{f\in K[t]:f(A)=0\}=(\mu_A)$ and $I'=\{f\in\overline K[t]:f(A_{\overline K})=0\}$. Since $\mu_A\in I'$, $(\mu_A)\overline K[t]\subseteq I'$. Conversely let $f\in I'$ and divide in the Euclidean domain $\overline K[t]$: $f=q\mu_A+r$ with $\deg r<\deg\mu_A$. Then $r(A_{\overline K})=f(A_{\overline K})-q(A_{\overline K})\mu_A(A_{\overline K})=0$. The $K$-linear map $\varphi:K[t]_{<\deg\mu_A}\to\mathrm{End}_K(V)$, $g\mapsto g(A)$, is injective by minimality of $\mu_A$; since $\overline K$ is flat over $K$, $\varphi\otimes\overline K$ is injective, and $r$ lies in its kernel. Hence $r=0$ and $f\in(\mu_A)\overline K[t]$. $\dashv$

FACT 3 (characteristic-0 semisimplicity criterion). Let $V$ be finite-dimensional over a characteristic-0 field $K$ and $A\in\mathrm{End}_K(V)$. Then $A$ is semisimple (i.e. $A_{\overline K}$ is diagonalisable) if and only if $\mu_A$ is square-free, equivalently a product of pairwise distinct irreducible polynomials.
Proof. ($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $A_{\overline K}$ is diagonalisable, with distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_s\in\overline K$. Then $V_{\overline K}=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{s}V_{\lambda_j}$ is an eigenspace decomposition. The polynomial $\prod_{j=1}^{s}(t-\lambda_j)$ annihilates $A_{\overline K}$ because it kills every vector of the eigenbasis. No proper subproduct does: omitting the factor $(t-\lambda_j)$ leaves a polynomial whose value at $\lambda_j$ is nonzero, and it therefore does not annihilate any nonzero vector of $V_{\lambda_j}$ (which is nonzero since $\lambda_j$ is an eigenvalue). Hence the minimal polynomial of $A_{\overline K}$ is $\prod_{j=1}^s(t-\lambda_j)$, which is square-free; by Fact 2 it equals $\mu_A$, so $\mu_A$ is square-free.
($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $\mu_A=p_1\cdots p_r$ with the $p_i$ pairwise distinct monic irreducibles in $K[t]$. Since $\operatorname{char}K=0$, each $p_i$ is separable: $p_i'\ne0$ and $\deg p_i'<\deg p_i$ with $p_i$ irreducible forces $\gcd(p_i,p_i')=1$, so $p_i$ has $\deg p_i$ distinct roots in $\overline K$. Give $V$ the $K[t]$-module structure with $t$ acting as $A$; since $\mu_A$ annihilates $A$, this factors through the Artinian ring $R:=K[t]/(\mu_A)$. By the Chinese remainder theorem the pairwise coprimality of the $p_i$ gives $R\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\prod_{i=1}^{r}K[t]/(p_i)$, an isomorphism onto a product of fields; let $e_i\in R$ be the idempotent mapping to $(0,\dots,0,1,0,\dots,0)$. Then $V=\bigoplus_{i=1}^r e_iV$ as $K$-vector spaces. We identify $e_iV$ with $\ker p_i(A)$: if $v=e_iv'$ then $p_i(A)v=p_i(A)e_iv'=\mu_A(A)\cdot\bigl(p_ie_i/\mu_A\bigr)(A)v'=0$, because $p_ie_i\equiv p_i\equiv0\pmod{p_i}$ and $p_ie_i\equiv0\pmod{p_j}$ for $j\ne i$, hence $p_ie_i\in(\mu_A)$; conversely if $p_i(A)v=0$, write $v=\sum_je_jv$, and for $j\ne i$ we have $e_j\in(p_i)$ in $R$, say $e_j=p_ig_j$, so $e_jv=g_j(A)p_i(A)v=0$, whence $v=e_iv\in e_iV$.
Now base-change to $\overline K$. Each $e_iV_{\overline K}=e_i\,(V_{\overline K})$ is stable under $A_{\overline K}$, and $V_{\overline K}=\bigoplus_i e_iV_{\overline K}$. The algebra $K[t]/(p_i)\otimes_K\overline K\cong\overline K[t]/(p_i)\cong\prod_{\lambda\,:\,p_i(\lambda)=0}\overline K$ (the last isomorphism by separability and the Chinese remainder theorem), so $e_iV_{\overline K}$ decomposes as a direct sum of the subspaces on which $t$, i.e. $A_{\overline K}$, acts as the scalar $\lambda$: explicitly, if $\varepsilon_\lambda$ is the idempotent of $\overline K[t]/(p_i)$ projecting to the $\lambda$-factor, then $e_iV_{\overline K}=\bigoplus_\lambda \varepsilon_\lambda(e_iV_{\overline K})$ and $A_{\overline K}=\lambda\,\mathrm{id}$ on $\varepsilon_\lambda(e_iV_{\overline K})$. Thus $A_{\overline K}$ is diagonalisable on each $e_iV_{\overline K}$ and hence on their direct sum $V_{\overline K}$. $\dashv$

Now we apply these facts.

STEP 1: $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ are square-free. By hypothesis $T|_W$ is semisimple, so Fact 3 ($\Rightarrow$) applied to $A=T|_W$ on $V=W$ gives that $\mu_1$ is square-free; likewise $\bar T$ semisimple on $E/W$ gives $\mu_2$ square-free. (In the degenerate cases $W=0$ or $W=E$ we set the corresponding minimal polynomial to $1$, which is square-free.)

STEP 2: $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ are coprime. By Fact 1, $\mu_1\mid\chi_1$ and $\mu_2\mid\chi_2$. By hypothesis $\gcd(\chi_1,\chi_2)=1$ in the UFD $K[t]$. Any common divisor of $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ divides both $\chi_1$ and $\chi_2$, hence is a unit; so $\gcd(\mu_1,\mu_2)=1$. (If $\chi_1=1$ or $\chi_2=1$ this is immediate.)

STEP 3: $m(t):=\mu_1(t)\mu_2(t)$ annihilates $T$. Let $e\in E$ and let $\bar e\in E/W$ be its class. Since $\mu_2$ is the minimal polynomial of $\bar T$, $\mu_2(\bar T)=0$, i.e. $\overline{\mu_2(T)e}=\mu_2(\bar T)\bar e=0$; thus $\mu_2(T)e\in W$. As $\mu_1$ annihilates $T|_W$ and $W$ is $T$-stable, $\mu_1(T)$ annihilates $W$, so $\mu_1(T)\mu_2(T)e=0$. Since $e$ was arbitrary and polynomials in $T$ commute, $m(T)=\mu_1(T)\mu_2(T)=0$ on $E$. (Degenerate cases: if $W=0$ then $\mu_1=1$ and $\mu_2(T)=0$ directly; if $W=E$ then $\mu_2=1$ and $\mu_1(T)=0$ since $T|_E=T$.)

STEP 4: $m$ is square-free. Write $\mu_1=\prod_{i\in I}p_i$ and $\mu_2=\prod_{j\in J}q_j$ into distinct monic irreducibles (possible by Step 1). By Step 2 no $p_i$ equals any $q_j$, so $m=\prod_{i\in I}p_i\prod_{j\in J}q_j$ is a product of pairwise distinct irreducible polynomials, hence square-free.

STEP 5: conclusion. Since $m(T)=0$, the minimal polynomial $\mu_T$ of $T$ divides $m$ in $K[t]$; a divisor of a square-free polynomial is square-free, so $\mu_T$ is square-free. By Fact 3 ($\Leftarrow$), $T_{\overline K}$ is diagonalisable on $E_{\overline K}=E\otimes_K\overline K$, i.e. $T$ is semisimple on $E$.

This covers all cases ($W=0$, $W=E$, $E=0$ included), and every step is justified above. Hence $T$ is semisimple on $E$. $\blacksquare$

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let T in GL_K(V) be semisimple, and let W be a T-stable K-linear subspace of V. Then the K-linear operator induced by T on the quotient V/W is semisimple.
proof:
PROOF.

CONVENTIONS. Fix once and for all an algebraic closure K̄ of K. For a K-vector space M write M̄ := M ⊗_K K̄, and for a K-linear endomorphism u of M write ū := u ⊗ id_{K̄}. Following the usage of the proved linear-algebra lemmas (where an operator is called semisimple precisely when its base change to V ⊗_K K̄ is diagonalizable), we take as the definition: u is semisimple on M iff ū is diagonalizable on M̄. We must prove that the operator induced by T on V/W has this property.

NOTATION FOR THE INDUCED OPERATOR. Define U: V/W → V/W by U(v + W) := Tv + W. This is well defined and K-linear: if v + W = v′ + W then v − v′ ∈ W, and since T(W) ⊆ W by hypothesis, Tv − Tv′ = T(v − v′) ∈ W, so Tv + W = Tv′ + W; K-linearity of U follows immediately from that of T. The hypothesis T ∈ GL_K(V) is only used through the inclusion T(W) ⊆ W.

EDGE CASE. If V/W = 0 (for instance V = 0 or W = V), then (V/W)̄ = 0 and Ū is the zero operator on the zero K̄-vector space, which is diagonalizable (the empty family is a basis of the zero space, and the diagonalizability condition is vacuous). Henceforth assume V/W ≠ 0; then V ≠ 0 and dim_{K̄} V̄ = dim_K V > 0.

STEP 1 (flatness of K̄/K; quotient commutes with base change). K̄ is a vector space over K, hence admits a K-basis, hence is a free K-module; every free module is flat. Tensoring the short exact sequence of K-modules 0 → W → V → V/W → 0 with the flat K-module K̄ gives an exact sequence 0 → W̄ → V̄ → (V/W)̄ → 0, where W̄ → V̄ is w ⊗ c ↦ w ⊗ c; it is injective and its image is the K̄-linear span of {w ⊗ 1 : w ∈ W}. We identify W̄ with this image, a K̄-subspace of V̄. The map Ψ: V̄ → (V/W)̄ given by Ψ(v ⊗ c) = (v + W) ⊗ c is well defined (it is the tensor product of the quotient map V ↠ V/W with id_{K̄}, applied to the universal bilinear map), it is K̄-linear and surjective (elements v ⊗ c generate V̄), and exactness gives ker Ψ = im(W̄ → V̄) = W̄. Therefore Ψ induces a canonical K̄-linear isomorphism
  Φ: (V/W)̄ →̃ V̄/W̄,   Φ((v + W) ⊗ c) = (v ⊗ c) + W̄.

STEP 2 (Φ is an isomorphism of K̄[t]-modules). Since T(W) ⊆ W we have T̄(W̄) ⊆ W̄: for w ∈ W and c ∈ K̄, T̄(w ⊗ c) = Tw ⊗ c ∈ W̄, and W̄ is the K̄-span of such tensors. Hence T̄ induces a well-defined K̄-linear operator Q on V̄/W̄, Q((v ⊗ c) + W̄) = T̄(v ⊗ c) + W̄. On elementary tensors,
  Φ(Ū((v + W) ⊗ c)) = Φ((Tv + W) ⊗ c) = (Tv ⊗ c) + W̄ = T̄(v ⊗ c) + W̄ = Q((v ⊗ c) + W̄) = Q(Φ((v + W) ⊗ c)),
where we used U(v + W) = Tv + W and T̄(v ⊗ c) = Tv ⊗ c. Both sides are K̄-linear in (v + W) ⊗ c, so Φ ∘ Ū = Q ∘ Φ; equivalently Φ is an isomorphism of K̄[t]-modules, where t acts on (V/W)̄ through Ū and on V̄/W̄ through Q. Consequently Ū is diagonalizable if and only if Q is diagonalizable. It remains to prove that Q is diagonalizable.

STEP 3 (eigenspace decomposition of V̄). By the semisimplicity hypothesis, T̄ is diagonalizable on V̄. Let Λ ⊂ K̄ be the set of eigenvalues of T̄. Then Λ is nonempty (a diagonalizable operator on a nonzero space has a basis of eigenvectors, and that basis is nonempty) and finite: choosing one nonzero eigenvector in each eigenspace gives |Λ| linearly independent vectors, because eigenvectors belonging to pairwise distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent (standard: a minimal linear relation among vectors from distinct eigenspaces, acted on by T̄ and by λ·id for one of the eigenvalues, and subtracted, yields a shorter relation, contradiction); hence |Λ| ≤ dim_{K̄} V̄ < ∞. Taking a basis of eigenvectors and grouping it according to its eigenvalues shows
  V̄ = ⊕_{λ ∈ Λ} E_λ,   E_λ := ker(T̄ − λ id),   T̄|_{E_λ} = λ·id,
since the grouped subfamilies span E_λ (each member is an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ, hence lies in E_λ, and every element of E_λ is a K̄-linear combination of basis vectors on which T̄ acts as λ, which must therefore all have eigenvalue λ). We record the elementary consequence used repeatedly: for every f(t) = Σ_i a_i t^i ∈ K̄[t], every λ ∈ Λ and every v ∈ E_λ,
  f(T̄)v = Σ_i a_i T̄^i v = Σ_i a_i λ^i v = f(λ)·v.      (∗)

STEP 4 (vanishing on Λ implies annihilation of T̄). Put m(t) := ∏_{λ∈Λ} (t − λ) ∈ K̄[t]. For v = Σ_λ v_λ with v_λ ∈ E_λ, (∗) gives m(T̄)v = Σ_λ m(T̄)v_λ = Σ_λ m(λ)v_λ = 0, since m(λ) = 0 for every λ ∈ Λ; thus m(T̄) = 0. Now let Q(t) ∈ K̄[t] be any polynomial with Q(μ) = 0 for all μ ∈ Λ. For each μ ∈ Λ, the division algorithm in the Euclidean domain K̄[t] yields Q = (t − μ)S_μ + Q(μ) = (t − μ)S_μ, so (t − μ) | Q. For μ ≠ μ′ the polynomials t − μ and t − μ′ are non-associate irreducibles of degree 1, hence coprime; by Euclid’s lemma and induction on |Λ| their product m divides Q, say Q = m·R. Since the evaluation map K̄[t] → End_{K̄}(V̄), f ↦ f(T̄), is a K̄-algebra homomorphism, Q(T̄) = m(T̄) ∘ R(T̄) = 0. Thus:
  (†)  Q(T̄) = 0 for every Q ∈ K̄[t] with Q|_Λ ≡ 0.
No restriction on deg Q is imposed or needed; this is the point where the earlier degree argument has been replaced by coprimality of the linear factors.

STEP 5 (Lagrange interpolation polynomials). For λ ∈ Λ set m_λ(t) := ∏_{λ′ ∈ Λ, λ′ ≠ λ} (t − λ′) and e_λ(t) := m_λ(t)/m_λ(λ) ∈ K̄[t]. The scalar m_λ(λ) = ∏_{λ′ ≠ λ}(λ − λ′) is a product of nonzero factors, hence nonzero, so e_λ is defined. Evaluating at μ ∈ Λ: if μ ≠ λ, the factor (t − μ) occurs among the factors of m_λ, so m_λ(μ) = 0 and e_λ(μ) = 0; if μ = λ then e_λ(λ) = m_λ(λ)/m_λ(λ) = 1. Hence e_λ(μ) = δ_{λμ} for all λ, μ ∈ Λ.

STEP 6 (the operators p_λ := e_λ(T̄) are commuting idempotents summing to the identity). For λ, λ′ ∈ Λ consider Q_{λ,λ′}(t) := e_λ(t)e_{λ′}(t) − δ_{λλ′}e_{λ′}(t). By Step 5, for every μ ∈ Λ,
  Q_{λ,λ′}(μ) = δ_{λμ}δ_{λ′μ} − δ_{λλ′}δ_{λ′μ}.
If λ ≠ λ′ both terms are 0 (a single μ cannot equal both λ and λ′). If λ = λ′ the two terms are both δ_{λμ}, so the difference is 0. Thus Q_{λ,λ′} vanishes on Λ, and (†) gives p_λ p_{λ′} = δ_{λλ′} p_{λ′}. With λ = λ′ this reads p_λ² = p_λ, so each p_λ is an idempotent, and the displayed relation also shows the p_λ commute pairwise. Next, R(t) := Σ_{λ∈Λ} e_λ(t) − 1 satisfies, for every μ ∈ Λ, R(μ) = Σ_λ δ_{λμ} − 1 = 1 − 1 = 0 (exactly one term of the sum is nonzero). By (†), Σ_{λ∈Λ} p_λ = id_{V̄}. (Note that deg(e_λ e_{λ′}) may be as large as 2(|Λ| − 1); no degree bound is used, only vanishing on Λ, exactly as prescribed.)

STEP 7 (image of p_λ). For λ ∈ Λ, (t − λ)e_λ(t) = (t − λ)m_λ(t)/m_λ(λ) = m(t)/m_λ(λ) as polynomials, so the polynomial (t − λ)e_λ(t) − m(t)/m_λ(λ) is identically zero and (†) gives (T̄ − λ id)∘p_λ = m(T̄)/m_λ(λ) = 0. Hence p_λ(V̄) ⊆ ker(T̄ − λ id) = E_λ. Conversely, (∗) gives p_λ v = e_λ(λ)v = v for every v ∈ E_λ, so E_λ ⊆ p_λ(V̄). Therefore p_λ(V̄) = E_λ.

STEP 8 (W̄ splits along the eigenspace decomposition). Because W̄ is T̄-stable (Step 2), it is stable under f(T̄) for every f ∈ K̄[t]; indeed the set {S ∈ End_{K̄}(V̄) : S(W̄) ⊆ W̄} is a K̄-subalgebra containing id and T̄, hence containing every polynomial in T̄. In particular p_λ(W̄) ⊆ W̄ for all λ. Let w ∈ W̄. By Step 6, w = Σ_{λ∈Λ} p_λ w, and each summand p_λ w lies in W̄ and, by Step 7, in E_λ. Hence w ∈ Σ_λ (W̄ ∩ E_λ), giving W̄ ⊆ Σ_λ (W̄ ∩ E_λ); the reverse inclusion is immediate. The sum is direct, being a sub-sum of the direct sum V̄ = ⊕_λ E_λ: if Σ_λ x_λ = 0 with x_λ ∈ W̄ ∩ E_λ ⊆ E_λ, uniqueness of the components in ⊕_λ E_λ forces x_λ = 0 for every λ. Thus
  W̄ = ⊕_{λ∈Λ} (W̄ ∩ E_λ).

STEP 9 (the quotient is a direct sum of eigenspaces of Q). Let q: V̄ → V̄/W̄ be the quotient map and, for λ ∈ Λ, set F_λ := q(E_λ) = (E_λ + W̄)/W̄ ⊆ V̄/W̄.
Spanning: given y ∈ V̄/W̄ write y = q(v) with v = Σ_λ v_λ, v_λ ∈ E_λ; then y = Σ_λ q(v_λ) ∈ Σ_λ F_λ.
Directness: suppose Σ_λ q(v_λ) = 0 with v_λ ∈ E_λ. Then q(Σ_λ v_λ) = 0, so Σ_λ v_λ ∈ ker q = W̄ = ⊕_μ (W̄ ∩ E_μ) by Step 8; writing Σ_λ v_λ = Σ_μ w_μ with w_μ ∈ W̄ ∩ E_μ and comparing components in the direct sum V̄ = ⊕_μ E_μ yields v_μ = w_μ ∈ W̄ for every μ, hence q(v_μ) = 0 for every μ. Therefore
  V̄/W̄ = ⊕_{λ∈Λ} F_λ.
Each F_λ is contained in the λ-eigenspace of Q: for v ∈ E_λ, Q(q(v)) = T̄v + W̄ = λv + W̄ = λ·q(v). Since the F_λ span V̄/W̄ and are mutually independent, choosing a K̄-basis B_λ of each F_λ, the union B = ⊔_{λ∈Λ} B_λ is a K̄-basis of V̄/W̄ (the sum being direct), and every element of B is an eigenvector of Q (with eigenvalue λ for elements of B_λ). Hence Q is diagonalizable on V̄/W̄.

STEP 10 (conclusion). By Step 2, Ū is diagonalizable on (V/W)̄ ≅ V̄/W̄. By the convention stated at the outset, U is semisimple on V/W. This is exactly the required conclusion, and the edge case V/W = 0 was settled at the beginning. ∎

NOTE. The argument used only the T-stability of W and the diagonalizability of T̄; the invertibility of T plays no role.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be prime, let m>=1 and put k=overline(F_q). Let X be a smooth projective variety over F_{q^m}, let E be a vector bundle of rank r+1 on X defined over F_{q^m}, and let P over F_{q^m} be the projective bundle of one-dimensional quotients of E. If the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (id x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) for every n>=0, then it is semisimple on H^n_et(P_k,Q_ell) for every n>=0.
proof:
We write F_0 := \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), \(\sigma:k\to k\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}\) (so \(\sigma\) fixes \(F_0\) pointwise), and \(F:=({\rm id}\times{\rm Spec}\,\sigma)^*\) for the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius. For \(e\ge 1\) we write \(F^{(e)}:=F^e=({\rm id}\times{\rm Spec}\,\sigma^e)^*\); note \(\sigma^e(c)=c^{q^{me}}\). By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a, \(F\) (and every \(F^{(e)}\)) is an invertible \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear operator on the étale cohomology of any \(F_0\)-scheme base-changed to \(k\); by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob these spaces are finite-dimensional over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) (all our schemes are proper over finite fields). By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5, an operator on a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-space is semisimple if and only if its base change to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) is diagonalizable; we use these two notions interchangeably.

STEP 0 (edge cases). If \(X=\varnothing\) then \(P=\varnothing\) and \(H^n_{\rm et}(P_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\), on which the zero operator is diagonalizable. If \(\operatorname{rk} E=r+1=0\), i.e. \(E=0\), then \({\mathcal P}=\mathbf P(E)={\rm Proj}_X(\bigoplus_{n\ge0}{\rm Sym}^n E)={\rm Proj}_X({\mathcal O}_X)=\varnothing\), and again the conclusion is trivial. Henceforth assume \(X\ne\varnothing\) and \(r\ge 0\) with \(r+1\ge 1\).

STEP 1 (linear algebra). Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, \(T\in{\rm GL}(V)\), \(e\ge1\). Then \(T\) is semisimple if and only if \(T^e\) is semisimple.
Proof. (\(\Rightarrow\)) If \(V_{\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell}\) has a basis of eigenvectors \(v\) with \(Tv=\lambda v\), then \(T^ev=\lambda^e v\), so \(T^e\) is diagonalizable. (\(\Leftarrow\)) Let \(T=T_sT_u\) be the Jordan–Chevalley decomposition over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Both \(T_s,T_u\) are polynomials in \(T\), they commute, and \(T^e=T_s^eT_u^e\) with \(T_s^e\) semisimple and \(T_u^e\) unipotent; by uniqueness of the Jordan–Chevalley decomposition, \((T^e)_u=T_u^e\). The Jordan–Chevalley decomposition is compatible with field extension, so \(T^e\) semisimple (i.e. diagonalizable over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), equivalently semisimple over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) by lemma_5) forces \(T_u^e={\rm id}\). The minimal polynomial of \(T_u\) then divides \(X^e-1\in\mathbb Q_\ell[X]\), which is separable in characteristic \(0\) (its only possible common roots with \(eX^{e-1}\) would be \(0\), and \(0^e-1\ne0\)); hence \(T_u\) is semisimple. A semisimple unipotent operator has only the eigenvalue \(1\) and is diagonalizable, hence is the identity. Thus \(T_u={\rm id}\) and \(T=T_s\) is semisimple. \(\square\)

STEP 2 (decomposition of \(X\) into components defined over finite extensions). Since \(X\) is proper over the finite field \(F_0\), \(A:={\Gamma}(X,{\mathcal O}_X)\) is a finite-dimensional \(F_0\)-algebra. Since \(X\) is smooth, \(X_{\overline F_0}\) is reduced, and by flat base change for quasi-coherent cohomology (\(X\) is quasi-compact and quasi-separated and \(\overline F_0/F_0\) is flat) \(A\otimes_{F_0}\overline F_0\cong{\Gamma}(X_{\overline F_0},{\mathcal O})\), which is reduced because \(X_{\overline F_0}\) is reduced; as \(F_0\) is perfect, a finite \(F_0\)-algebra that becomes reduced over \(\overline F_0\) is étale. Hence \(A\cong\prod_{i\in I}K_i\) is a finite product of finite field extensions \(K_i/F_0\); write \(K_i\cong\mathbb F_{q^{me_i}}\) and \(e_i=[K_i:F_0]\). Let \(\pi:X\to{\rm Spec}\,A\) be the canonical morphism (adjunction for \(A={\Gamma}(X,{\mathcal O}_X)\); \(\pi\) is over \({\rm Spec}\,F_0\)). Put \(X_i:=X\times_{{\rm Spec}\,A}{\rm Spec}\,K_i\). Since \({\rm Spec}\,K_i\to{\rm Spec}\,A\) is an open-and-closed immersion, each \(X_i\) is an open-and-closed \(F_0\)-subscheme of \(X\) (defined over \(F_0\), because everything is over \({\rm Spec}\,F_0\)), and \(X=\bigsqcup_{i\in I}X_i\). Moreover \({\Gamma}(X_i,{\mathcal O})=A\otimes_A K_i=K_i\), so the structure morphism \(X_i\to{\rm Spec}\,F_0\) factors as \(X_i\xrightarrow{\;\rho_i\;}{\rm Spec}\,K_i\to{\rm Spec}\,F_0\).

Smoothness and properness of \(X_i\) over \(K_i\): we do NOT argue by fpqc descent. Let \(L:=K_i\) and \(A_L:=L\otimes_{F_0}L\). Because \(L/F_0\) is finite separable (finite fields are perfect), \(A_L\) is a finite étale \(L\)-algebra, hence \(A_L\cong\prod_{j=1}^{n}F_j\) with each \(F_j/F_0\) a field (finite separable over \(L\)). The multiplication map \(\mu:A_L\to L\), \(a\otimes b\mapsto ab\), is a surjective \(L\)-algebra homomorphism onto a field; its kernel is a maximal ideal of \(\prod_jF_j\), and every maximal ideal of a finite product of fields is generated by an idempotent. Hence \(\mu\) is the projection onto a direct factor, so \({\rm Spec}\,\mu:{\rm Spec}\,L\to{\rm Spec}\,A_L\) is an open-and-closed immersion. Consider the morphism \(\gamma:X_i\to X_i\times_{F_0}{\rm Spec}\,L\) induced by \(({\rm id},\rho_i)\); it is a section of the first projection \({\rm pr}_1\). On an affine \({\rm Spec}\,B\subseteq X_i\) (with \(B\) an \(L\)-algebra) the corresponding ring map is \(B\otimes_{F_0}L\to B\), \(b\otimes\lambda\mapsto b\lambda\). Using \(B\otimes_{F_0}L\xrightarrow\sim B\otimes_L A_L\), \(b\otimes\lambda\mapsto b\otimes(1\otimes\lambda)\), this map identifies with \({\rm id}_B\otimes\mu:B\otimes_LA_L\to B\otimes_LL\cong B\), which is the quotient by the ideal generated by the idempotent \(1\otimes(1-e)\) (\(e\) the direct-factor idempotent of \(\mu\)). Hence \(\gamma\) is an open-and-closed immersion. Now \({\rm pr}_1:X_i\times_{F_0}{\rm Spec}\,L\to{\rm Spec}\,L\) is the base change of the smooth projective \(F_0\)-scheme \(X_i\), hence is smooth and projective over \(L\). Since \(\gamma\) is an open immersion (hence étale, hence smooth) and also a closed immersion (hence proper), the composite \(\rho_i={\rm pr}_1|_{X_i}\circ\gamma\) is smooth (composition of smooth morphisms) and proper (composition of proper morphisms). Projectivity over \(L\) holds because \(X_i\) is a closed subscheme of the \(L\)-projective scheme \(X_i\times_{F_0}{\rm Spec}\,L\), and the restriction of a relatively ample line bundle to a closed subscheme is ample. Thus \(X_i\) is smooth projective over \(L=K_i\).

Geometric connectedness of \(X_i\) over \(K_i\): for any field extension \(K_i\subseteq K'\), flat base change for the qcqs \(X_i\) gives \({\Gamma}(X_i\times_{{\rm Spec}\,K_i}{\rm Spec}\,K',{\mathcal O})={\Gamma}(X_i,{\mathcal O})\otimes_{K_i}K'=K_i\otimes_{K_i}K'=K'\). In particular \({\Gamma}(X_i\times_{{\rm Spec}\,K_i}{\rm Spec}\,\overline{K_i},{\mathcal O})=\overline{K_i}\), which has only the trivial idempotents; since open-and-closed decompositions of a scheme correspond bijectively to idempotents of its ring of global sections, \(X_i\times\overline{K_i}\) is connected. So \(X_i\) is geometrically connected over \(K_i\).

STEP 3 (the pieces of \({\mathcal P}\)). Put \(E_i:=E|_{X_i}\), a vector bundle of rank \(r+1\ge1\) on the \(K_i\)-scheme \(X_i\) (it is \({\rm Spec}_{X_i}({\rm Sym}_{\mathcal O_{X_i}}E_i^\vee)\), hence naturally a \(K_i\)-scheme), and \({\mathcal P}_i:={\mathcal P}\times_X X_i\). Projective bundles commute with base change, so \({\mathcal P}_i={\mathbf P}(E_i)\) as \(K_i\)-schemes, and since \(X_i\hookrightarrow X\) is open-and-closed, \({\mathcal P}_i\hookrightarrow{\mathcal P}\) is open-and-closed and \({\mathcal P}=\bigsqcup_{i\in I}{\mathcal P}_i\); the \({\mathcal P}_i\) are defined over \(F_0\) because the \(X_i\) are \(F_0\)-subschemes of \(X\).

STEP 4 (splitting \(H^n(X_k)\) over the \(X_i\), equivariantly for \(F\)). Each \(X_i\) is open-and-closed in \(X\) and defined over \(F_0\), and \(\sigma\) fixes \(F_0\), so \({\rm id}\times{\rm Spec}\,\sigma\) restricts to \({\rm id}_{X_i}\times{\rm Spec}\,\sigma\) on \((X_i)_k:=X_i\times_{{\rm Spec}\,F_0}{\rm Spec}\,k\); thus each \((X_i)_k\) is \(F\)-stable. Applying Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_cohom_open_closed_sum inductively to the finite open-and-closed decomposition \(X_k=\bigsqcup_i (X_i)_k\) (all schemes involved are proper, hence separated of finite type, over \(k\)) gives \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphisms \(H^n_{\rm et}(X_k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\cong\bigoplus_i H^n_{\rm et}((X_i)_k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\). By naturality of restriction maps for étale cohomology, this is an isomorphism of \(F\)-modules: \(F\) acts as \(\bigoplus_i F|_{H^n((X_i)_k)}\). By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_9 (the summands are finite-dimensional and \(F\) is invertible on each, by lemma_45_finite_frob and lemma_6a) and the hypothesis that \(F\) is semisimple on \(H^n(X_k)\) for every \(n\), we conclude:
\[(*)\qquad F\ \text{is semisimple on } H^n_{\rm et}((X_i)_k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\ \text{for every } i\in I,\ n\ge0.\]

STEP 5 (refining \((X_i)_k\) over the \(F_0\)-embeddings \(K_i\hookrightarrow k\)). Fix \(i\in I\) and write \(L:=K_i\), \(e:=e_i\), \({\rm Hom}:=\hom_{F_0}(L,k)\) (so \(|{\rm Hom}|=e\)). Choose \(\tau_0\in{\rm Hom}\) and put \(L_0:=\tau_0(L)=\mathbb F_{q^{me}}\subseteq k\). Since \(L=F_0[\alpha]\) with \(\alpha\) separable of degree \(e\) and minimal polynomial \(f\in F_0[X]\) splitting over \(k\) as \(\prod_{\tau\in{\rm Hom}}(X-\tau(\alpha))\) with distinct roots, the Chinese remainder theorem gives a \(k\)-algebra isomorphism
\[\varphi:\;k\otimes_{F_0}L\;\xrightarrow\sim\;\prod_{\tau\in{\rm Hom}}k,\qquad a\otimes b\longmapsto (a\,\tau(b))_{\tau}.\]
Let \(e_\tau\in k\otimes_{F_0}L\) be the primitive idempotent corresponding to the \(\tau\)-factor. Since \(X_i\to{\rm Spec}\,F_0\) factors through \({\rm Spec}\,L\),
\[(X_i)_k=X_i\times_{{\rm Spec}\,F_0}{\rm Spec}\,k\;=\;X_i\times_{{\rm Spec}\,L}{\rm Spec}\,(L\otimes_{F_0}k)=\bigsqcup_{\tau\in{\rm Hom}}X_i^{(\tau)},\qquad X_i^{(\tau)}:=X_i\times_{{\rm Spec}\,L,\tau}{\rm Spec}\,k,\]
a disjoint union into open-and-closed \(k\)-subschemes; likewise \(({\mathcal P}_i)_k=\bigsqcup_\tau{\mathcal P}_i^{(\tau)}\) with \({\mathcal P}_i^{(\tau)}:={\mathcal P}_i\times_{{\rm Spec}\,L,\tau}{\rm Spec}\,k\). Each \(X_i^{(\tau)}\) is nonempty: \(X_i\ne\varnothing\) of finite type over the field \(L\) has a closed point \(x\) with \(\kappa(x)/L\) finite, and \(\kappa(x)\otimes_{L,\tau}k\ne0\) because \(\kappa(x)\) admits an \(L\)-embedding into the algebraically closed \(k\).

Action of \(F\) on these idempotents: on \(k\otimes_{F_0}L\) the morphism \({\rm id}\times{\rm Spec}\,\sigma\) induces the ring automorphism \(\sigma\otimes1\). Writing \(e_\tau\) as the class in \(k[X]/(f)\) of the interpolation polynomial \(P_\tau\in k[X]\) with \(P_\tau(\upsilon(\alpha))=\delta_{\tau\upsilon}\), the automorphism \(\sigma\otimes1\) sends it to the class of \(\sigma(P_\tau)\), whose value at \(\upsilon(\alpha)\) is \(\sigma(P_\tau(\sigma^{-1}\upsilon(\alpha)))=\delta_{\tau,\sigma^{-1}\upsilon}=\delta_{\sigma\tau,\upsilon}\). Hence
\[(\sigma\otimes1)(e_\tau)=e_{\sigma\circ\tau}.\]
Consequently \(F={\rm id}\times{\rm Spec}\,\sigma\) restricts to an isomorphism of \(k\)-schemes \(f_\tau:X_i^{(\tau)}\xrightarrow\sim X_i^{(\sigma\circ\tau)}\) (and likewise \({\mathcal P}_i^{(\tau)}\xrightarrow\sim{\mathcal P}_i^{(\sigma\circ\tau)}\)), and \(F\) permutes the summands accordingly. The subgroup \(\langle\sigma\rangle\) acts on \({\rm Hom}\): the stabiliser of \(\tau_0\) is \(\{j\ge0:\sigma^j|_L={\rm id}\}=e\mathbb Z\), since \(\sigma^j|_L={\rm id}\iff c^{q^{mj}}=c\ \forall c\in L\iff me\mid mj\iff e\mid j\). Thus the orbit of \(\tau_0\) has \(e=|{\rm Hom}|\) elements, i.e. \({\rm Hom}=\{\sigma^j\circ\tau_0:0\le j\le e-1\}\) is a single \(\langle\sigma\rangle\)-orbit. In particular \(\sigma^e\) fixes \(L\) pointwise, so \(\sigma^e\circ\tau=\tau\) for every \(\tau\), and therefore \(F^{(e)}={\rm id}\times{\rm Spec}\,\sigma^e\) preserves every summand \(X_i^{(\tau)}\) and \({\mathcal P}_i^{(\tau)}\).

Finally, on the \(\tau_0\)-summand the restricted operator is exactly the \(q^{me}\)-power arithmetic Frobenius of the \(L_0\)-scheme \(X_i\): identifying \(L\) with \(L_0=\tau_0(L)=\mathbb F_{q^{me}}\subseteq k\) via \(\tau_0\), we have \(X_i^{(\tau_0)}=X_i\times_{{\rm Spec}\,L_0}{\rm Spec}\,k\), \(\sigma^e(c)=c^{q^{me}}\) fixes \(L_0\) pointwise, and by naturality of restriction the operator \(F^{(e)}|_{H^n(X_i^{(\tau_0)})}\) equals \(({\rm id}\times{\rm Spec}\,\sigma^e)^*\) on \(H^n_{\rm et}(X_i\times_{{\rm Spec}\,L_0}{\rm Spec}\,k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\), i.e. the \(q^{me}\)-power arithmetic Frobenius. The same holds for \({\mathcal P}_i^{(\tau_0)}={\mathbf P}(E_i)\).

STEP 6 (transfer of semisimplicity to the \(\tau_0\)-summand for \(X_i\)). From \((*)\) and Step 1 (with \(T=F|_{H^n((X_i)_k)}\), \(e=e_i\)), \(F^{(e)}\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\rm et}((X_i)_k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\). Applying Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_cohom_open_closed_sum inductively over the finite set \({\rm Hom}\) to the open-and-closed decomposition \((X_i)_k=\bigsqcup_\tau X_i^{(\tau)}\), and using that \(F^{(e)}\) preserves each summand, we get an \(F^{(e)}\)-equivariant isomorphism \(H^n((X_i)_k)\cong\bigoplus_{\tau}H^n(X_i^{(\tau)})\). By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_9 (each summand finite-dimensional, \(F^{(e)}\) invertible by lemma_6a), \(F^{(e)}\) is semisimple on each \(H^n(X_i^{(\tau)})\). Note that we apply lemma_9 only to \(F^{(e)}\), never to \(F\) itself, which permutes these summands. Thus
\[(\dagger)\qquad F^{(e)}\ \text{is semisimple on } H^n_{\rm et}(X_i^{(\tau)},{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\ \text{for every }\tau\in{\rm Hom},\ n\ge0.\]

STEP 7 (apply the projective-bundle theorem on the \(\tau_0\)-summand). The \(K_i\cong\mathbb F_{q^{me}}\)-scheme \(X_i\) is smooth, projective and geometrically connected (Step 2), and \(E_i\) is a vector bundle of rank \(r+1\ge1\) on it, defined over \(K_i\) (Step 3). Taking \((q,m)\) in eoinm/ebe471c6ef5b2d01/6f77f7 to be \((q,me)\) (note \(\overline{\mathbb F}_{q^{me}}=\overline{\mathbb F}_q=k\), since an element of \(k\) is algebraic over \(\mathbb F_{q^{me}}\) iff it is algebraic over \(\mathbb F_q\)), the hypothesis of that lemma is precisely (\(\dagger\)) at \(\tau=\tau_0\): the \(q^{me}\)-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on \(H^n_{\rm et}(X_i\times_{{\rm Spec}\,L_0}k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)=H^n(X_i^{(\tau_0)},{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\) for every \(n\). Its conclusion is that the \(q^{me}\)-power arithmetic Frobenius, i.e. \(F^{(e)}\) (Step 5), is semisimple on \(H^n_{\rm et}({\mathbf P}(E_i)_k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)=H^n_{\rm et}({\mathcal P}_i^{(\tau_0)},{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\).

STEP 8 (conjugacy to the other summands, then reassembly over \(\tau\)). Let \(\tau=\sigma^j\circ\tau_0\) with \(0\le j\le e-1\), and let \(g_j:{\mathcal P}_i^{(\tau_0)}\xrightarrow\sim{\mathcal P}_i^{(\tau)}\) be the restriction of \({\rm id}\times{\rm Spec}\,\sigma^j=F^j\). Set \(\alpha:=(g_j^{-1})^*:H^n({\mathcal P}_i^{(\tau_0)})\to H^n({\mathcal P}_i^{(\tau)})\), a \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear isomorphism. The morphisms \({\rm id}\times{\rm Spec}\,\sigma^e\) and \({\rm id}\times{\rm Spec}\,\sigma^{-j}\) of \(({\mathcal P}_i)_k\) commute (both are powers of \({\rm id}\times{\rm Spec}\,\sigma\)), so their pullbacks commute; as \(g_j^{-1}\) is the restriction of \({\rm id}\times{\rm Spec}\,\sigma^{-j}\) and \(F^{(e)}\) preserves both summands, we obtain \(\alpha\circ F^{(e)}|_{H^n({\mathcal P}_i^{(\tau_0)})}=F^{(e)}|_{H^n({\mathcal P}_i^{(\tau)})}\circ\alpha\). By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_8, \(F^{(e)}\) is semisimple on \(H^n({\mathcal P}_i^{(\tau)},{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\) for every \(\tau\in{\rm Hom}\) and every \(n\). Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_9 to the \(F^{(e)}\)-equivariant decomposition \(H^n(({\mathcal P}_i)_k)\cong\bigoplus_\tau H^n({\mathcal P}_i^{(\tau)})\) (from lemma_cohom_open_closed_sum, as in Step 6) gives: \(F^{(e)}\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\rm et}(({\mathcal P}_i)_k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\).

STEP 9 (descent from \(F^{(e)}\) to \(F\) on \(({\mathcal P}_i)_k\)). Apply Step 1 with \(T=F|_{H^n(({\mathcal P}_i)_k)}\) and \(e=e_i\): since \(F^{(e)}\) is semisimple, \(F\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\rm et}(({\mathcal P}_i)_k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\).

STEP 10 (reassembly over \(i\)). The \({\mathcal P}_i\) are open-and-closed \(F_0\)-subschemes of \({\mathcal P}\) with \({\mathcal P}=\bigsqcup_i{\mathcal P}_i\), so each \(({\mathcal P}_i)_k\) is \(F\)-stable in \({\mathcal P}_k\), and lemma_cohom_open_closed_sum (applied inductively) yields an \(F\)-equivariant isomorphism \(H^n_{\rm et}({\mathcal P}_k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\cong\bigoplus_{i\in I}H^n_{\rm et}(({\mathcal P}_i)_k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\). By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_9 and Step 9, \(F\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\rm et}({\mathcal P}_k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\) for every \(n\ge0\).

This is exactly the required conclusion: the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius \(({\rm id}\times{\rm Spec}\,\sigma)^*\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}\), is semisimple on \(H^n_{\rm et}({\mathcal P}_k,{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\) for all \(n\ge0\). \(\blacksquare\)

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be prime, let m>=1, and put k=overline(F_q). Let X be smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d>=2 over F_{q^m}, let Y subset X be a nonempty effective very ample Cartier divisor defined over F_{q^m}, smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension d-1, and let U=X\Y. Fix a nonzero element of Q_ell(1) and identify Tate twists with Q_ell. Let xi in H^2_et(X_k,Q_ell) be the cycle class of Y and let L denote cup product with xi. Suppose L^{d-n}:H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_ell) is an isomorphism for every 0<=n<=d. If the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (id x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^d_et(U_k,Q_ell), then the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on P^d=ker(L:H^d_et(X_k,Q_ell) -> H^{d+2}_et(X_k,Q_ell)).
proof:
Notation. Write $H^n(X)=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, $H^n(Y)=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, $H^n(U)=H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$. Let $F$ denote the $q^m$-power arithmetic Frobenius $(\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*$, $\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}$, on each of these spaces (it acts on $U_k$ because $U=X\setminus Y$ is defined over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$, $Y$ being defined over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$). Let $i:Y\hookrightarrow X$ and $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusions, $\xi=\mathrm{cl}(Y)\in H^2(X)$, $L=x\mapsto x\cup\xi$, and $P^d=\ker(L:H^d(X)\to H^{d+2}(X))$. Throughout, $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$ is identified with $\mathbb Q_\ell$ by the fixed nonzero element, so Tate twists are ignored as far as the underlying vector spaces are concerned.

Step 1. The Gysin sequence and the subspace $K\subset H^d(U)$.
Apply the Gysin long exact sequence of the pair $(X,Y)$ (lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_ordinary_gysin_sequence_open_complement, with $\mathbb F_{q^m}$ in place of $\mathbb F_q$; $q^m$ is again a prime power) to the smooth projective geometrically connected $\mathbb F_{q^m}$-scheme $X$ of pure dimension $d\ge 1$ and the smooth effective divisor $Y$ of pure dimension $d-1$. In the degrees we need it reads
\[
H^{d-2}(Y)(-1)\xrightarrow{i_!} H^d(X)\xrightarrow{j^*} H^d(U)\xrightarrow{\partial} H^{d-1}(Y)(-1)\xrightarrow{i_!} H^{d+1}(X),
\]
and is exact. After the fixed identification $\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell$, write $\delta:H^d(U)\to H^{d-1}(Y)$ for $\partial$ composed with this identification; clearly $\ker\delta=\ker\partial$. Set
\[
K:=\ker\delta=\operatorname{im}(j^*:H^d(X)\to H^d(U)),
\]
where the second equality is exactness at $H^d(U)$.

Step 2. $K$ is $F$-stable, and $K$, $H^d(U)$ are finite-dimensional.
(a) $F$-stability: the restriction map $j^*$ is $\mathbb F_{q^m}$-rational (both $U$ and $X$ are defined over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$ and $j$ is defined over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$), so by functoriality of pullback along the cartesian squares defining Frobenius one has $j^*\circ F_X=F_U\circ j^*$, i.e. $j^*$ is a morphism of $\mathbb Q_\ell[F]$-modules. Since $K=\operatorname{im} j^*$, it follows that $F(K)\subseteq K$. (Equivalently, $\partial$ is the boundary morphism of the functorial localisation triangle $j_!\mathbb Q_\ell\to\mathbb Q_\ell\to Ri_*\mathbb Q_\ell\xrightarrow{+1}$, hence is Frobenius-equivariant up to the invertible scalar by which Frobenius acts on the Tate twist; either way $\ker\partial$ is $F$-stable.)
(b) Finiteness: $X$ and $Y$ are proper over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$, so by lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob applied to $\mathbb Q_\ell$ with its natural arithmetic Frobenius structure, $H^n(X)$ and $H^n(Y)$ are finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector spaces for every $n$. Consequently $K\cong H^d(X)/\ker j^*$ is finite-dimensional, and $H^d(U)/K\cong\operatorname{im}\delta\subseteq H^{d-1}(Y)$ is finite-dimensional, so $H^d(U)$ itself is finite-dimensional.
(c) By lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a, $F$ is an invertible $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear operator on the finite-dimensional spaces $H^d(U)$ and $H^d(X)$; its restriction $F|_K:K\to K$ is then injective (being the restriction of an injection) and hence, by finite-dimensionality of $K$, an element of $\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(K)$.

Step 3. $P^d$ is $F$-stable.
By lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_frob_lefschetz_stable (again with $\mathbb F_{q^m}$, $q^m$ in place of $\mathbb F_q$, $q$), $F\circ L=q^m\,L\circ F$ on $H^d(X)$. Hence for $x\in P^d$ one has $L(Fx)=q^{-m}F(Lx)=0$, so $Fx\in P^d$; since $F$ is invertible on $H^d(X)$, $F(P^d)=P^d$.

Step 4. Identification of $P^d$ with $K$ as $\mathbb Q_\ell[F]$-modules.
All hypotheses of lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_primitive_middle_as_affine_kernel are satisfied: $d\ge2$; $Y\subset X$ is a nonempty effective very ample Cartier divisor defined over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$, smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension $d-1$; $\xi=\mathrm{cl}(Y)$; $L$ is cup product with $\xi$; and $L^{d-n}:H^n(X)\to H^{2d-n}(X)$ is an isomorphism for every $0\le n\le d$ by assumption. That lemma asserts that $j^*$ restricts to an isomorphism of $\mathbb Q_\ell[F]$-modules
\[
\varphi:=j^*|_{P^d}\;:\;P^d\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;\ker\bigl[H^d(U)\xrightarrow{\ \partial\ }H^{d-1}(Y)\bigr]=K .
\]
Concretely, $\varphi$ is the restriction of the $F$-equivariant map $j^*$ of Step 2(a) to the $F$-stable subspace $P^d$ of Step 3, and it is bijective onto $K$ by the cited lemma; thus $\varphi\circ F_{P^d}=F_K\circ\varphi$.

Step 5. Semisimplicity passes to $F$-stable subspaces.
We prove the following general fact: if $T$ is a semisimple $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear operator on a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space $V$ and $W\subseteq V$ is a $T$-stable $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspace, then $T|_W$ is semisimple. By lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5 (applied to $V$), $T$ is diagonalizable on $\overline V:=V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$; so $\overline V=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda}E_\lambda$ with $\Lambda\subset\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ the finite set of eigenvalues and $E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda)$. Since $\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ is flat (indeed free) over $\mathbb Q_\ell$, $\overline W:=W\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell$ embeds in $\overline V$, and $\overline W$ is $T$-stable because $W$ is. For each $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $p_\lambda\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell[t]$ be the Lagrange interpolation polynomial with $p_\lambda(\lambda)=1$ and $p_\lambda(\mu)=0$ for $\mu\in\Lambda\setminus\{\lambda\}$ (possible since $\Lambda$ is finite); then the projection $\pi_\lambda:\overline V\to E_\lambda$ equals $p_\lambda(T)$. As $\overline W$ is $T$-stable it is stable under every $p_\lambda(T)$, so for $w\in\overline W$ we have $w=\sum_{\lambda}p_\lambda(T)w$ with $p_\lambda(T)w\in\overline W\cap E_\lambda$. Hence $\overline W=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda}(\overline W\cap E_\lambda)$ is a direct sum of eigenspaces, i.e. $T|_{\overline W}$ is diagonalizable. Applying lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5 to $W$ gives that $T|_W$ is semisimple. This proves the claim.

Step 6. Conclusion.
By hypothesis the $q^m$-power arithmetic Frobenius $F$ is semisimple on $H^d(U)$. By Step 2, $K\subseteq H^d(U)$ is an $F$-stable $\mathbb Q_\ell$-subspace of a finite-dimensional space; applying the claim of Step 5 with $V=H^d(U)$, $T=F$, $W=K$, we obtain that $F|_K$ is semisimple.
Finally, $\varphi:P^d\xrightarrow{\sim}K$ is an isomorphism of $\mathbb Q_\ell[F]$-modules (Step 4), so $F|_{P^d}$ and $F|_K$ are conjugate operators: they have the same minimal polynomial in $\mathbb Q_\ell[t]$, and after any extension of scalars they are simultaneously conjugate, hence one is diagonalizable if and only if the other is. Since $F|_K$ is semisimple, $F|_{P^d}$ is semisimple.

Thus the $q^m$-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on $P^d=\ker\bigl(L:H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)$, which is exactly the required conclusion.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power and m>=1. Let X be a smooth projective variety over F_{q^m} of pure dimension d, and let X_1,...,X_s be the geometrically connected components of X_{\overline{F}_q}. Then there exists an integer m' divisible by m such that each X_j is defined over F_{q^{m'}} and, as a scheme over F_{q^{m'}}, is smooth, projective and geometrically connected; equivalently X_{F_{q^{m'}}} is the disjoint union of s smooth projective geometrically connected F_{q^{m'}}-schemes.
proof:
We write F := \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) and \(k := \overline{\mathbb F}_q = \overline F\). For an \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)-scheme \(Z\) and a field extension \(K/\mathbb F_{q^m}\) we write \(Z_K := Z \times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}} \operatorname{Spec} K\).

We first record three standard facts that we use repeatedly, with proofs, so that nothing is hidden.

**Claim 0 (idempotents and clopen subsets).** For any scheme \(Y\), the map \(e \mapsto D(e) := \{y \in |Y| : e_y \neq 0\}\) is a bijection from the set of idempotents of \(\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y)\) onto the set of open-and-closed subschemes of \(Y\); equivalently, \(Y\) is connected if and only if \(\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y)\) has only the idempotents \(0,1\).
*Proof.* Let \(e^2=e\). For an affine open \(U=\operatorname{Spec} B\subset Y\), the restriction \(e|_U\in B\) is idempotent and \(D(e|_U)=V((1-e)|_U)\), so \(D(e)\cap U\) is both open and closed in \(U\). These local sets glue to a subset \(D(e)\subset |Y|\) which is open (being locally open) and whose complement is \(D(1-e)\), also open; hence \(D(e)\) is clopen, and it is an open subscheme of \(Y\). Conversely, if \(|Y|=Y_1\sqcup Y_2\) with \(Y_1,Y_2\) open, the sheaf axiom for the open cover \(\{Y_1,Y_2\}\) gives \(\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y)\cong \Gamma(Y_1,\mathcal O)\times \Gamma(Y_2,\mathcal O)\), and \((1,0)\) is an idempotent. The two constructions are mutually inverse: for an idempotent \(e\), \(D(e)\cap D(1-e)=\varnothing\) because \(e(1-e)=0\) lies in every prime, \(D(e)\cup D(1-e)=|Y|\), \(e|_{D(e)}=1\) (on \(D(e)\), \(e\) is invertible and \(e^2=e\)), and \(e|_{D(1-e)}=0\); and if \(e\) comes from a clopen decomposition \(Y_1\sqcup Y_2\) then \(D(e)=Y_1\), because \(e|_{Y_1}=1\) gives \(Y_1\subset D(e)\) while \(e|_{Y_2}=0\) gives \(D(e)\cap Y_2=\varnothing\) (on \(D(e)\) the element \(e\) is invertible). Finally, if \(D(e)=\varnothing\) then \(e|_U\) is nilpotent for every affine \(U\), so \(e|_U=0\) as it is idempotent, hence \(e=0\); thus \(e\neq 0,1\) yields a genuine disconnection \(|Y|=D(e)\sqcup D(1-e)\), and a disconnection yields a non-trivial idempotent by the construction above. ∎

**Claim 1 (global functions and flat base change).** Let \(Y\) be a proper scheme over a field \(K\), and let \(L/K\) be a field extension. Then the natural map \(\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y)\otimes_K L \to \Gamma(Y_L,\mathcal O_{Y_L})\) is an isomorphism.
*Proof.* \(Y\) is quasi-compact, so choose a finite affine open cover \(Y=\bigcup_{i=1}^{r} V_i\). Since \(Y\) is proper over \(K\) it is separated, so every finite intersection \(V_{i_0\dots i_p}=V_{i_0}\cap\cdots\cap V_{i_p}\) is affine. For a quasi-coherent sheaf on a quasi-compact separated scheme, Čech cohomology computes sheaf cohomology, so \(\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y)\) is the equaliser (kernel) of \(\prod_i \mathcal O(V_i) \rightrightarrows \prod_{i,j}\mathcal O(V_i\cap V_j)\). Each \(V_i\times_K L\) is affine with \(\mathcal O(V_i\times_K L)=\mathcal O(V_i)\otimes_K L\), and the same for the intersections; \(\{V_i\times_K L\}\) is an affine open cover of \(Y_L\), which is again separated over \(L\). Hence \(\Gamma(Y_L,\mathcal O)\) is the equaliser of \(\prod_i(\mathcal O(V_i)\otimes_K L)\rightrightarrows\prod_{i,j}(\mathcal O(V_i\cap V_j)\otimes_K L)\). Since \(L\) is flat over \(K\), tensoring the exact sequence of \(K\)-vector spaces \(0\to\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y)\to\prod_i\mathcal O(V_i)\rightrightarrows\prod_{i,j}\mathcal O(V_i\cap V_j)\) with \(L\) keeps it exact, which is exactly the claimed isomorphism. ∎

**Claim 2 (finiteness).** If \(Y\) is proper over a field \(K\), then \(\Gamma(Y,\mathcal O_Y)\) is a finite-dimensional \(K\)-vector space (Grothendieck's finiteness theorem for the coherent cohomology of a proper scheme over a field, applied to \(\mathcal F=\mathcal O_Y\) and \(i=0\)).

**Step 0 (the empty case).** If \(X=\varnothing\), then \(X_k=\varnothing\) has \(s=0\) connected components, and \(m':=m\) works: \(X_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}=\varnothing\) is the disjoint union of zero smooth projective geometrically connected \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\)-schemes. Henceforth assume \(X\neq\varnothing\).

**Step 1 (the components of \(X_k\), and their geometric connectedness).** \(X_k\) is of finite type over the field \(k\), hence its underlying space is noetherian. A noetherian space has only finitely many irreducible components \(Z_1,\dots,Z_t\), each closed; every connected component is a union of irreducible components, and since the list \(Z_1,\dots,Z_t\) is finite, both a union of \(Z_i\)'s and its complement are finite unions of closed sets. Hence the connected components of \(X_k\) are open and closed, and there are finitely many of them; call them \(X_1,\dots,X_s\) (\(s\ge 1\) since \(X_k\neq\varnothing\)). Each \(X_j\) is an open subscheme of the smooth \(k\)-scheme \(X_k\), hence smooth, hence regular, hence reduced, over \(k\); each is closed in \(X_k\), hence proper over \(k\) (as \(X_k\) is projective, being the base change of the projective \(X\)). By Claim 2, \(\Gamma(X_j,\mathcal O)\) is a finite-dimensional \(k\)-algebra; being reduced and artinian it is a product \(\prod_{i=1}^{t_j} k/\mathfrak m_i\) of fields finite over \(k\), and since \(k\) is algebraically closed each factor is \(k\); so \(\Gamma(X_j,\mathcal O)\cong k^{t_j}\). This ring has \(2^{t_j}\) idempotents, so by Claim 0 the space \(X_j\) has \(2^{t_j}\) clopen subsets, hence exactly \(t_j\) connected components; \(X_j\) is connected, so \(t_j=1\) and \(\Gamma(X_j,\mathcal O)\cong k\).
Now let \(K/k\) be any field extension. By Claim 1, \(\Gamma(X_j\times_k K,\mathcal O)=\Gamma(X_j,\mathcal O)\otimes_k K\cong K\), whose only idempotents are \(0,1\); by Claim 0, \(X_j\times_k K\) is connected. Thus each \(X_j\) is geometrically connected over \(k\), which justifies the terminology "geometrically connected components" in the statement.

**Step 2 (the algebra of global functions of \(X\)).** \(X\) is projective, hence proper, over the field \(F\); by Claim 2, \(A:=\Gamma(X,\mathcal O_X)\) is a finite-dimensional \(F\)-algebra. For every field extension \(F'/F\), Claim 1 gives a natural isomorphism of \(F'\)-algebras \(\Gamma(X_{F'},\mathcal O)\cong A\otimes_F F'\); in particular \(\Gamma(X_k,\mathcal O)\cong A\otimes_F k\).

**Step 3 (the idempotents of \(X_j\) are defined over finite subextensions).** For each \(j\), the decomposition \(X_k = X_j \sqcup \bigsqcup_{j'\neq j} X_{j'}\) into open-and-closed subschemes gives, by Claim 0, a unique idempotent \(e_j\in\Gamma(X_k,\mathcal O)=A\otimes_F k\) which restricts to \(1\) on \(X_j\) and to \(0\) on every other \(X_{j'}\); then \(D(e_j)=X_j\) as open subschemes of \(X_k\). Write \(k=\varinjlim_{L} L\), the filtered colimit over the directed set of finite extensions \(L/F\) contained in \(k\) (directed under compositum). Tensoring commutes with colimits, so \(A\otimes_F k=\varinjlim_L (A\otimes_F L)\). Idempotents commute with filtered colimits of rings: indeed, if \(\bar e\in\varinjlim R_i\) satisfies \(\bar e^2=\bar e\) and \(\bar e\) is the image of \(a_i\in R_i\), then the two elements \(a_i^2,a_i\in R_i\) have the same image in the colimit, so they become equal in some \(R_{i'}\), where the image of \(a_i\) is an idempotent mapping to \(\bar e\); and two idempotents equal in the colimit are already equal at some later stage. Applying this to \(\bar e=e_j\), we obtain a finite extension \(L_j/F\) inside \(k\) and an idempotent \(\tilde e_j\in A\otimes_F L_j\) mapping to \(e_j\). Every finite extension of \(F=\mathbb F_{q^m}\) inside \(k\) is of the form \(\mathbb F_{q^{m n}}\); write \(L_j=\mathbb F_{q^{m n_j}}\). Put \(N:=\mathrm{lcm}(n_1,\dots,n_s)\) and \(F' := \mathbb F_{q^{mN}}\), which contains every \(L_j\). Let \(e_j'\in A\otimes_F F'\) be the image of \(\tilde e_j\) under the transition map \(A\otimes_F L_j\to A\otimes_F F'\). Each \(e_j'\) is an idempotent. The map \(A\otimes_F F' \to A\otimes_F k\) is injective: writing \(M:=A\otimes_F F'\) (an \(F'\)-vector space), this map is \(M\to M\otimes_{F'} k\), \(m\mapsto m\otimes 1\), obtained by tensoring the injective \(F'\)-linear map \(F'\hookrightarrow k\) with the flat \(F'\)-module \(k\). The elements \(e_j'e_{j'}'\) (\(j\neq j'\)) and \(\sum_j e_j'-1\) map in \(A\otimes_F k\) to \(e_je_{j'}=0\) and \(\sum_j e_j-1=0\) (the latter because the \(e_j\) are the characteristic functions of a decomposition of \(X_k\) into clopen pieces, so their sum is the constant section \(1\)). By injectivity, \(e_j'e_{j'}'=0\) for \(j\neq j'\) and \(\sum_{j=1}^{s} e_j'=1\) already in \(A\otimes_F F'\). (Note that these relations are asserted only after passing to the common stage \(F'\), where all the \(e_j'\) live.)

**Step 4 (descent of the components).** Let \(U_j := D(e_j')\subset X_{F'}\), an open-and-closed subscheme by Claim 0. Since the \(e_j'\) are pairwise orthogonal idempotents summing to \(1\), the clopen sets \(D(e_j')\) are pairwise disjoint and cover \(|X_{F'}|\); hence \(X_{F'} = \bigsqcup_{j=1}^{s} U_j\) as a disjoint union of open-and-closed subschemes. Base change to \(k\) gives \(U_j\times_{F'} k = D(e_j'\otimes 1)=D(e_j)=X_j\) as open subschemes of \(X_k\); in particular each \(U_j\) is non-empty (the map \(|X_k|\to|X_{F'}|\) is surjective, \(k/F'\) being faithfully flat, and \(X_j\neq\varnothing\)), and the \(U_j\) are pairwise distinct. Thus each \(X_j\) is defined over \(F'=\mathbb F_{q^{mN}}\): \(U_j\times_{F'}k\cong X_j\).

**Step 5 (smoothness and projectivity of \(U_j\)).** \(X_{F'}\) is smooth and projective over \(F'\) (base change of \(X\)). \(U_j\) is an open subscheme of \(X_{F'}\), hence smooth over \(F'\); and \(U_j\) is also closed in \(X_{F'}\) (its complement is the union of the open sets \(U_{j'}\), \(j'\neq j\)), so \(U_j\hookrightarrow X_{F'}\) is a closed immersion and \(U_j\to\operatorname{Spec} F'\) is the composite of a closed immersion with the projective morphism \(X_{F'}\to\operatorname{Spec} F'\), hence projective.

**Step 6 (pure dimension).** We argue by base change, not on \(U_j\) itself. By Step 4, \(U_j\times_{F'} k\) is (isomorphic to) \(X_j\) as a subscheme of \(X_k\), so its underlying space is \(|X_j|\). Now \(X\) is smooth of pure dimension \(d\) over the perfect field \(F\): since \(X\) is smooth it is normal and noetherian, so its irreducible components are open and closed, and each is integral and smooth of dimension \(d\) over \(F\) (purity of dimension). Base-changing an integral \(F\)-scheme of finite type to \(k\) gives a scheme all of whose irreducible components have the same dimension (\(F\) perfect, so the extension is separable), and a scheme smooth of relative dimension \(d\) over a field has all local rings at closed points of dimension \(d\) (the sheaf of differentials has rank \(d\), preserved by base change), so each component has dimension \(d\). Hence \(X_k\) is of pure dimension \(d\). Since \(X_j\) is open and closed in \(X_k\), it is a union of irreducible components of \(X_k\), hence of pure dimension \(d\); so \(U_j\times_{F'}k\) is of pure dimension \(d\). Finally, \(U_j\) is smooth, hence normal and noetherian, so its irreducible components \(C\) are open and closed, and \(U_j\times_{F'}k=\bigsqcup_C (C\times_{F'}k)\) with each \(C\times_{F'}k\) non-empty of pure dimension \(\dim C\). Comparing with the pure dimension \(d\) of \(U_j\times_{F'}k\) gives \(\dim C=d\) for every \(C\). Thus \(U_j\) is of pure dimension \(d\) over \(F'\).

**Step 7 (geometric connectedness of \(U_j\)).** Put \(A_j:=\Gamma(U_j,\mathcal O_{U_j})\). Since \(U_j\) is projective, hence proper, over \(F'\), Claim 2 gives \(\dim_{F'}A_j<\infty\), and Claim 1 gives, for every field extension \(K/F'\), a natural isomorphism \(\Gamma(U_j\times_{F'}K,\mathcal O)\cong A_j\otimes_{F'}K\). Taking \(K=k\) and using Step 4 (\(U_j\times_{F'}k\cong X_j\)) and Step 1 (\(\Gamma(X_j,\mathcal O)\cong k\)), we get an isomorphism of \(k\)-algebras \(A_j\otimes_{F'}k \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \Gamma(X_j,\mathcal O)\cong k\). Hence \(\dim_{F'}A_j=\dim_k(A_j\otimes_{F'}k)=1\), and the unit map \(u:F'\to A_j\) becomes, after \(-\otimes_{F'}k\), the structure map \(k\to A_j\otimes_{F'}k\cong k\), which is an isomorphism. Since \(k/F'\) is faithfully flat, a map of \(F'\)-modules that becomes an isomorphism after tensoring with \(k\) is an isomorphism; thus \(u\) is an isomorphism \(F'\xrightarrow{\sim}A_j\). Therefore for every field extension \(K/F'\), \(\Gamma(U_j\times_{F'}K,\mathcal O)\cong A_j\otimes_{F'}K\cong K\), whose only idempotents are \(0,1\); by Claim 0, \(U_j\times_{F'}K\) is connected. This says precisely that \(U_j\) is geometrically connected over \(F'\). (No Chevalley/specialisation argument is needed.)

**Step 8 (conclusion).** Take \(m' := mN\) with \(N=\mathrm{lcm}(n_1,\dots,n_s)\) from Step 3; then \(m'\) is divisible by \(m\), \(F'=\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}\), each \(X_j\) is defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}\) (namely by \(U_j\), with \(U_j\times_{\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}}k\cong X_j\)), and by Steps 5, 6 and 7 each \(U_j\) is smooth, projective (and of pure dimension \(d\)) and geometrically connected over \(\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}\). By Step 4, \(X_{\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}}=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^{s} U_j\), which is the asserted disjoint union of \(s\) smooth projective geometrically connected \(\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}\)-schemes.

It remains only to note the announced equivalence. We have just proved that the first property (each \(X_j\) defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}\) and smooth, projective, geometrically connected over it) implies the second. Conversely, if \(X_{\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}}=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^{s}V_j\) with the \(V_j\) smooth, projective and geometrically connected over \(\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}\), then base change to \(k\) gives \(X_k=\bigsqcup_j (V_j)_k\) with each \((V_j)_k\) connected (geometric connectedness), so the \((V_j)_k\) are exactly the connected components \(X_1,\dots,X_s\) in some order; each \(X_j\) is therefore defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}\), and smoothness, projectivity and geometric connectedness over \(\mathbb F_{q^{m'}}\) hold for the corresponding \(V_j\). This completes the proof. ∎

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(m\ge1\) and \(d\ge2\) be integers, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and let \(\mathcal A\) be an ample line bundle on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Then there exist an integer \(r\ge1\) divisible by \(m\), an integer \(N\ge1\), and a section \(s\in H^0\!\left(X_{\mathbb F_{q^r}},\mathcal A^{\otimes N}\right)\) whose zero scheme \(Y=V(s)\) is an effective Cartier divisor on \(X_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}\) that is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^r}\).
proof:
We keep the notation of the statement: q=p^a, m>=1, d>=2, X smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over k_0:=F_{q^m}, and A an ample line bundle on X defined over k_0. We must produce r>=1 divisible by m, N>=1 and s in H^0(X_{F_{q^r}}, A^{\otimes N}) whose zero scheme is an effective Cartier divisor, smooth, geometrically connected and of pure dimension d-1 over F_{q^r}.

STEP 1 (Bertini over a finite extension).
Put Q:=q^m=p^{am}; then F_{q^m}=F_Q is a finite field of characteristic p, so the proved lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_bertini_finite_extension may be applied with the prime power q replaced by Q. Its hypotheses are satisfied: X is smooth, projective, geometrically connected of pure dimension d>=2 over F_Q, and A is an ample line bundle on X defined over F_Q. The lemma yields integers rho>=1 and N>=1 and a section
   s in H^0(X_{F_{Q^rho}}, A^{\otimes N}),   X_{F_{Q^rho}}:=X x_{Spec F_Q} Spec F_{Q^rho},
whose zero scheme Y:=V(s) is an effective Cartier divisor on X_{F_{Q^rho}}, smooth over F_{Q^rho} and of pure dimension d-1.
Set r:=m*rho and k':=F_{Q^rho}=F_{q^{m rho}}=F_{q^r}. Then r>=1 is divisible by m, N>=1, and s is a global section of A^{\otimes N} on X_{k'}=X_{F_{q^r}} (note X_{F_{Q^rho}}=X_{k'} since F_{Q^rho}=F_{q^r}). Moreover Y is an effective Cartier divisor on X_{k'}, smooth over k', and of pure dimension d-1. Only geometric connectedness remains to be proved.

STEP 2 (Y is an AMPLE divisor).
The k'-scheme X_{k'} is smooth over k' and, X being geometrically connected over k_0 and k'/k_0 being a field extension, connected; a connected regular noetherian scheme is integral, so X_{k'} is integral. The zero scheme of a section s of the invertible sheaf A^{\otimes N} gives the standard exact sequence
   0 -> (A^{\otimes N})^{-1} --x s--> O_{X_{k'}} -> O_Y -> 0,
whence O_{X_{k'}}(Y) \cong A^{\otimes N}.
We check A^{\otimes N} is ample. Since A is ample on the projective k'-scheme X_{k'}, Serre's vanishing theorem and its converse (the cohomological characterisation of ample line bundles on a scheme projective over a field) give: for every coherent sheaf F on X_{k'} and every i>0 one has H^i(X_{k'}, F \otimes A^{\otimes t})=0 for t>>0, and conversely a line bundle satisfying this vanishing is ample. Given F and i>0, applying this vanishing with t=Nn gives H^i(X_{k'}, F\otimes A^{\otimes Nn})=0 for n>>0 (as Nn->infty with n). Thus A^{\otimes N} satisfies the same characterisation, hence is ample. Consequently Y is an effective ample Cartier divisor on X_{k'}.

STEP 3 (Base change to an algebraic closure).
Let \bar k:=\overline{F_{q^r}}. Since Spec \bar k -> Spec k' is flat:
(a) Y_{\bar k}:=Y x_{k'} \bar k = V(s_{\bar k}) is an effective Cartier divisor on X_{\bar k}:=X_{k'} x_{k'} \bar k, with O(Y_{\bar k}) \cong (A^{\otimes N})_{\bar k}.
(b) (A^{\otimes N})_{\bar k} is ample: by Step 2 and the same Serre-criterion argument, (A^{\otimes N})^{\otimes t} is ample for t>>0, hence very ample for t>>0 (a sufficiently high power of an ample line bundle on a projective k'-scheme is very ample); thus for such t there is a closed immersion j:X_{k'} -> P^V_{k'} with (A^{\otimes N})^{\otimes t}=j^*O(1). Base change preserves closed immersions, so j_{\bar k}:X_{\bar k} -> P^V_{\bar k} is a closed immersion with ((A^{\otimes N})_{\bar k})^{\otimes t}=j_{\bar k}^*O(1), which is ample; by the closure of ampleness under taking roots (Serre criterion again), (A^{\otimes N})_{\bar k} is ample.
(c) Y_{\bar k} is smooth of pure dimension d-1 over \bar k: smoothness is stable under base change; for the dimension, if Z is an irreducible component of Y_{\bar k} then its image Z_0 in Y is an irreducible component (the projection is closed and surjective, and Z is maximal with this property), and for a field extension the dimension of every irreducible component of W x_{k'} \bar k equals dim W_0 for the finite type k'-scheme W_0; hence dim Z = dim Z_0 = d-1.
(d) Y_{\bar k} is nonempty: Y has pure dimension d-1>=1, so Y\neq\emptyset; a nonempty scheme of finite type over a field stays nonempty after any field extension (take a closed point: the tensor product of a nonzero finite-dimensional k'-algebra with \bar k is a nonzero \bar k-algebra).
(e) Y_{\bar k} \neq X_{\bar k}: dim Y_{\bar k}=d-1 < d = dim X_{\bar k}, while X_{\bar k} is equidimensional of dimension d and nonempty.
(f) X_{\bar k} is smooth, projective and connected over \bar k (connectedness is exactly geometric connectedness of X_{k'}/k', which holds because X is geometrically connected over k_0 and k'/k_0 is a field extension). Thus X_{\bar k} is a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d>=2 over the algebraically closed field \bar k.

STEP 4 (Degree-zero Lefschetz isomorphism).
Fix a prime \ell\neq p (e.g. \ell=2 if p\neq2 and \ell=3 if p=2). Applying Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_420 to X_{\bar k}/\bar k and the divisor Y_{\bar k}\subsetneq X_{\bar k} -- all its hypotheses were verified in Step 3 -- we obtain that for every integer m<d-1 the pullback
   i^*: H^m_et(X_{\bar k},Q_\ell) -> H^m_et(Y_{\bar k},Q_\ell)
is an isomorphism. Since d>=2 we have 0<d-1, so m=0 is admissible:
   i^*: H^0_et(X_{\bar k},Q_\ell) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^0_et(Y_{\bar k},Q_\ell).

STEP 5 (H^0 of a smooth scheme over an algebraically closed field counts components).
Claim. Let \kappa be algebraically closed, let Z be a scheme of finite type and smooth over \kappa, and let \ell\neq char\kappa. Then H^0_et(Z,Q_\ell) \cong Q_\ell^{\pi_0(Z)}; in particular dim_{Q_\ell} H^0_et(Z,Q_\ell)=#\pi_0(Z).
Proof of the claim. Z is noetherian, so \pi_0(Z)={Z_1,...,Z_t} is finite; each Z_j is closed, and since there are only finitely many components each Z_j is also open. Hence Z=\coprod_j Z_j and the étale topos decomposes, giving H^0_et(Z,-)=\prod_j H^0_et(Z_j,-).
Next, for any set S the étale sheaf \underline S associated to the constant presheaf S is, on the site of locally noetherian \kappa-schemes, the sheaf U\mapsto{Zariski-locally constant functions U->S}: indeed (i) this presheaf is an étale sheaf, because if p:V->U is surjective étale with U,V locally noetherian and f:U->S has f\circ p locally constant, then p is open and surjective, so f^{-1}(s) is open for every s, i.e. f is locally constant; (ii) it is the sheafification of the constant presheaf, because every object U of the site is noetherian and hence a finite disjoint union of its open-and-closed connected components, on each of which the presheaf already takes the value S.
Therefore H^0_et(Z_j,\underline S) is the set of locally constant S-valued functions on the connected space Z_j, namely S. Applying this with S=Q_\ell (as a set) gives H^0_et(Z_j,Q_\ell)=Q_\ell for each j (equivalently, H^0_et(Z_j,Q_\ell)=colim_\nu H^0_et(Z_j,Z/\ell^\nu\mathbb Z)=colim_\nu Z/\ell^\nu\mathbb Z=Q_\ell, using that Z_j is quasi-compact and quasi-separated so that H^0 commutes with filtered colimits of sheaves). Hence H^0_et(Z,Q_\ell)=\prod_{j=1}^t Q_\ell=Q_\ell^{\pi_0(Z)}. This proves the claim.

STEP 6 (Y is geometrically connected).
Apply the claim of Step 5 to Z=X_{\bar k}, which is connected by Step 3(f): H^0_et(X_{\bar k},Q_\ell)\cong Q_\ell. By the isomorphism of Step 4, dim_{Q_\ell} H^0_et(Y_{\bar k},Q_\ell)=1. Applying the claim to Z=Y_{\bar k} (smooth of finite type over \bar k by Step 3(c)) gives #\pi_0(Y_{\bar k})=1. In particular Y_{\bar k}\neq\emptyset and Y_{\bar k} is connected, which is precisely the statement that Y is geometrically connected over k'.

STEP 7 (Conclusion).
With r=m\rho (divisible by m), the integer N>=1 and the section s\in H^0(X_{F_{q^r}},A^{\otimes N}) of Step 1, the zero scheme Y=V(s) is: an effective Cartier divisor on X_{F_{q^r}} (Step 1), smooth over F_{q^r} (Step 1), of pure dimension d-1 over F_{q^r} (Step 1), and geometrically connected over F_{q^r} (Step 6). This is exactly the required conclusion. QED.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be prime, let m>=1, and put k=overline(F_q). Let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension 2 over F_{q^m}. Then the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (id_{X_k} x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k, Q_ell) for every integer n>=0 with n != 2.
proof:
Fix a prime power q=p^a, a prime \ell\neq p, and write k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q. We must show: for every m\ge 1 and every smooth projective geometrically connected variety X of pure dimension 2 over \mathbb F_{q^m}, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius F_m=(\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*, \sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every n\ge 0 with n\neq 2.

STEP 0 (Preliminaries: the objects we speak about are finite dimensional, and the range of n is bounded).
Let X be as above, of pure dimension 2 over \mathbb F_{q^m}. Since X is proper over the finite field \mathbb F_{q^m}, with structure morphism f:X\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^m}, the constant sheaf \mathbb Q_\ell on X_k carries its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism, so eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob applies (with the base field \mathbb F_{q^m} in place of \mathbb F_q; this is legitimate because \mathbb F_{q^m}=\mathbb F_{p^{am}} is again a finite field, and the lemma is a statement about a proper variety over an arbitrary finite field): each H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is a finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space, and the lemma equips it with a canonical \mathbb Q_\ell-linear arithmetic Frobenius automorphism, which under the Ext-identification is u\mapsto\psi\circ f^*(u)\circ\psi^{-1}; this canonical automorphism is precisely the operator (\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*, \sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, appearing in the statement. Hence "F_m is semisimple" is an assertion about an automorphism of a finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector space.
Moreover, X_k is projective over the algebraically closed field k and equidimensional of dimension 2, so by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_projective_cohomology_vanishes_above_twice_dimension, H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0 for every n>4. Thus the only degrees in which the assertion is not vacuous are n\in\{0,1,3,4\}; the degrees n\ge 5 are trivially semisimple (the zero operator on the zero space is diagonalisable). This observation is only a sanity check on the range: the argument below covers all n\neq 2 at once.

STEP 1 (Reduction to a compactly supported vanishing statement).
Consider the following assertion (\star):
  for every integer t\ge 1, every smooth projective geometrically connected surface X' over \mathbb F_{q^t}, and every effective ample divisor Y'\subset X' defined over \mathbb F_{q^t} that is smooth of pure dimension 1, putting U'=X'\setminus Y', one has H^j_{c,\mathrm{\acute et}}(U'_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0 for every integer j<2.
The lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_379_surface_away_from_middle states exactly: if (\star) holds, then for every integer m\ge 1 and every smooth projective geometrically connected surface X over \mathbb F_{q^m}, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*, \sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for every n\ge 0 with n\neq 2. This is verbatim the target statement (same q, same \ell, same k, same normalisation of the Frobenius, same range of degrees). Therefore it suffices to prove (\star).

STEP 2 (Verification of (\star): setup).
Let t\ge 1 be arbitrary; put Q:=q^t=p^{at}, which is again a prime power, and let X' be a smooth projective geometrically connected surface over \mathbb F_{Q}=\mathbb F_{q^t}. Let Y'\subset X' be an effective ample divisor defined over \mathbb F_{Q} which is smooth of pure dimension 1 over \mathbb F_{Q}, and set U'=X'\setminus Y' with open immersion j:U'\hookrightarrow X'. We must prove H^j_{c,\mathrm{\acute et}}(U'_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0 for j<2.

We first check the three hypotheses of Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_hc_vanishing_ample_complement that are not literally identical to what we are given: non-emptiness of Y', the Cartier property, and Y'\subsetneq X'.
