STEP 2a (X' is integral and H^0(X',\mathcal O_{X'})=\mathbb F_{Q}).
X' is smooth over the field \mathbb F_{Q}, hence regular; regular local rings are domains, so X' is locally integral, and for a locally Noetherian locally integral scheme the irreducible components coincide with the connected components. Since X' is geometrically connected over \mathbb F_{Q} it is connected, hence integral; it is reduced because it is smooth (hence geometrically reduced) over a field. Since X' is proper over \mathbb F_{Q}, the \mathbb F_{Q}-algebra H^0(X',\mathcal O_{X'}) is a finite \mathbb F_{Q}-algebra (standard finiteness for proper morphisms); as X' is reduced and connected it is a finite field extension L/\mathbb F_{Q}. If L were strictly larger than \mathbb F_{Q}, then L\otimes_{\mathbb F_{Q}}\overline{\mathbb F}_{\mathbb Q} would be a product of [L:\mathbb F_{Q}]>1 copies of \overline{\mathbb F}_{\mathbb Q} (\mathbb F_{Q} is perfect, so L/\mathbb F_{Q} is separable), which would make H^0(X'_{\overline{\mathbb F}_{\mathbb Q}},\mathcal O) a product of more than one field, i.e. X'_{\overline{\mathbb F}_{\mathbb Q}} disconnected, contradicting geometric connectedness. Hence H^0(X',\mathcal O_{X'})=\mathbb F_{Q}.

STEP 2b (Y' is nonempty).
Let \mathcal A:=\mathcal O_{X'}(Y') be the ample invertible sheaf associated with the effective divisor Y'. The exact sequence of an effective Cartier/Weil divisor 0\to\mathcal O_{X'}(-Y')\to\mathcal O_{X'}\to\mathcal O_{Y'}\to 0 shows that Y'=\varnothing if and only if \mathcal O_{X'}(-Y')=\mathcal O_{X'}, i.e. if and only if \mathcal A\simeq\mathcal O_{X'}. Suppose for contradiction that Y'=\varnothing. Then \mathcal O_{X'} is ample on X'. Since \dim X'=2>0, X' has a closed point x; let \mathcal I_x\subset\mathcal O_{X'} be its ideal sheaf, a coherent \mathcal O_{X'}-module. By Serre's characterisation of ampleness, for every coherent sheaf \mathcal F on X' the twist \mathcal F\otimes\mathcal O_{X'}^{\otimes n}=\mathcal F is generated by global sections for n\gg 0; applying this to \mathcal F=\mathcal I_x says that \mathcal I_x is globally generated. Taking the stalk at x, the evaluation map H^0(X',\mathcal I_x)\to \mathcal I_{x,x}/\mathfrak m_x\mathcal I_{x,x} must then be surjective. But H^0(X',\mathcal I_x)=\{g\in H^0(X',\mathcal O_{X'}):g(x)=0\}=\{g\in\mathbb F_{Q}:g=0\}=0 by Step 2a (a constant function vanishing at one point is zero). On the other hand \mathcal I_{x,x} is the maximal ideal of the regular local ring \mathcal O_{X',x} of dimension 2, hence is nonzero, so \mathcal I_{x,x}/\mathfrak m_x\mathcal I_{x,x}\neq 0. A surjection 0\twoheadrightarrow \mathcal I_{x,x}/\mathfrak m_x\mathcal I_{x,x} is impossible. This contradiction proves Y'\neq\varnothing. (Equivalently: \mathcal O_{X'} ample forces X' affine by Serre's criterion for affineness, and X' would then be both affine and proper over \mathbb F_{Q}, hence finite over \mathbb F_{Q}, of dimension 0, contradiction.)

STEP 2c (Y' is an effective ample Cartier divisor, and Y'\subsetneq X').
By hypothesis Y' is an effective ample divisor on X'. If one reads "divisor" as a Weil divisor, then since X' is smooth over a field it is regular, and regular local rings are unique factorisation domains (Auslander--Buchsbaum), so every Weil divisor on X' is Cartier; hence Y' is an effective ample Cartier divisor. If one reads "effective ample divisor" as already meaning an effective Cartier divisor with ample associated invertible sheaf, nothing needs to be shown. In either reading, Y' is an effective ample Cartier divisor on X', defined over \mathbb F_{Q}, nonempty by Step 2b. Finally Y'\subsetneq X' because Y' is of pure dimension 1 while X' is of pure dimension 2, so they cannot be equal as sets.

STEP 2d (Applying the ample-complement vanishing).
We now apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_hc_vanishing_ample_complement with the base field taken to be \mathbb F_{Q}=\mathbb F_{p^{at}} (the lemma is stated for a prime power, and Q=p^{at} is a prime power; this is simply the substitution q\leftarrow q^t, a\leftarrow at), with X:=X', Y:=Y', d:=2, and \ell as given (\ell\neq p). Its hypotheses are all satisfied:
 - Q=p^{at} is a prime power and \ell\neq p;
 - X' is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d=2\ge 2 over \mathbb F_{Q};
 - Y'\subsetneq X' is a nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor defined over \mathbb F_{Q} (Steps 2b, 2c);
 - Y' is smooth of pure dimension d-1=1 over \mathbb F_{Q} (hypothesis of (\star)).
The lemma then yields H^j_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U'_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0 for every integer j<d=2, where k denotes an algebraic closure of \mathbb F_{Q}. But \mathbb F_{q^t}\subset\overline{\mathbb F}_q is a subfield, and \overline{\mathbb F}_q is algebraic over \mathbb F_{q^t} and algebraically closed, hence is an algebraic closure of \mathbb F_{q^t}; so we may and do identify k=\overline{\mathbb F}_{q^t}=\overline{\mathbb F}_q, and under this identification U'_k is exactly the base change U'_{\overline{\mathbb F}_q} appearing in (\star). Thus H^j_{c,\mathrm{\acute et}}(U'_{\overline{\mathbb F}_q},\mathbb Q_\ell)=0 for all j<2, which is the required conclusion of (\star). Since t, X' and Y' were arbitrary, (\star) is established.

STEP 3 (Conclusion).
Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_379_surface_away_from_middle to (\star), we obtain: for every integer m\ge 1 and every smooth projective geometrically connected surface X over \mathbb F_{q^m}, the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (\mathrm{id}_{X_{\overline{\mathbb F}_q}}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*, \sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_{\overline{\mathbb F}_q},\mathbb Q_\ell) for every integer n\ge 0 with n\neq 2. This is exactly the statement to be proved. (For n\ge 5 the groups vanish by Step 0, so the content is in degrees 0,1,3,4, all of which are covered by the cited lemma.)

This completes the proof. The genuine obstruction to the full conjecture for surfaces is thereby isolated in the middle degree n=2, which is not addressed here.

statement: Let \(\ell\) be a prime, let \(\iota:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\) be an embedding, let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space, and let \(T\in\operatorname{GL}_{\mathbb Q_\ell}(V)\). Suppose there exist real numbers \(C>0\) and \(R>0\) such that \(\left|\iota\!\left(\operatorname{Tr}_V(T^n)\right)\right|\le C\,R^{n}\) for every integer \(n\ge 1\). Then every eigenvalue \(\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) of \(T\) on \(V\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) satisfies \(|\iota(\alpha)|\le R\).
proof:
We prove the statement by a purely analytic (linear-algebraic) argument; no geometry and no semisimplicity hypothesis is used.

=== 0. Setup and the vacuous case ===
Put k := Q_\ell and \bar k := \overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell, and let N := dim_k V.

If N = 0, then V \otimes_k \bar k = 0 has no eigenvalues at all, so the conclusion "every eigenvalue \alpha satisfies |\iota(\alpha)| \le R" is vacuously true. Henceforth assume N \ge 1.

Let \chi_T(t) \in k[t] be the characteristic polynomial of T. Since \bar k is algebraically closed, \chi_T splits over \bar k; write its distinct roots as \beta_1,\dots,\beta_s \in \bar k with algebraic multiplicities d_1,\dots,d_s \in \mathbb Z_{>0}. Thus
  \chi_T(t) = \prod_{j=1}^{s} (t-\beta_j)^{d_j},   \qquad \sum_{j=1}^{s} d_j = N.   (1)
The characteristic polynomial is computed in any k-basis of V, and the matrix of T \otimes \mathrm{id}_{\bar k} in the induced \bar k-basis is the same matrix; hence \chi_{T\otimes\mathrm{id}} = \chi_T. So the eigenvalues of T on V\otimes_k\bar k are exactly \beta_1,\dots,\beta_s with the same multiplicities d_j, as the statement requires.

Because T \in \mathrm{GL}_k(V), \det(T) \neq 0, and \prod_{j} \beta_j^{d_j} = (-1)^N \det(T) \neq 0; hence
  \beta_j \neq 0 \quad\text{for every } j.   (2)

=== 1. The trace identity ===
Fix n \ge 1. We claim
  \operatorname{Tr}_V(T^n) = \sum_{j=1}^{s} d_j\, \beta_j^{n}   \quad \text{in } \bar k.   (3)

Justification. Trace is unchanged by the scalar extension k \to \bar k (same matrix in the extended basis), so \iota(\operatorname{Tr}_V(T^n)) = \iota(\operatorname{Tr}_{\bar k}(T^n\otimes\mathrm{id})). To identify the eigenvalues of T^n\otimes\mathrm{id} we invoke part (2) of eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_69. That lemma is stated for a nonzero finite-dimensional k-vector space equipped with a perfect bilinear pairing and a scalar c\in k^\times; these auxiliary data do not enter the assertion of its part (2), and they are available here because V\neq 0: choose a k-basis e_1,\dots,e_N of V and set \langle v,w\rangle := \sum_{i=1}^N v_i w_i (coordinates in that basis), which is a perfect pairing, and take c := 1. Applying part (2) of that lemma to the operator T and to the Laurent polynomial P(t) := t^n \in k[t^{\pm 1}], and using (2) to ensure the \beta_j lie in \bar k^\times as that part requires, we obtain: the eigenvalues of T^n on V\otimes_k\bar k, counted with algebraic multiplicity, are \beta_1^n,\dots,\beta_s^n with the same multiplicities d_1,\dots,d_s.

For completeness we record the elementary reason for this special case, so that the identity (3) is fully justified here. Over \bar k, since \chi_T splits, T\otimes\mathrm{id} is represented by an upper-triangular matrix whose diagonal, in a suitable ordering, is \beta_1,\dots,\beta_1 (d_1 times), \beta_2,\dots (d_2 times), etc. Then (T\otimes\mathrm{id})^n is again upper triangular, with diagonal entries the n-th powers of the diagonal entries of T\otimes\mathrm{id}; the trace of an upper-triangular matrix is the sum of its diagonal entries. Hence
  \operatorname{Tr}_{\bar k}(T^n\otimes\mathrm{id}) = \sum_{j=1}^{s} d_j \beta_j^n,\nwhich is (3).

Applying \iota (a field homomorphism \bar k\hookrightarrow\mathbb C) gives
  \iota(\operatorname{Tr}_V(T^n)) = \sum_{j=1}^{s} d_j\, \iota(\beta_j)^{n} \in \mathbb C.   (4)

=== 2. Grouping by complex modulus ===
For each j put r_j := |\iota(\beta_j)| \in \mathbb R_{>0} (strictly positive by (2)). Let
  \rho_1 > \rho_2 > \cdots > \rho_t \ (>0)   (5)\nbe the distinct values among \{r_1,\dots,r_s\}, listed in strictly decreasing order; t \ge 1 since s\ge 1. For 1\le i\le t set
  J_i := \{\, j \in \{1,\dots,s\} : r_j = \rho_i \,\},\nso that \{J_1,\dots,J_t\} partitions \{1,\dots,s\}. For j \in J_i define
  z_j := \iota(\beta_j)/\rho_i \in \mathbb C, \qquad |z_j| = r_j/\rho_i = 1.   (6)
Thus each z_j lies on the unit circle \mathbb S^1 \subset \mathbb C^\times. For 1\le i\le t and n\ge 1 define the finite exponential sum
  S_i(n) := \sum_{j\in J_i} d_j\, z_j^{\,n} \in \mathbb C.   (7)
Then \iota(\beta_j)^n = \rho_i^{\,n} z_j^{\,n} for j\in J_i, and (4) becomes
  \iota(\operatorname{Tr}_V(T^n)) = \sum_{i=1}^{t} \rho_i^{\,n} S_i(n).   (8)
Two elementary bounds, valid for all n\ge 1 and all i, will be used repeatedly:
  |S_i(n)| \le D_i := \sum_{j\in J_i} d_j, \qquad \text{and} \qquad \sum_{i=1}^{t} D_i = \sum_{j=1}^{s} d_j = N.   (9)
(The first is the triangle inequality together with |z_j|=1; the second is (1).)

=== 3. Mean-square orthogonality: limsup_n |S_i(n)| > 0 ===
Fix i with 1\le i\le t. Write M_i := \sum_{j\in J_i} d_j^{2}. Since J_i\neq\emptyset and each d_j\ge 1, we have
  M_i \ge 1 > 0.   (10)
We first compute the Cesàro mean of |S_i(n)|^2. By (7),
  |S_i(n)|^2 = S_i(n)\,\overline{S_i(n)} = \sum_{j\in J_i}\sum_{j'\in J_i} d_j d_{j'}\, z_j^{\,n}\, \overline{z_{j'}^{\,n}} = \sum_{j,j'\in J_i} d_j d_{j'}\, w_{jj'}^{\,n},\nwhere w_{jj'} := z_j\overline{z_{j'}} satisfies |w_{jj'}| = 1 by (6). Hence for N_0\ge 1,
  \frac{1}{N_0}\sum_{n=1}^{N_0} |S_i(n)|^2 = \sum_{j,j'\in J_i} d_j d_{j'}\, A_{jj'}(N_0), \qquad A_{jj'}(N_0) := \frac1{N_0}\sum_{n=1}^{N_0} w_{jj'}^{\,n}.   (11)
We evaluate the two kinds of terms.
(a) If w_{jj'} = 1, then A_{jj'}(N_0) = \frac1{N_0}\cdot N_0 = 1 for every N_0.
(b) If w_{jj'}\neq 1, then w_{jj'}-1\neq 0 and the geometric sum gives
  \Bigl|\sum_{n=1}^{N_0} w_{jj'}^{\,n}\Bigr| = \Bigl|\frac{w_{jj'}(1-w_{jj'}^{N_0})}{1-w_{jj'}}\Bigr| \le \frac{|w_{jj'}|+|w_{jj'}|^{N_0}}{|1-w_{jj'}|} = \frac{2}{|1-w_{jj'}|},\nusing |w_{jj'}|=1. Therefore |A_{jj'}(N_0)| \le \frac{2}{N_0\,|1-w_{jj'}|} \xrightarrow[N_0\to\infty]{} 0.
Since the index set J_i\times J_i is finite, passing to the limit in (11) yields
  \lim_{N_0\to\infty} \frac1{N_0}\sum_{n=1}^{N_0} |S_i(n)|^2 = \sum_{\substack{j,j'\in J_i\\ w_{jj'}=1}} d_j d_{j'}.   (12)
Now w_{jj'}=1 means z_j\overline{z_{j'}}=1, i.e. z_j = z_{j'} (as |z_{j'}|=1 gives \overline{z_{j'}}=z_{j'}^{-1}). For distinct indices j\neq j' in J_i we have \beta_j\neq\beta_j' (the \beta_j are the *distinct* eigenvalues), hence \iota(\beta_j)\neq\iota(\beta_{j'}) and therefore z_j = \iota(\beta_j)/\rho_i \neq \iota(\beta_{j'})/\rho_i = z_{j'}. So w_{jj'}=1 occurs exactly when j=j'. Thus the right-hand side of (12) equals \sum_{j\in J_i} d_j^2 = M_i, and
  \lim_{N_0\to\infty} \frac1{N_0}\sum_{n=1}^{N_0} |S_i(n)|^2 = M_i > 0.   (13)
Finally, let L_i := \limsup_{n\to\infty} |S_i(n)|^2 \in [0,\infty]. For any sequence of non-negative reals a_n with limsup L, and any \varepsilon>0, one has a_n \le L+\varepsilon for all sufficiently large n, whence \limsup_{N_0}\frac1{N_0}\sum_{n=1}^{N_0} a_n \le L+\varepsilon; letting \varepsilon\to 0 gives \lim_{N_0}\frac1{N_0}\sum_{n=1}^{N_0} a_n \le L (the limit on the left exists by (13)). Applying this to a_n = |S_i(n)|^2 and using (13):
  M_i \le \limsup_{n\to\infty} |S_i(n)|^2, \qquad\text{so}\qquad \limsup_{n\to\infty} |S_i(n)| \ge \sqrt{M_i} \ge 1 > 0.   (14)
In particular, for \delta_i := \sqrt{M_i}/2 > 0 there exist infinitely many integers n with |S_i(n)| > \delta_i.   (15)

=== 4. The dominant term: limsup_n |\iota(\operatorname{Tr}_V(T^n))|^{1/n} = \rho_1 ===

Upper bound. By (8) and (9), for every n\ge 1,
  |\iota(\operatorname{Tr}_V(T^n))| \le \sum_{i=1}^{t} \rho_i^{\,n} |S_i(n)| \le \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{t} D_i\Bigr) \rho_1^{\,n} = N\,\rho_1^{\,n}.
Taking n-th roots and letting n\to\infty (N^{1/n}\to 1 since N\ge 1 is fixed):
  \limsup_{n\to\infty} |\iota(\operatorname{Tr}_V(T^n))|^{1/n} \le \rho_1.   (16)

Lower bound. By (15) applied to i=1, choose a strictly increasing sequence of integers n_1<n_2<\cdots with |S_1(n_k)| > \delta_1 for all k. Using (8) and (9),
  |\iota(\operatorname{Tr}_V(T^{n}))| \ge \rho_1^{\,n}\Bigl(|S_1(n)| - \sum_{i=2}^{t} (\rho_i/\rho_1)^{n} |S_i(n)|\Bigr) \ge \rho_1^{\,n}\Bigl(|S_1(n)| - \sum_{i=2}^{t} D_i (\rho_i/\rho_1)^{n}\Bigr).
By (5), \rho_i/\rho_1 < 1 for every i\ge 2, so \sum_{i=2}^{t} D_i(\rho_i/\rho_1)^{n} \to 0 as n\to\infty (a finite sum of geometric sequences with ratio <1; the sum is empty and equal to 0 when t=1). Choose n_0 such that this sum is < \delta_1/2 for all n\ge n_0. Passing to the subsequence n_k with n_k\ge n_0 (possible since n_k\to\infty),
  |\iota(\operatorname{Tr}_V(T^{n_k}))| \ge \rho_1^{\,n_k}\bigl(\delta_1 - \delta_1/2\bigr) = (\delta_1/2)\, \rho_1^{\,n_k}.   (17)
Since \delta_1/2 > 0 and \rho_1 > 0, taking n_k-th roots gives
  |\iota(\operatorname{Tr}_V(T^{n_k}))|^{1/n_k} \ge (\delta_1/2)^{1/n_k}\, \rho_1 \xrightarrow[k\to\infty]{} \rho_1,\nas x^{1/n_k}\to 1 for every fixed x>0. Hence
  \limsup_{n\to\infty} |\iota(\operatorname{Tr}_V(T^n))|^{1/n} \ge \rho_1.   (18)
Combining (16) and (18):
  \limsup_{n\to\infty} |\iota(\operatorname{Tr}_V(T^n))|^{1/n} = \rho_1.   (19)

=== 5. Conclusion ===
By hypothesis there are C>0 and R>0 with |\iota(\operatorname{Tr}_V(T^n))| \le C R^{n} for all n\ge 1. Taking n-th roots, using R>0 and C>0,
  |\iota(\operatorname{Tr}_V(T^n))|^{1/n} \le C^{1/n} R,\nand since C^{1/n}\to 1,
  \limsup_{n\to\infty} |\iota(\operatorname{Tr}_V(T^n))|^{1/n} \le R.   (20)
From (19) and (20) we obtain \rho_1 \le R. Now let \alpha \in \bar k be any eigenvalue of T on V\otimes_k\bar k; then \alpha = \beta_j for some j, and with i such that j\in J_i,
  |\iota(\alpha)| = |\iota(\beta_j)| = \rho_i \le \rho_1 \le R\nby (5). This is exactly the required conclusion, and the proof is complete. \quad\blacksquare

Remark on the argument, as required by the guidance: the key point is the mean-square orthogonality (13), which rules out the possibility that a dominant group of terms cancels identically; the coefficients d_j are positive integers and the characters n\mapsto z_j^{\,n} are orthogonal on the unit circle for distinct z_j, so no cancellation can make all S_i(n) small. No Kronecker/subsequence argument tending to 1 is used, no semisimplicity of T is assumed (the trace identity (3) holds with multiplicities for arbitrary T), and no assertion is made that \iota(\mathbb Q_\ell)\subset\mathbb R; all conjugations are complex conjugations in \mathbb C of the numbers \iota(\beta_j).

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), and fix an embedding \(\iota:\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\). Let \(r\ge1\) and let \(C_1,\dots,C_r\) be smooth projective geometrically connected curves over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). Suppose that for every \(j\) and every eigenvalue \(\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) of the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius on \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((C_j)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) one has \(\iota(\alpha)\overline{\iota(\alpha)}=q^m\). Then for every integer \(n\ge0\) and every eigenvalue \(\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) of the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((C_1\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\cdots\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}C_r)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\), one has \(\iota(\alpha)\overline{\iota(\alpha)}=q^{mn}\).
proof:
We write \(\mathbb F:=\mathbb F_{q^m}\) for the ground field and \(\sigma:k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\to k\), \(\sigma(c)=c^{q^m}\), for its \(q^m\)-power automorphism. Since \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\subset \overline{\mathbb F}_q\) and \(\overline{\mathbb F}_q\) is algebraic and separable over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), \(k\) is an algebraic closure of \(\mathbb F\), and \(\sigma\) is the \(q^m\)-power Frobenius automorphism of that algebraic closure. For a scheme \(Z\) over \(\mathbb F\) we write \(F_Z=(\mathrm{id}_{Z_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma)^*\) for the induced \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-linear automorphism of \(H^*_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\); this is a well-defined automorphism by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a (applied with the prime power \(q\) replaced by the prime power \(q^m=p^{am}\)), and it is invertible with inverse the geometric Frobenius pullback. Put \(X=C_1\times_{\mathbb F}\cdots\times_{\mathbb F}C_r\); each \(C_j\) and each partial product is smooth projective over \(\mathbb F\), hence proper, so eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob guarantees that every \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((C_j)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) and \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is finite-dimensional over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\); in particular the characteristic polynomials of the Frobenius operators are defined and their roots (the eigenvalues) lie in \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\).

STEP 1. Two pieces of linear algebra.

(1a) Direct sums. If \(V=\bigoplus_{\lambda}V_\lambda\) is a finite direct sum of \(K\)-subspaces stable under \(A\in\operatorname{End}_K(V)\), then \(\chi_A(t)=\prod_\lambda\chi_{A|_{V_\lambda}}(t)\): take the block-diagonal matrix of \(A\) in a basis adapted to the decomposition. Hence the multiset of eigenvalues of \(A\) on \(V\) (in \(\overline K\), with algebraic multiplicity) is the disjoint union of the multisets for the \(V_\lambda\).

(1b) Tensor products. Let \(K\) be a field, \(\overline K\) an algebraic closure, \(V,W\) finite-dimensional \(K\)-vector spaces, \(T\in\operatorname{End}_K(V)\), \(S\in\operatorname{End}_K(W)\). Then the multiset of eigenvalues of \(T\otimes S\) on \(V\otimes_K W\) is \(\{\alpha\beta:\alpha\in\operatorname{Spec}(T),\ \beta\in\operatorname{Spec}(S)\}\), counted with multiplicity. Proof: extend scalars to \(\overline K\) (the characteristic polynomial is unchanged by extension of scalars, since it is computed from a matrix with entries in \(K\)), and triangularise. Triangularisability over an algebraically closed field: induct on \(\dim U\) for \(A\in\operatorname{End}_{\overline K}(U)\); for \(\dim U>0\) the characteristic polynomial of \(A\) splits, so \(A\) has an eigenvector \(e_1\) with eigenvalue \(\alpha\); \(A\) induces \(\bar A\) on \(U/\overline Ke_1\), which by induction has a basis \(\bar e_2,\dots,\bar e_d\) with upper-triangular matrix; lifting to \(e_2,\dots,e_d\in U\), one has \(Ae_k=\sum_{l\le k}c_{kl}e_l+\mu_k e_1\), so \(e_1,\dots,e_d\) is a basis in which \(A\) is upper triangular with diagonal \(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_d\) (the eigenvalues with multiplicity). Applying this to \(T\) and \(S\) gives bases \((v_i)\), \((w_k)\) with upper-triangular matrices \(A=(a_{ij})\), \(B=(b_{kl})\). In the lexicographically ordered tensor basis \((v_i\otimes w_k)\) the matrix of \(T\otimes S\) has entries \((T\otimes S)_{(i,k),(j,l)}=a_{ij}b_{kl}\), which vanishes unless \(i\ge j\) and \(k\ge l\), i.e. unless \((i,k)\ge (j,l)\) lexicographically; so the matrix is upper triangular with diagonal entries \(a_{ii}b_{kk}=\alpha_i\beta_k\). Hence \(\chi_{T\otimes S}(t)=\prod_{i,k}(t-\alpha_i\beta_k)\). \(\square\)

(1c) Multiplicativity of the norm. For \(z,w\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), \(\iota(zw)=\iota(z)\iota(w)\) since \(\iota\) is a field homomorphism, and complex conjugation is multiplicative with \(\overline{zw}=\bar z\bar w\); hence \(\iota(zw)\overline{\iota(zw)}=\big(\iota(z)\overline{\iota(z)}\big)\big(\iota(w)\overline{\iota(w)}\big)\). Also, for the positive rational number \(q^{mt}\), \(\iota\) fixes it, so \(\iota(q^{mt})\overline{\iota(q^{mt})}=q^{2mt}\).

STEP 2. Eigenvalues of Frobenius on the cohomology of a single curve.
Fix \(j\in\{1,\dots,r\}\) and write \(V_j^i=H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((C_j)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). We claim:
(*) for every \(i\ge 0\), every eigenvalue \(\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) of \(F_{C_j}\) on \(V_j^i\) satisfies \(\iota(\alpha)\overline{\iota(\alpha)}=q^{mi}\) (the statement being vacuous when \(V_j^i=0\)).

Case \(i>2\): \(C_j\) is a projective scheme over the algebraically closed field \(k\), equidimensional of dimension \(1\) (smooth, geometrically connected curve), so eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_projective_cohomology_vanishes_above_twice_dimension with \(n=1\) gives \(V_j^i=0\). Vacuous.

Case \(i=0\): \(V_j^0=\Gamma((C_j)_k,\underline{\mathbb Q}_\ell)\) is the \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector space of locally constant functions from the profinite space \(\pi_0((C_j)_k)\) to the discrete group \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Since \(C_j\) is geometrically connected, \((C_j)_k\) is connected, so \(\pi_0\) is a single point and \(V_j^0=\mathbb Q_\ell\cdot 1\) with \(1\) the constant function. The pullback of a section of a constant sheaf along an endomorphism is precomposition with that endomorphism, and precomposition fixes the constant function \(1\). Hence \(F_{C_j}|_{V_j^0}=\mathrm{id}\), its only eigenvalue is \(1\), and \(\iota(1)\overline{\iota(1)}=1=q^{m\cdot 0}\).

Case \(i=2\): apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77(a) to \(Y=C_j\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) with \(d=1\) and \(F=F_{C_j}\). It gives a canonical isomorphism of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces \(\operatorname{tr}:V_j^2\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)\) which is arithmetic-Frobenius-equivariant, where \(F\) acts on \(\mathbb Q_\ell(-1)\) as multiplication by the positive rational number \(q^{m\cdot 1}=q^m\). Thus \(V_j^2\) is \(1\)-dimensional. Let \(e\ne 0\) span it and write \(F_{C_j}e=\lambda e\). Equivariance says \(\operatorname{tr}(F_{C_j}e)=q^m\operatorname{tr}(e)\), i.e. \(\lambda\operatorname{tr}(e)=q^m\operatorname{tr}(e)\); since \(\operatorname{tr}(e)\ne 0\) we get \(\lambda=q^m\). So the only eigenvalue is \(q^m\), and by (1c), \(\iota(q^m)\overline{\iota(q^m)}=q^{2m}=q^{m\cdot 2}\).

Case \(i=1\): this is exactly the hypothesis of the lemma: every eigenvalue \(\alpha\) of \(F_{C_j}\) on \(H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((C_j)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) satisfies \(\iota(\alpha)\overline{\iota(\alpha)}=q^m=q^{m\cdot 1}\).

This proves (*).

STEP 3. Künneth decomposition of the \(r\)-fold product, Frobenius-equivariantly.
For \(1\le s\le r\) put \(X_s=C_1\times_{\mathbb F}\cdots\times_{\mathbb F}C_s\) and consider the iterated cross-product map
\[\kappa_s:\bigoplus_{i_1+\cdots+i_s=n}\;H^{i_1}((C_1)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}\cdots\otimes_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^{i_s}((C_s)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^n((X_s)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\quad x_1\otimes\cdots\otimes x_s\longmapsto \mathrm{pr}_1^*x_1\cup\cdots\cup\mathrm{pr}_s^*x_s .\]
We claim that \(\kappa_s\) is an isomorphism of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces and that \(F_{X_s}\circ\kappa_s=\kappa_s\circ\big(\bigoplus F_{C_1}|_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes F_{C_s}|_{i_s}\big)\), so that each multi-graded summand is \(F_{X_s}\)-stable and \(F_{X_s}\) acts on it as the tensor product of the individual Frobenius operators.

Induction on \(s\). For \(s=1\) this is the identity. For the step, apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_146 to the smooth projective \(\mathbb F\)-schemes \(X=X_s\) and \(Y=C_{s+1}\) (with its prime power \(q\) taken to be \(q^m\)): the map
\[\bigoplus_{a+b=n}H^a((X_s)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\otimes H^b((C_{s+1})_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n((X_{s+1})_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\quad u\otimes y\mapsto \mathrm{pr}_1^*u\cup\mathrm{pr}_2^*y\]\nis an isomorphism under which \(F_{X_{s+1}}\) corresponds to \(F_{X_s}\otimes F_{C_{s+1}}\) on the \((a,b)\)-summand. Substituting the induction hypothesis, \(H^a((X_s)_k)\cong\bigoplus_{i_1+\cdots+i_s=a}\bigotimes_{j\le s}V_j^{i_j}\) as an \(F_{X_s}\)-module, and using that tensor product distributes over finite direct sums, the \((a,b)\)-summand identifies with \(\bigoplus_{i_1+\cdots+i_s=a,\,i_{s+1}=b}\bigotimes_{j\le s+1}V_j^{i_j}\), and \(F_{X_s}\otimes F_{C_{s+1}}\) corresponds, under associativity \((\bigotimes_{j\le s}V_j^{i_j})\otimes V_{s+1}^{i_{s+1}}\cong\bigotimes_{j\le s+1}V_j^{i_j}\), to \(\bigotimes_{j\le s+1}F_{C_j}|_{V_j^{i_j}}\), because associativity of the tensor product is strictly compatible with the operators \((T_1\otimes\cdots\otimes T_s)\otimes T_{s+1}\) and \(T_1\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{s+1}\). Finally the resulting composite equals \(\kappa_{s+1}\): writing \(\mathrm{pr}'_j:X_s\to C_j\) for the projections, we have \(\mathrm{pr}_j^{(s+1)}=\mathrm{pr}'_j\circ\mathrm{pr}_1\) for \(j\le s\), hence \(\mathrm{pr}_1^*(\mathrm{pr}'_1{}^*x_1\cup\cdots\cup\mathrm{pr}'_s{}^*x_s)=\mathrm{pr}_1^{(s+1)*}x_1\cup\cdots\cup\mathrm{pr}_s^{(s+1)*}x_s\) by functoriality of pullback and the fact that pullback is a ring homomorphism; thus \(\mathrm{pr}_1^*u\cup\mathrm{pr}_2^*x_{s+1}=\mathrm{pr}_1^{(s+1)*}x_1\cup\cdots\cup\mathrm{pr}_{s+1}^{(s+1)*}x_{s+1}\). This completes the induction. Taking \(s=r\) (so \(X_r=X\)) gives the claimed decomposition
\[H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\bigoplus_{i_1+\cdots+i_r=n}\;W(i_1,\dots,i_r),\qquad W(i_1,\dots,i_r):=V_1^{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes V_r^{i_r},\]\nas a direct sum of \(F_X\)-stable subspaces on which \(F_X\) acts as \(\bigotimes_j F_{C_j}|_{V_j^{i_j}}\).

STEP 4. Eigenvalue count.
Let \(\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) be an eigenvalue of \(F_X\) on \(H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). If \(n>2r\) then every summand with some \(i_j>2\) vanishes by Step 2 (case \(i>2\)), and there are no tuples \((i_1,\dots,i_r)\) with all \(i_j\le 2\) and \(\sum i_j=n\); hence \(H^n(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) and there is nothing to prove. Assume therefore that some summand is nonzero.

By (1a) applied to the direct-sum decomposition of Step 3, \(\alpha\) is an eigenvalue of \(F_X\) on \(W(i_1,\dots,i_r)\) for some tuple \((i_1,\dots,i_r)\) with \(i_1+\cdots+i_r=n\). By (1b) applied repeatedly, the eigenvalues of \(F_X|_{W(i_1,\dots,i_r)}=\bigotimes_{j=1}^rF_{C_j}|_{V_j^{i_j}}\) are exactly the products \(\alpha_1\cdots\alpha_r\) with \(\alpha_j\) an eigenvalue of \(F_{C_j}\) on \(V_j^{i_j}\). Thus \(\alpha=\alpha_1\cdots\alpha_r\) for such \(\alpha_j\). By (*) each \(\alpha_j\) satisfies \(\iota(\alpha_j)\overline{\iota(\alpha_j)}=q^{mi_j}\) (note that the summand is nonzero, so \(V_j^{i_j}\ne 0\) and \(\alpha_j\) exists). Therefore, using (1c),
\[\iota(\alpha)\overline{\iota(\alpha)}=\prod_{j=1}^r\iota(\alpha_j)\overline{\iota(\alpha_j)}=\prod_{j=1}^r q^{mi_j}=q^{m(i_1+\cdots+i_r)}=q^{mn}.\]

STEP 5. Edge cases. For \(n=0\) the only tuple is \((0,\dots,0)\), \(W(0,\dots,0)=\mathbb Q_\ell\) and \(F_X=\mathrm{id}\), giving the eigenvalue \(1\) with \(\iota(1)\overline{\iota(1)}=1=q^{m\cdot 0}\), consistent with Step 4 (the argument above already covers it, since each \(V_j^0\) is \(1\)-dimensional with eigenvalue \(1\)). The case \(r=1\) is covered verbatim: the Künneth decomposition is the identity decomposition. All eigenvalues are taken in \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\), which is legitimate because each \(H^n\) is finite-dimensional over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) (Step 0), so eigenvalues are roots of characteristic polynomials in \(\mathbb Q_\ell[t]\).

This establishes that for every \(n\ge 0\) and every eigenvalue \(\alpha\in\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) of the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}((C_1\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\cdots\times_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}C_r)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) one has \(\iota(\alpha)\overline{\iota(\alpha)}=q^{mn}\), as required.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge 2\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), and let \(\mathcal L\) be an ample line bundle on \(X\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\). Then there exist integers \(r\ge 1\) and \(m\ge 1\) and a global section \(s\in H^0\!\left(X_{\mathbb F_{q^r}},\mathcal L^{\otimes m}\right)\) whose zero scheme \(Y=V(s)\) is a nonempty effective Cartier divisor on \(X_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}\), smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^r}\).
proof:
We prove the statement in ten steps. Write $X':=X_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}=X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^r}$ once $r$ is chosen, and fix once and for all a prime $\ell\neq p$ (such a prime exists since there are infinitely many primes). Put $k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q$; note that $k$ is also an algebraic closure of $\mathbb F_{q^r}$, because $\mathbb F_q\subseteq\mathbb F_{q^r}\subseteq k$, $k/\mathbb F_{q^r}$ is algebraic, and $k$ is algebraically closed.

Step 1 (Bertini over a finite extension). Apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_bertini_finite_extension to $q$, $X$ and $\mathcal L$ (the hypotheses $d\ge2$, $X$ smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $d$ over $\mathbb F_q$, $\mathcal L$ ample over $\mathbb F_q$ are exactly those of the target). It yields integers $m\ge1$, $r\ge1$ and a section $s\in H^0(X',\mathcal L^{\otimes m})$ whose zero scheme $Y=V(s)$ is an effective Cartier divisor on $X'$, smooth over $\mathbb F_{q^r}$ and of pure dimension $d-1$. We keep this $r,m,s$ and show that $Y$ has the two extra required properties: nonemptiness and geometric connectedness.

Step 2 (properties of $X'$). Smoothness, projectivity, geometric connectedness and pure dimension are all preserved by arbitrary base change of the ground field. Hence $X'$ is smooth, projective, geometrically connected and of pure dimension $d\ge2$ over $\mathbb F_{q^r}$. In particular $X'$ is nonempty (pure dimension $d\ge2$), and $X'$ is integral: $X'$ is smooth over the perfect field $\mathbb F_{q^r}$, so all its local rings are regular local rings, hence domains, i.e. $X'$ is locally integral; a connected locally Noetherian locally integral scheme is integral (its irreducible components are pairwise disjoint and open, so connectedness leaves exactly one, giving irreducibility, and reducedness is local).

Step 3 ($Y$ is nonempty). Suppose for contradiction that $V(s)=\varnothing$. Let $\mathcal M:=\mathcal L^{\otimes m}$; since $\mathcal L$ is ample and $m\ge1$, $\mathcal L^{\otimes n}$ is very ample for all $n\gg0$, so we may choose $N\ge1$ with $\mathcal M^{\otimes N}=\mathcal L^{\otimes mN}$ very ample. Very ampleness gives a closed immersion (closed because $X'$ is proper over $\mathbb F_{q^r}$) $\iota:X'\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^{M}_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}$ with $\mathcal M^{\otimes N}\simeq\iota^{*}\mathcal O(1)$ and with $H^0(\mathbb P^M,\mathcal O(1))\to H^0(X',\mathcal M^{\otimes N})$ surjective. The section $t:=s^{\otimes N}\in H^0(X',\mathcal M^{\otimes N})$ is nowhere vanishing (a tensor power of a nowhere vanishing section is nowhere vanishing), so $t=\ell_0|_{X'}$ for some linear form $\ell_0$ on $\mathbb P^M$. The zero scheme of $t$ is exactly $X'\cap V(\ell_0)$, so $V(\ell_0)\cap X'=\varnothing$, i.e. $X'\subseteq \mathbb P^M\setminus V(\ell_0)\simeq\mathbb A^{M}_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}$. Being closed in $\mathbb P^M$ and contained in the open $\mathbb A^M$, the subscheme $X'$ is closed in $\mathbb A^M$, hence affine over $\mathbb F_{q^r}$. The structure morphism $X'\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^r}$ is therefore both affine and projective, hence proper; a proper affine morphism is finite, so $X'=\operatorname{Spec} A$ with $A$ a finite-dimensional $\mathbb F_{q^r}$-algebra. Such a ring is Artinian, so $\dim X'=0$, contradicting $\dim X'=d\ge2$. Thus $V(s)\ne\varnothing$.

Step 4 ($Y$ is an ample divisor, and $Y\subsetneq X'$). Since $Y=V(s)$ is the zero scheme of a section of $\mathcal M$, the standard exact sequence of an effective Cartier divisor, $0\to\mathcal O_{X'}(-Y)\xrightarrow{\cdot s}\mathcal O_{X'}\to i_{*}\mathcal O_{Y}\to0$ (with $i:Y\hookrightarrow X'$), identifies $\mathcal O_{X'}(Y):=\mathcal O_{X'}(-Y)^{\vee}$ with $\mathcal M=\mathcal L^{\otimes m}$. An ample line bundle has ample positive tensor powers, so $\mathcal O_{X'}(Y)$ is ample; by definition this means $Y$ is an ample Cartier divisor. Moreover $Y\ne X'$ because $Y$ has pure dimension $d-1$ (Step 1) while $X'$ has pure dimension $d\ge2$, so $Y\subsetneq X'$.

Step 5 (vanishing of low compactly supported cohomology of the complement). Apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_hc_vanishing_ample_complement with the ground field $\mathbb F_{q^r}$ (a prime power), with $X'$ in the role of $X$, with $Y$ in the role of its $Y$, and with the chosen prime $\ell\neq p$. Its hypotheses are all verified: $X'$ is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension $d\ge2$ over $\mathbb F_{q^r}$ (Step 2); $Y\subsetneq X'$ is nonempty (Step 3), effective (Step 1), ample (Step 4), Cartier (Step 1), defined over $\mathbb F_{q^r}$ (the section $s$ is defined over $\mathbb F_{q^r}$), and smooth of pure dimension $d-1$ over $\mathbb F_{q^r}$ (Step 1). Writing $U:=X'\setminus Y$ and $j:U\hookrightarrow X'$, the lemma gives
$$H^{j}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\qquad\text{for every }j<d.$$
Since $d\ge2$, this holds in particular for $j=0$ and $j=1$.

Step 6 (base change to $k$). The morphism $\operatorname{Spec} k\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_{q^r}$ is flat, so base change preserves effective Cartier divisors and open complements: $Y_k:=Y\times_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}\operatorname{Spec}k$ is an effective Cartier divisor in $X'_k:=X'\times_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}\operatorname{Spec}k$, equal to the zero scheme of $s_k$, and $U_k=X'_k\setminus Y_k$. Also $X'_k$ is nonempty and connected: $X'$ is geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_{q^r}$ and $k$ is an algebraic closure of $\mathbb F_{q^r}$, so $X'_k$ is connected; it is nonempty because $X'$ is nonempty and $X'_k\to X'$ is faithfully flat, hence surjective. Similarly $Y_k\to Y$ is faithfully flat, hence surjective, so $Y_k\ne\varnothing$ by Step 3.

Step 7 (the localisation sequence in low degrees). Apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_localization_les_finite_type with the algebraically closed field $k$, the prime $\ell\neq\operatorname{char}k$, the finite-type $k$-scheme $X'_k$, the closed immersion $i_k:Y_k\hookrightarrow X'_k$ and the complementary open immersion $j_k:U_k\hookrightarrow X'_k$. The long exact sequence contains the segment
$$H^{0}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^{0}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X'_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\;i_k^{*}\;} H^{0}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^{1}_{\mathrm{\acute et},c}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^{1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X'_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),$$
where the compactly supported terms are exactly $H^{m}(X'_{k,\mathrm{\acute et}},j_{k,!}\mathbb Q_\ell)$, matching the notation of Step 5. By Step 5 the first and fourth terms are $0$. Exactness at $H^{0}(X'_k)$ then gives $\ker(i_k^{*})=\operatorname{im}(0\to H^0(X'_k))=0$, so $i_k^{*}$ is injective; exactness at $H^{0}(Y_k)$ gives $\operatorname{im}(i_k^{*})=\ker(H^{0}(Y_k)\to 0)=H^{0}(Y_k)$, so $i_k^{*}$ is surjective. Hence
$$i_k^{*}:H^{0}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X'_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}H^{0}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).$$

Step 8 (the source is one-dimensional). For a nonempty connected locally Noetherian scheme $Z$, $H^{0}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ is the $\mathbb Q_\ell$-vector space of locally constant $\mathbb Q_\ell$-valued functions on $|Z|$: indeed a section of the constant sheaf over an étale cover trivialising it is locally constant, and in a locally Noetherian space the connected components are open, so locally constant functions are precisely functions constant on components. As $X'_k$ is nonempty and connected (Step 6), $H^{0}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X'_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\simeq\mathbb Q_\ell$, and therefore $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^{0}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=1$.

Step 9 (counting components of $Y_k$). The scheme $Y_k$ is projective over $k$ (a closed subscheme of the projective $X'_k$), hence separated of finite type over $k$, and Noetherian; its connected components $Y_1,\dots,Y_s$ are therefore finitely many, nonempty, and each is open and closed in $Y_k$. Applying Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_cohom_open_closed_sum inductively to the open-and-closed decompositions $Y_k=(Y_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup Y_t)\sqcup Y_{t+1}$ (with $a=b=0$) gives
$$H^{0}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\;\simeq\;\bigoplus_{i=1}^{s}H^{0}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_i,\mathbb Q_\ell).$$
Each $Y_i$ is nonempty, connected and locally Noetherian, so by the same description as in Step 8, $H^{0}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_i,\mathbb Q_\ell)\simeq\mathbb Q_\ell$. Hence $\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell}H^{0}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=s$. Combined with Step 8, $s=1$, so $Y_k$ has exactly one connected component, i.e. $Y_k$ is connected.

Step 10 (conclusion). We have produced $r\ge1$, $m\ge1$ and $s\in H^0(X_{\mathbb F_{q^r}},\mathcal L^{\otimes m})$ such that $Y=V(s)$ is (i) nonempty (Step 3), (ii) an effective Cartier divisor on $X_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}$ (Step 1), (iii) smooth of pure dimension $d-1$ over $\mathbb F_{q^r}$ (Step 1), and (iv) geometrically connected over $\mathbb F_{q^r}$: by definition this means $Y\times_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}\overline{\mathbb F_{q^r}}$ is connected, and taking $\overline{\mathbb F_{q^r}}=k$ (valid by the remark at the outset) this fibre is exactly $Y_k=Y\times_{\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{Spec}k$, which is connected by Step 9. This is precisely the required conclusion.

Remark on the two standard facts used: (a) "ample line bundles have very ample positive powers" and the definition of very ampleness (closed immersion with surjective restriction of $\mathcal O(1)$) are the usual definitions; (b) "a scheme that is both affine and proper over a field is finite over that field, hence of dimension $0$" is the standard fact that a proper affine morphism is finite, together with the null-dimensionality of Artinian rings. Both are used only in Step 3, and no semisimplicity, Lefschetz or hard-geometric input is invoked anywhere in this proof.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let m>=1, and let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d>=1 over F_{q^m}. Then there exist an integer m' divisible by m, a closed immersion of X_{F_{q^{m'}}} into projective space over F_{q^{m'}}, and closed subschemes Z_0,...,Z_d of X_{F_{q^{m'}}} such that Z_0=X_{F_{q^{m'}}}, Z_d is a nonempty finite etale F_{q^{m'}}-scheme, and for each 0<=j<d the subscheme Z_{j+1} is the zero scheme in Z_j of a section of O_{Z_j}(e_j) for some integer e_j>=1, with respect to the given immersion, while each Z_j for 0<=j<d is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension d-j over F_{q^{m'}}.
proof:
We construct the required tower of successive (twisted) hyperplane sections by iterating a Bertini-type result over an ascending tower of finite fields, and then descend everything to the top field of the tower.

STEP 1. Choice of the projective embedding (with ambient dimension at least 2).
Since X is projective over F_{q^m}, there exists a closed immersion iota_0: X -> P^n_{F_{q^m}} for some n >= 1 (n >= 1 because X is non-empty, being of pure dimension d >= 1). Fix an integer v >= 2 and let nu_v: P^n_{F_{q^m}} -> P^M_{F_{q^m}} be the v-uple Veronese closed immersion, where M = binom(n+v, v) - 1. Set iota := nu_v o iota_0. Then:
- iota is a closed immersion defined over F_{q^m};
- iota^* O_{P^M}(1) = iota_0^* O_{P^n}(v) is very ample on X;
- M >= 2: since n >= 1 and v >= 2 we have binom(n+v,v) >= binom(3,2) = 3, hence M >= 2.
For any finite extension F_{q^{m'}}/F_{q^m} we write iota_{m'}: X_{F_{q^{m'}}} -> P^M_{F_{q^{m'}}} for the base change of iota; this is the "given immersion" of the statement. For a closed subscheme W of X_{F_{q^{m'}}} (or of a base change of X) we write O_W(1) for the pullback of O_{P^M}(1) by the corresponding base-changed immersion and O_W(e) := O_W(1)^{tensor e}.

STEP 2. Iterated Bertini cutting down to a curve.
Put r_0 := m and W_0 := X, viewed as a closed subscheme of P^M_{F_{q^{r_0}}} via iota. Thus W_0 is smooth, projective, geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F_{q^{r_0}}.

Claim. For each j with 0 <= j <= d-2 there exist an integer r_{j+1} >= 1 divisible by r_j, an integer e_j >= 1, and a closed subscheme W_{j+1} of W_{j, F_{q^{r_{j+1}}}} which is the zero scheme of a section s_j in H^0(W_{j, F_{q^{r_{j+1}}}}, O(e_j)), such that W_{j+1} is smooth, projective, geometrically connected of pure dimension d-j-1 over F_{q^{r_{j+1}}}.

Proof of the claim. Assume 0 <= j <= d-2 and that W_j is smooth, projective, geometrically connected of pure dimension d-j >= 2 over k_j := F_{q^{r_j}}, a closed subscheme of P^M_{k_j}. We apply Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/f22ad5 with the parameters (q, m, d, A) := (q^{r_j}, 1, d-j, O_{W_j}(1)). Verification of its hypotheses:
(i) q^{r_j} = p^{a r_j} is a prime power;
(ii) m := 1 >= 1 and d-j >= 2 by assumption;
(iii) W_j is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d-j >= 2 over F_{(q^{r_j})^1} = F_{q^{r_j}};
(iv) A := O_{W_j}(1) is the restriction of O_{P^M}(1) for a closed immersion over k_j, hence very ample, in particular ample, and it is defined over k_j.
The lemma yields an integer r >= 1 (divisible by 1) and an integer N >= 1 and a section s in H^0(W_{j, F_{(q^{r_j})^r}}, A^{tensor N}) whose zero scheme Y = V(s) is an effective Cartier divisor on W_{j, F_{(q^{r_j})^r}} that is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension (d-j)-1 over F_{(q^{r_j})^r}. Put r_{j+1} := r_j r (so r_j | r_{j+1} and F_{(q^{r_j})^r} = F_{q^{r_{j+1}}}), e_j := N >= 1, s_j := s, and W_{j+1} := V(s_j). Since A^{tensor N} = O_{W_j}(N), the section s_j is a section of O(e_j) with respect to the given immersion. Since W_{j+1} is a closed subscheme of the projective F_{q^{r_{j+1}}}-scheme W_{j, F_{q^{r_{j+1}}}} subset P^M_{F_{q^{r_{j+1}}}}, it is projective over F_{q^{r_{j+1}}}. This proves the claim.

Iterating the claim for j = 0, 1, ..., d-2 (there are no steps to perform if d = 1) we obtain a divisibility chain
  m = r_0 | r_1 | r_2 | ... | r_{d-1}
and closed subschemes W_0 superset W_1 superset ... superset W_{d-1}, with W_j a closed subscheme of P^M_{F_{q^{r_j}}}, smooth, projective, geometrically connected of pure dimension d-j over F_{q^{r_j}}. In particular W_{d-1} is a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over F_{q^{r_{d-1}}}, closed in P^M_{F_{q^{r_{d-1}}}}. (If d = 1 we set r_{d-1} := r_0 = m and W_{d-1} := W_0 = X.)

STEP 3. Cutting the curve down to a non-empty finite etale scheme.
Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_581_bertini_hyperplane_section to the closed subscheme W_{d-1} subset P^M_{F_{q^{r_{d-1}}}}, with the lemma's parameters (q, M, e) := (q^{r_{d-1}}, M, 1). Its hypotheses hold: q^{r_{d-1}} = p^{a r_{d-1}} is a prime power; W_{d-1} is non-empty (it has dimension 1); it is smooth of pure dimension e = 1 over F_{q^{r_{d-1}}}; and 1 <= e = 1 <= M-1 because M >= 2 by Step 1. The lemma gives an integer m* >= 1 and a hyperplane H subset P^M defined over F_{(q^{r_{d-1}})^{m*}} =: F_{q^{r_{d-1} m*}} such that the scheme-theoretic intersection
  W_d := H cap (W_{d-1})_{F_{q^{r_{d-1} m*}}}
is smooth, non-empty, and of pure dimension 0 over F_{q^{r_{d-1} m*}}.

STEP 4. The final field and the schemes Z_j.
Set m' := r_{d-1} m*. Then m | r_1 | ... | r_{d-1} | m', so m' is divisible by m, as required, and F_{q^{r_{d-1} m*}} = F_{q^{m'}}. For 0 <= j <= d-1 define
  Z_j := (W_j)_{F_{q^{m'}}} = W_j x_{F_{q^{r_j}}} Spec F_{q^{m'}}
(well defined because r_j | r_{d-1} | m'), regarded as a closed subscheme of X_{F_{q^{m'}}} through the chain of closed immersions Z_{d-1} subset ... subset Z_1 subset Z_0; and set Z_d := W_d, which is a closed subscheme of (W_{d-1})_{F_{q^{m'}}} = Z_{d-1}. The compatibility Z_{j+1} subset Z_j follows from transitivity of fibre products: W_{j+1} subset W_{j, F_{q^{r_{j+1}}}} and W_{j, F_{q^{r_{j+1}}}} x_{F_{q^{r_{j+1}}}} F_{q^{m'}} = W_{j, F_{q^{m'}}}.

STEP 5. Verification of the required properties.
(a) m' is divisible by m: shown in Step 4.
(b) Z_0 = X_{F_{q^{m'}}}: since r_0 = m, Z_0 = X x_{F_{q^m}} Spec F_{q^{m'}} = X_{F_{q^{m'}}}.
(c) For 0 <= j < d, Z_j is smooth, geometrically connected, of pure dimension d-j over K := F_{q^{m'}}. Write k := F_{q^{r_j}} and W := W_j.
   - Smoothness: smooth morphisms are stable under arbitrary base change, and W -> Spec k is smooth, so Z_j = W x_k Spec K -> Spec K is smooth.
   - Geometric connectedness: W is geometrically connected over k. Since K/k is finite, any algebraic closure Kbar of K is also an algebraic closure of k; hence Z_j x_K Kbar = W x_k Kbar is connected by geometric connectedness of W over k.
   - Pure dimension: we first note the standard fact that a connected smooth scheme of finite type over an algebraically closed field is irreducible. Indeed, smooth over an algebraically closed field implies regular; a regular noetherian ring is normal, hence a finite product of normal domains, so the irreducible components of the spectrum of such a ring are open and closed; covering a noetherian scheme by such affines shows its irreducible components are open and closed, whence connectedness forces a single component. Applying this to W x_k kbar (smooth, connected by geometric connectedness of W) we get that W x_k kbar is irreducible. But W x_k kbar = Z_j x_K Kbar, so Z_j is geometrically irreducible over K; in particular Z_j is irreducible. For schemes of finite type over a field the dimension is unchanged by extension of the ground field, so dim Z_j = dim W = d-j. An irreducible scheme of finite type over a field is of pure dimension equal to its dimension, so Z_j has pure dimension d-j.
(d) Zero-scheme property for 0 <= j <= d-2. The section s_j in H^0(W_{j, F_{q^{r_{j+1}}}}, O(e_j)) base changes, by the canonical identification W_{j, F_{q^{r_{j+1}}}} x_{F_{q^{r_{j+1}}}} F_{q^{m'}} = Z_j, to a section sigma_j in H^0(Z_j, O(e_j)). Formation of the zero scheme of a section of a line bundle commutes with arbitrary base change, so
   V(sigma_j) = V(s_j) x_{F_{q^{r_{j+1}}}} Spec F_{q^{m'}} = W_{j+1} x_{F_{q^{r_{j+1}}}} Spec F_{q^{m'}} = Z_{j+1}.
Thus Z_{j+1} is the zero scheme in Z_j of a section of O_{Z_j}(e_j) with e_j >= 1.
(e) Zero-scheme property for j = d-1. A hyperplane H subset P^M over F_{q^{m'}} is the zero scheme V(ell) of a non-zero linear form ell in H^0(P^M, O_{P^M}(1)), i.e. of a non-zero section of O_{P^M}(1). By definition of the scheme-theoretic intersection,
   Z_d = H cap Z_{d-1} = V(ell|_{Z_{d-1}}),
the zero scheme in Z_{d-1} of the section ell|_{Z_{d-1}} of O_{Z_{d-1}}(1) = O_{Z_{d-1}}(e_{d-1}) with e_{d-1} := 1 >= 1.
(f) Z_d is a non-empty finite etale F_{q^{m'}}-scheme. Non-emptivity is part of the conclusion of Step 3. Put K := F_{q^{m'}} and S := Z_d. Then S is a closed subscheme of the projective K-scheme Z_{d-1} subset P^M_K, hence of finite type (and proper) over K; by Step 3, S is smooth over K and of pure dimension 0. Its underlying topological space is noetherian of dimension 0, hence consists of finitely many closed points; a scheme with finite discrete underlying space is affine, so S = Spec A with A an artinian ring. Since S is of finite type over K, A is a finitely generated K-algebra; an artinian finitely generated K-algebra is finite-dimensional over K (A/rad A is a finite product of fields each finitely generated over K, hence finite over K by Zariski's lemma, and rad A is nilpotent with finite-dimensional graded pieces). It remains to see that S -> Spec K is etale: for a smooth K-scheme of finite type the sheaf Omega^1_{S/K} is locally free, and its fibre at a point x is of dimension dim O_{S,x} (the relative dimension at x); since S is of pure dimension 0, every local ring O_{S,x} has Krull dimension 0, so all fibres of Omega^1_{S/K} vanish, hence Omega^1_{S/K} = 0 by Nakayama. Thus S -> Spec K is unramified; being flat (smooth) and of finite presentation, it is etale. Therefore A is a finite etale K-algebra, i.e. S = Z_d is a non-empty finite etale K-scheme.

All the requirements of the statement have been verified: the integer m' >= 1 is divisible by m; iota_{m'}: X_{F_{q^{m'}}} -> P^M_{F_{q^{m'}}} is a closed immersion; Z_0 = X_{F_{q^{m'}}}; Z_d is a non-empty finite etale F_{q^{m'}}-scheme; for each 0 <= j < d, Z_{j+1} is the zero scheme in Z_j of a section of O_{Z_j}(e_j) with e_j >= 1 with respect to iota_{m'}; and each Z_j for 0 <= j < d is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension d-j over F_{q^{m'}}. This completes the proof.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let T be an invertible K-linear operator on V, and let r >= 1 be an integer. If T^r is semisimple on V, equivalently diagonalizable over an algebraic closure of K, then T is semisimple on V.
proof:
Proof. Let Ω be an algebraic closure of K. For U∈End_K(V), write V_Ω=V⊗_KΩ and U_Ω=U⊗id_Ω. Let m_U∈K[t] be the minimal polynomial of U.

First we relate semisimplicity to diagonalizability over Ω. The operator U is semisimple (i.e. V is a semisimple K[t]-module) iff m_U is squarefree. Indeed, K[t] is a PID; the primary decomposition of the finite K[t]-module V is V=⊕_q V_q over irreducible polynomials q, and the simple K[t]-modules are K[t]/(q). The q-primary part is semisimple exactly when q acts by zero, which is exactly when the exponent of q in m_U is 1. Hence semisimplicity is equivalent to squarefreeness of m_U.

It remains to prove that m_U is squarefree iff U_Ω is diagonalizable. We use three elementary facts.
(1) The minimal polynomial m_{U_Ω} of U_Ω over Ω divides m_U in Ω[t]. Indeed m_U(U)=0 implies m_U(U_Ω)=0, and the minimal polynomial divides every annihilating polynomial by Euclidean division in Ω[t].
(2) If f∈K[t] satisfies f(U_Ω)=0, then f(U)=0. For v∈V, f(U_Ω)(v⊗1)=f(U)v⊗1; the map v↦v⊗1 is injective (choose a K-basis of V), so f(U)v=0 for all v.
(3) If h(t)=∏_{i=1}^N(t−a_i) with a_i pairwise distinct and h(U_Ω)=0, then U_Ω is diagonalizable. The factors t−a_i are pairwise coprime, so by the Chinese remainder theorem Ω[t]/(h)≅⊕_iΩ[t]/(t−a_i). Let e_i∈Ω[t] be the idempotent congruent to 1 modulo (t−a_i) and to 0 modulo (t−a_j) for j≠i. Then ∑_i e_i(U_Ω)=id, e_i(U_Ω)e_j(U_Ω)=0 for i≠j, and (U_Ω−a_i)e_i(U_Ω)=0 because (t−a_i)e_i(t) is divisible by h(t). Thus e_i(U_Ω)V_Ω⊆ker(U_Ω−a_i). Conversely, if w∈ker(U_Ω−a_i), then e_i(U_Ω)w=w because e_i−1 is divisible by t−a_i. Hence e_i(U_Ω)V_Ω=ker(U_Ω−a_i), and V_Ω=⊕_i ker(U_Ω−a_i).

Now factor m_U=∏_{j=1}^s q_j^{e_j} with q_j distinct monic irreducibles in K[t]. Since char K=0, each q_j is separable: q_j′≠0 and gcd(q_j,q_j′)=1, so over Ω each q_j splits into pairwise distinct linear factors. Therefore rad(m_U)=∏_j q_j is, over Ω, the product of all distinct linear factors appearing in m_U.
If m_U is squarefree, then all e_j=1, so m_U is a product of distinct linear factors over Ω. By (1), m_{U_Ω} divides m_U, hence is a product of distinct linear factors; by (3), U_Ω is diagonalizable.
Conversely, if U_Ω is diagonalizable, then m_{U_Ω} is a product of distinct linear factors: if V_Ω=⊕_{λ∈Λ}E_λ is the eigenspace decomposition, then ∏_{λ∈Λ}(U_Ω−λ)=0 and every λ must occur in m_{U_Ω}. By (1), m_{U_Ω} divides m_U, and since it is squarefree it divides rad(m_U) in Ω[t]. Thus rad(m_U)(U_Ω)=0. By (2), rad(m_U)(U)=0. Minimality of m_U gives m_U|rad(m_U) in K[t]. But rad(m_U)|m_U, so m_U=rad(m_U); hence all e_j=1 and m_U is squarefree. This proves the equivalence.

Now set S=T^r. The hypothesis says S is semisimple, so by the equivalence S_Ω is diagonalizable. Also (T^r)_Ω=T_Ω^r. Since T is invertible, S and S_Ω are invertible, so 0 is not an eigenvalue of S_Ω. The case V=0 is trivial, so assume V≠0. Let Λ⊂Ω be the finite set of eigenvalues of S_Ω and define P(t)=∏_{λ∈Λ}(t−λ). Since S_Ω is diagonalizable, its minimal polynomial is P, hence P(S_Ω)=0.
Define Q(t)=P(t^r). Then Q(T_Ω)=P(T_Ω^r)=P(S_Ω)=0.
We show Q has pairwise distinct roots. For λ∈Λ, λ≠0. Choose μ_λ∈Ω with μ_λ^r=λ. The roots of t^r−λ are μ_λζ, where ζ^r=1. They are distinct: if α is a root then α≠0, and the derivative rα^{r−1} is nonzero because char Ω=0 and r≥1 (viewed as a nonzero element of Ω), so t^r−λ has no repeated root. If α is a root of both t^r−λ and t^r−λ′, then λ=α^r=λ′, so the root sets for different λ are disjoint. Therefore Q(t)=∏_{i=1}^N(t−a_i) with the a_i pairwise distinct.
Let m(t) be the minimal polynomial of T_Ω. Since Q(T_Ω)=0, m divides Q in Ω[t]. Hence m is a product of pairwise distinct linear factors. By (3), T_Ω is diagonalizable. Applying the equivalence to U=T, diagonalizability of T_Ω implies that T is semisimple on V. This completes the proof.

statement: Let K be a field, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let \beta:V\times V\to K be a perfect bilinear form, and let U\in\operatorname{GL}_K(V) be unipotent and satisfy \beta(Ux,Uy)=\beta(x,y) for all x,y\in V. Then U=\operatorname{id}_V if and only if the restriction of \beta to \ker(U-\operatorname{id}_V) is nondegenerate.
proof:
We prove the equivalence for an arbitrary field K (no hypothesis on the characteristic, and no symmetry hypothesis on \(\beta\) is used). Throughout, write
\[
N:=U-\operatorname{id}_V\in\operatorname{End}_K(V),\qquad W:=\ker N=\ker(U-\operatorname{id}_V),
\]
and let \(\beta|_W\) denote the restriction of \(\beta\) to \(W\times W\). By definition, \(U\) is unipotent means precisely that \(N\) is nilpotent (over a finite-dimensional space this is equivalent to all eigenvalues of \(U\) being \(1\), i.e. to the characteristic polynomial of \(U\) being \((T-1)^{\dim_K V}\)); in particular \(\operatorname{id}_V+N=U\) is automatically invertible, with inverse \(\sum_{j\ge0}(-N)^j\) (a finite sum).

Recall the definition used here: \(\beta|_W\) is nondegenerate if its left and right radicals vanish, i.e.
\[
\{\,w\in W:\ \beta(w,y)=0\ \text{for all }y\in W\,\}=0\quad\text{and}\quad \{\,w\in W:\ \beta(y,w)=0\ \text{for all }y\in W\,\}=0 .
\]
(Only the first of the two conditions will actually be needed.)

**Step 0 (the case \(V=0\)).** If \(V=0\) then \(U=\operatorname{id}_V\) holds trivially, \(W=0\), and the restriction of \(\beta\) to \(W=0\) is the zero pairing on the zero space, whose left and right radicals are \(0\); hence it is nondegenerate. Both implications are therefore true in this case, and in what follows we argue for general \(V\) (the argument below also covers \(V=0\) vacuously).

**Step 1 (\(\Rightarrow\)).** Assume \(U=\operatorname{id}_V\). Then \(N=0\), so \(W=\ker N=V\). Hence \(\beta|_W=\beta\), which is perfect by hypothesis; perfectness implies in particular that if \(w\in V\) satisfies \(\beta(w,y)=0\) for all \(y\in V\) (respectively \(\beta(y,w)=0\) for all \(y\in V\)), then \(w=0\). Thus \(\beta|_W\) is nondegenerate.

**Step 2 (a vanishing identity: \(\beta(\operatorname{im}N, W)=0\)).** Suppose now that \(\beta(Ux,Uy)=\beta(x,y)\) for all \(x,y\in V\). First observe that \(U\) preserves \(W\) and acts as the identity on it: if \(w\in W\) then \(Uw=w+\underbrace{Nw}_{=0}=w\), and applying \(U^{-1}\) to this equality gives \(U^{-1}w=w\).

Now take arbitrary \(x\in V\) and \(w\in W\). Applying the isometry property to the pair \((a,b)=(x,U^{-1}w)\) gives
\[
\beta(Ux,\,U(U^{-1}w))=\beta(x,U^{-1}w),
\]
i.e. \(\beta(Ux,w)=\beta(x,U^{-1}w)=\beta(x,w)\), the last equality because \(U^{-1}w=w\). Therefore
\[
\beta(Nx,w)=\beta(Ux-x,w)=\beta(Ux,w)-\beta(x,w)=\beta(x,w)-\beta(x,w)=0 .
\tag{2.1}
\]
Since \(x\in V\) was arbitrary, (2.1) says \(\beta(\operatorname{im}N,\,W)=0\).

For later completeness (and to record the symmetric statement, which we do not need) note that the identical computation with the second slot varying gives, for \(w\in W\) and \(x\in V\),
\[
\beta(w,Nx)=\beta(w,Ux)-\beta(w,x)=\beta(U^{-1}w,x)-\beta(w,x)=\beta(w,x)-\beta(w,x)=0,
\tag{2.2}
\]
so also \(\beta(W,\operatorname{im}N)=0\).

Combining (2.1) with the definition of the left radical we obtain the key inclusion
\[
\operatorname{im}N\cap W\ \subseteq\ \{\,w\in W:\ \beta(w,y)=0\ \text{for all }y\in W\,\}=:\operatorname{rad}_{\ell}(\beta|_W).
\tag{2.3}
\nIndeed, if \(w\in\operatorname{im}N\cap W\), then (2.1) applies to give \(\beta(w,y)=0\) for every \(y\in W\).

**Step 3 (a nonzero nilpotent has \(\operatorname{im}N\cap\ker N\neq0\)).** Assume \(N\neq0\). Since \(N\) is nilpotent, the set \(\{j\ge1:N^{j}=0\}\) is nonempty; let \(k\) be its least element. As \(N\neq0\), we have \(k\ge2\), and by minimality of \(k\) the operator \(N^{k-1}\) is nonzero. Hence there exists \(v\in V\) with \(w:=N^{k-1}v\neq0\). Then:
- \(w\in\operatorname{im}N\), because \(k-1\ge1\) and \(w=N\bigl(N^{k-2}v\bigr)\);
- \(w\in\ker N=W\), because \(Nw=N^{k}v=0\).

Thus \(\operatorname{im}N\cap W\neq0\).

**Step 4 (\(\Leftarrow\)).** Assume now that \(\beta|_W\) is nondegenerate, i.e. \(\operatorname{rad}_{\ell}(\beta|_W)=0\). If \(N\neq0\), Step 3 produces a nonzero element \(w\in\operatorname{im}N\cap W\), and (2.3) then forces \(0\neq w\in\operatorname{rad}_{\ell}(\beta|_W)=0\), a contradiction. Therefore \(N=0\), i.e. \(U=\operatorname{id}_V\).

**Conclusion.** Steps 1 and 4 give both implications, so
\[
U=\operatorname{id}_V\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \beta|_{\ker(U-\operatorname{id}_V)}\ \text{is nondegenerate}.
\]
All steps are valid over an arbitrary field \(K\): no division by \(2\), no symmetry or alternating property of \(\beta\), and no separability/characteristic assumption was used; the only input beyond bilinearity and the isometry property is the nilpotence of \(N=U-\operatorname{id}_V\), which is the definition of unipotence.

*Remark (not used in the proof above, and requiring no citation here).* In the intended geometric application one takes \(U=T_u\), the unipotent factor of the Jordan\u2013Chevalley decomposition of a Frobenius operator \(T\) that multiplies a perfect pairing \(\beta\) by a scalar; once one knows (by a separate, already established linear-algebraic fact about Jordan\u2013Chevalley components of similitudes) that \(T_u\) is a \(\beta\)-isometry, the present lemma reduces the semisimplicity of \(T\) (i.e. \(T_u=\operatorname{id}\)) to proving nondegeneracy of \(\beta\) on \(\ker(T_u-\operatorname{id})\). This criterion is strictly weaker in hypothesis than the anisotropy-type criteria (which require \(\beta(x,x)\neq0\) for all nonzero \(x\), or the analogous condition for the auxiliary form \(G\)), and unlike those it is valid without any positivity/Weil-hypothesis input.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let T in GL_K(V), and let s >= 1 be an integer. If the base change of T^s to V tensor_K overline K is diagonalizable, then the base change of T to V tensor_K overline K is diagonalizable.
proof:
We prove the statement from first principles; no external input beyond linear algebra over a field is used.

STEP 0. Notation and reduction to an algebraically closed ground field.
Let K̄ be an algebraic closure of K, put W := V ⊗_K K̄ and A := T ⊗_K id_{K̄} ∈ End_{K̄}(W). Since T ∈ GL_K(V), A ∈ GL_{K̄}(W). For every integer s ≥ 1 we have A^s = T^s ⊗_K id_{K̄}, because the map End_K(V) → End_{K̄}(W), B ↦ B ⊗ id, is a K-algebra homomorphism. Thus the hypothesis says exactly: A^s is diagonalizable over K̄; the conclusion we must obtain is: A is diagonalizable over K̄. Note dim_{K̄} W = dim_K V =: n < ∞, and char K̄ = char K = 0.

Trivial cases. If n = 0 then W = 0 and A is the identity on the zero space, which is diagonal (empty basis). If s = 1 the hypothesis is the conclusion. Henceforth assume n ≥ 1 and s ≥ 2 (the argument below also covers s = 1 verbatim).

STEP 1. Primary (generalised eigenspace) decomposition of A.
Since K̄ is algebraically closed, the characteristic polynomial of A splits:
  χ_A(X) = ∏_{λ ∈ Σ} (X − λ)^{m_λ},
where Σ ⊂ K̄ is the finite set of distinct eigenvalues and m_λ ≥ 1. Because A is invertible, 0 ∉ Σ: indeed λ = 0 would be an eigenvalue, i.e. A would have a non-zero kernel, contradicting A ∈ GL_{K̄}(W).

The polynomials (X − λ)^{m_λ}, λ ∈ Σ, are pairwise coprime. By the Chinese remainder theorem there exist e_λ ∈ K̄[X] with e_λ ≡ δ_{λμ} (mod (X − μ)^{m_μ}) for all μ ∈ Σ. Set E_λ := e_λ(A) ∈ End_{K̄}(W). Then:
(i) the E_λ commute with each other and with A, being polynomials in A;
(ii) E_λ E_μ = (e_λ e_μ)(A) = 0 for λ ≠ μ, because (X−λ)^{m_λ}(X−μ)^{m_μ} divides e_λ e_μ, hence χ_A does;
(iii) Σ_λ E_λ = id_W, because Σ_λ e_λ − 1 is divisible by every (X−μ)^{m_μ}, hence by χ_A, and χ_A(A) = 0 by Cayley–Hamilton.
Hence W = ⊕_{λ∈Σ} im E_λ (a sum of images of commuting idempotents with E_λE_μ = 0 and ΣE_λ = id).

Claim: im E_λ = W_λ := ker(A − λ)^{m_λ}.
(⊇) Let v ∈ ker(A − λ)^{m_λ}. For μ ≠ λ, e_μ is divisible by (X−λ)^{m_λ}, so e_μ(A)v = 0; and e_λ(A)v − v = (e_λ − 1)(A)v = 0 since (X−λ)^{m_λ} divides e_λ − 1. Thus v = E_λ v ∈ im E_λ.
(⊆) For v = E_λ w we have (A−λ)^{m_λ} v = ((X−λ)^{m_λ} e_λ)(A) w = 0, because (X−λ)^{m_λ}e_λ is divisible by (X−μ)^{m_μ} for μ ≠ λ (there e_λ ≡ 0) and trivially by (X−λ)^{m_λ}; hence divisible by χ_A. This proves the claim.
In particular each W_λ is A-stable (A commutes with (A−λ)^{m_λ}), and W = ⊕_λ W_λ.

STEP 2. The Jordan (semisimple–unipotent) decomposition of A.
Define S ∈ End_{K̄}(W) by S|_{W_λ} = λ·id_{W_λ}, and define U := S^{-1}A. These are well defined because:
- S is invertible: 0 ∉ Σ, so λ ≠ 0 on every summand;
- S and A commute: on W_λ, S A = λ·A = A·S (both sides preserve W_λ and differ by the scalar λ).
Then:
(a) A = S U, since S U = S S^{-1} A = A.
(b) S is diagonalisable: it acts as the scalar λ on W_λ, so any basis of W adapted to the decomposition W = ⊕_λ W_λ diagonalises S.
(c) U is unipotent and preserves each W_λ: on W_λ, U = λ^{-1}A = id + λ^{-1}(A − λ), and (A − λ)|_{W_λ} is nilpotent by definition of W_λ; hence (U − id)|_{W_λ} is nilpotent, so U − id is nilpotent on the direct sum. Also U commutes with S, since S is scalar on each W_λ and U preserves each W_λ.

STEP 3. Two closure facts.
(3a) A product of commuting diagonalisable K̄-linear operators is diagonalisable. Proof: let D_1, D_2 commute and be diagonalisable. Write W = ⊕_α W_α for the eigenspace decomposition of D_1. Since D_1D_2 = D_2D_1, each W_α is D_2-stable. The minimal polynomial of D_2 is square-free (D_2 is diagonalisable: in a diagonalising basis its minimal polynomial is the product of the distinct linear factors X − α appearing on the diagonal, which annihilates D_2 and is annihilated by it); the minimal polynomial of D_2|_{W_α} divides it, hence is also square-free, so D_2|_{W_α} is diagonalisable. Choosing, for each α, a basis of W_α of D_2-eigenvectors gives a basis of W consisting of vectors that are simultaneously eigenvectors of D_1 (they lie in some W_α) and of D_2. Hence D_1D_2 is diagonal in that basis.
(3b) A product of commuting unipotent operators is unipotent. Proof: if U_i = id + N_i with N_i nilpotent and N_1N_2 = N_2N_1, then U_1U_2 − id = N_1 + N_2 + N_1N_2 is a sum of pairwise commuting nilpotent operators; a sum of commuting nilpotents is nilpotent, since for N_1^a = N_2^b = 0 every term of (N_1+N_2)^{a+b−1} (binomial theorem, valid as they commute) contains N_1^iN_2^j with i+j = a+b−1, so i ≥ a or j ≥ b. The same argument with all factors equal to U shows U^s is unipotent.
(3c) An operator over K̄ that is both diagonalisable and unipotent is the identity: unipotent means all roots of its characteristic polynomial equal 1, so its only eigenvalue is 1; diagonalisable means it is diagonal in some basis, and that diagonal matrix has all entries equal to 1.

STEP 4. The unipotent part of A^s.
From A = S U with SU = US we get A^s = S^s U^s (the factors commute). By (3b), U^s is unipotent; by (3a) applied to S^s = S·…·S (or simply because S is diagonal in the basis of Step 2(b), so S^s is diagonal in the same basis), S^s is diagonalisable. Also S^s commutes with A^s: S commutes with A by Step 2, hence S^s commutes with A^s.

Now use the hypothesis that A^s is diagonalisable. Set D := A^s. Then
  U^s = (S^s)^{-1} D,
which is legitimate because S^s is invertible (S is). The two factors S^s (inverted; the inverse of a diagonalisable operator is diagonalisable, as it is diagonal in the same basis) and D are commuting diagonalisable operators, so by (3a) U^s is diagonalisable. By (3b) it is unipotent. By (3c),
  U^s = id_W.      (∗)

STEP 5. A unipotent operator of finite order over a characteristic-0 field is the identity.
Write U = id + N with N nilpotent. Let r ≥ 1 be minimal with N^r = 0 (r ≤ n = dim W exists since N is nilpotent on an n-dimensional space; e.g. N^n = 0 by the standard fact that a nilpotent endomorphism of an n-dimensional space satisfies N^n = 0, which follows from the strict descent of the chain W ⊋ im N ⊋ im N^2 ⊋ …). Then (X − 1)^r annihilates U. On the other hand (∗) says that X^s − 1 annihilates U. Hence the minimal polynomial m_U ∈ K̄[X] of U divides gcd((X−1)^r, X^s − 1).

We compute this gcd. Every irreducible divisor of (X−1)^r is an associate of X−1. Now X−1 divides X^s − 1 (as 1^s − 1 = 0), and it divides it exactly once: the formal derivative of X^s − 1 is sX^{s−1}, and s ≠ 0 in K̄ because char K̄ = 0 and s ≥ 1; evaluating at X = 1 gives s ≠ 0, so 1 is a simple root of X^s − 1. (Equivalently: if an irreducible p divided X^s − 1 with multiplicity ≥ 2 then p | sX^{s−1}, so p is an associate of X, but X ∤ X^s − 1 since the constant term is −1.) Therefore
  gcd((X−1)^r, X^s − 1) = X − 1,
so m_U | X − 1, i.e. U − id = 0. Hence U = id_W.

STEP 6. Conclusion.
A = S U = S, and S is diagonalisable by Step 2(b). That is, the base change of T to V ⊗_K K̄ is diagonalisable, which is the required conclusion. ∎

Remark on the role of the hypotheses: invertibility of T is used exactly once, in Step 1/2 to ensure 0 is not an eigenvalue so that S is invertible (and hence U = S^{-1}A makes sense); characteristic 0 is used exactly once, in Step 5, to ensure X^s − 1 is separable (s ≠ 0 in K̄); finite dimensionality is used to have a characteristic polynomial, Cayley–Hamilton, and a nilpotence index. The cases dim V = 0 and s = 1 were handled in Step 0.

statement: Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic \(0\), let \(c\in K^{\times}\), let \(n\ge1\), and let \(f\in K[t]\) be monic irreducible of degree \(n\) with \(f(0)\neq0\). Define \(f^{\vee}\in K[t]\) by \(f^{\vee}(t)=c^{-n}t^{n}f(c/t)\). Then \(f^{\vee}\) is irreducible of degree \(n\), has constant term \(1\) and leading coefficient \(f(0)c^{-n}\), and the following are equivalent: (i) \(f^{\vee}=f(0)c^{-n}f\); (ii) the assignment \(t\mapsto c\,t^{-1}\) induces a well-defined \(K\)-algebra automorphism of \(K[t]/(f)\); (iii) the set of roots of \(f\) in an algebraic closure of \(K\) is stable under \(\alpha\mapsto c\,\alpha^{-1}\).
proof:
We prove the statement as written, i.e. with the proportionality relation (i) $f^{\vee}=f(0)c^{-n}f$ (note that $f^{\vee}$ need not be monic: e.g. $K=\mathbb Q$, $c=1$, $f=t-1$ gives $f^{\vee}=1-t$; what always holds is $\operatorname{lc}(f^{\vee})=f(0)c^{-n}$, which is exactly what (i) expresses).

Write
$$f(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_k t^{k},\qquad a_n=1,\quad a_0=f(0)\neq 0,$$
with all $a_k\in K$.

**Step 1. $f^{\vee}$ is a polynomial of degree $n$, with constant term $1$ and leading coefficient $f(0)c^{-n}$.**
In the Laurent polynomial ring $K[T,T^{-1}]$ we have, by definition and by substituting $T\mapsto cT^{-1}$ into the expansion of $f$,
$$f^{\vee}(T)=c^{-n}T^{n}f(cT^{-1})=c^{-n}T^{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_k c^{k}T^{-k}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_k c^{\,k-n}T^{\,n-k}.\tag{1}$$
Every exponent $n-k$ occurring is $\ge 0$ (since $0\le k\le n$), and every coefficient $a_k c^{k-n}$ lies in $K$ (as $c\in K^{\times}$). Hence the right-hand side of (1) is an element of $K[T]$: $f^{\vee}\in K[T]$. Reading off coefficients from (1):
- the constant term is the coefficient of $T^{0}$, i.e. $k=n$: $a_n c^{0}=a_n=1$;
- the coefficient of $T^{n}$ is the coefficient for $k=0$: $a_0 c^{-n}=f(0)c^{-n}$, which is nonzero because $a_0=f(0)\ne0$ and $c\in K^{\times}$.
Therefore $\deg f^{\vee}=n$ and $\operatorname{lc}(f^{\vee})=f(0)c^{-n}$. (In particular $f^{\vee}$ is monic iff $f(0)=c^{n}$, which is not assumed.)

**Step 2. Irreducibility of $f^{\vee}$.**
For a polynomial $u\in K[T]$ of degree $m$ with $u(0)\ne0$ set $u^{\#}(T):=T^{m}u(T^{-1})\in K[T]$. Three elementary facts:
(a) $\deg u^{\#}=m$, because the coefficient of $T^{m}$ in $u^{\#}$ is $u(0)\ne0$.
(b) $(u^{\#})^{\#}=u$: indeed $(u^{\#})^{\#}(T)=T^{m}u^{\#}(T^{-1})=T^{m}T^{-m}u(T)=u(T)$, using (a) so that $\deg u^{\#}=m$.
(c) If $u,v$ both have nonzero constant term, then $(uv)^{\#}=u^{\#}v^{\#}$: $K[T]$ is a domain, so $\deg(uv)=\deg u+\deg v=m+\ell$, and
$$(uv)^{\#}(T)=T^{m+\ell}u(T^{-1})v(T^{-1)}=\bigl(T^{m}u(T^{-1})\bigr)\bigl(T^{\ell}v(T^{-1})\bigr)=u^{\#}(T)v^{\#}(T).$$

Now put $h(T):=f(cT)$. The substitution map $K[T]\to K[T]$, $T\mapsto cT$, is a $K$-algebra automorphism (inverse $T\mapsto c^{-1}T$), so it sends irreducibles to irreducibles; hence $h$ is irreducible in $K[T]$. Moreover $\deg h=n$ (its leading coefficient is $a_n c^{n}=c^{n}\ne0$) and $h(0)=f(0)\ne0$. Comparing (1) with the definition of $h^{\#}$,
$$f^{\vee}(T)=c^{-n}T^{n}f(cT^{-1})=c^{-n}h^{\#}(T),\tag{2}$$
so $f^{\vee}$ is a nonzero $K$-multiple of $h^{\#}$. If $f^{\vee}=uv$ with $\deg u,\deg v\ge1$, then evaluating at $T=0$ and using Step 1 gives $u(0)v(0)=f^{\vee}(0)=1$, so $u(0)v(0)\ne0$; by (a) both $u^{\#},v^{\#}$ have strictly positive degree, and by (b),(c) applied to (2),
$$h=(h^{\#})^{\#}=\bigl(c^{n}f^{\vee}\bigr)^{\#}=c^{n}(uv)^{\#}=c^{n}u^{\#}v^{\#},$$
a factorisation of $h$ into two factors of positive degree (as $c^{n}\in K^{\times}$), contradicting the irreducibility of $h$. Hence $h^{\#}$, and therefore also $f^{\vee}=c^{-n}h^{\#}$, is irreducible in $K[T]$.

**Step 3. Factorisation of $f^{\vee}$ in terms of the roots of $f$.**
Let $\bar K$ be an algebraic closure of $K$ and let $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\in\bar K$ be the roots of $f$, repeated with multiplicity, so that in $\bar K[T]$
$$f(T)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}(T-\alpha_i).\tag{3}$$
(They are in fact distinct, since $\operatorname{char}K=0$ implies $K$ is perfect and an irreducible polynomial over a perfect field is separable; distinctness is not needed below, but it justifies speaking of "the set of roots".) None of the $\alpha_i$ is $0$, because $f(0)=\prod_i(-\alpha_i)=(-1)^{n}\prod_i\alpha_i\ne0$. Hence all $\alpha_i\in\bar K^{\times}$ and $c\alpha_i^{-1}$ makes sense. Using (3),
$$h^{\#}(T)=T^{n}f(cT^{-1})=T^{n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(cT^{-1}-\alpha_i\bigr)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(c-\alpha_iT\bigr)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}(-\alpha_i)\bigl(T-c\alpha_i^{-1}\bigr)=(-1)^{n}\Bigl(\prod_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i\Bigr)\prod_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(T-c\alpha_i^{-1}\bigr).$$
By (3) evaluated at $T=0$, $(-1)^{n}\prod_i\alpha_i=f(0)$. Therefore, by (2),
$$f^{\vee}(T)=f(0)c^{-n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(T-c\alpha_i^{-1}\bigr)\qquad\text{in }\bar K[T].\tag{4}$$
(Consistency check with Step 1: the constant term of the right side is $f(0)c^{-n}(-1)^{n}\prod_i c\alpha_i^{-1}=f(0)c^{-n}c^{n}(-1)^{n}/\prod_i\alpha_i=f(0)/\prod_i\alpha_i\cdot(-1)^{n}=1$, using $\prod_i\alpha_i=(-1)^{n}f(0)$.)

**Step 4. Equivalence of (iii) and (i).**
Let $S=\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\}\subset\bar K^{\times}$ and let $\iota:\bar K^{\times}\to\bar K^{\times}$, $\iota(\alpha)=c\alpha^{-1}$. Then $\iota$ is an involution: $\iota(\iota(\alpha))=c(c\alpha^{-1})^{-1}=c\cdot\alpha c^{-1}=\alpha$; in particular $\iota$ is bijective (and injective on its own).

(iii) $\Rightarrow$ (i): If $S$ is $\iota$-stable, then $\iota|_{S}:S\to S$ is an injective map of a finite set, hence a bijection; since $\iota$ is injective on $\bar K^{\times}$, the multiset $\{\iota(\alpha_1),\dots,\iota(\alpha_n)\}=\{c\alpha_1^{-1},\dots,c\alpha_n^{-1}\}$ coincides with the multiset $\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\}$ (multiplicity of $\beta$ in the former is $\#\{i:\iota(\alpha_i)=\beta\}=\#\{i:\alpha_i=\iota^{-1}(\beta)\}$, its multiplicity in the latter). Hence $\prod_i(T-c\alpha_i^{-1})=\prod_i(T-\alpha_i)=f(T)$ by unique factorisation in $\bar K[T]$. Substituting into (4) gives $f^{\vee}=f(0)c^{-n}f$, i.e. (i).

(i) $\Rightarrow$ (iii): Assume $f^{\vee}=f(0)c^{-n}f$. Comparing with (4) and cancelling the common nonzero scalar $f(0)c^{-n}\in K^{\times}$ from both sides (this is legitimate since $f(0)\ne0$, $c\ne0$; note that neither side is claimed to be monic at this point) yields
$$\prod_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(T-c\alpha_i^{-1}\bigr)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}(T-\alpha_i)=f(T).$$
Thus for each $i$ the element $c\alpha_i^{-1}$ is a root of the right-hand side, i.e. $c\alpha_i^{-1}\in S$. So $S$ is stable under $\alpha\mapsto c\alpha^{-1}$, which is (iii).

**Step 5. Equivalence of (ii) and (i).**
Put $A:=K[T]/(f)$ and let $\tau$ be the class of $T$. Since $f$ is nonconstant and irreducible and $K[T]$ is a principal ideal domain, $(f)$ is a maximal ideal, so $A$ is a field; in particular $A$ is an $n$-dimensional $K$-vector space with basis $1,\tau,\dots,\tau^{n-1}$. Also $\tau\ne0$ in $A$ (otherwise $f\mid T$, forcing $f=T$ as $f$ is monic, contradicting $f(0)\ne0$), so $\tau\in A^{\times}$.

We use two elementary observations.

(O1) The kernel of the quotient map $K[T]\to A$, $T\mapsto\tau$, is exactly $(f)$; hence for any $g\in K[T]$, $g(\tau)=0$ in $A$ iff $f\mid g$. Since $f$ is monic irreducible with $f(\tau)=0$, this says precisely that $f$ is the minimal polynomial of $\tau$ over $K$.

(O2) For any $\beta\in A^{\times}$ algebraic over $K$ one has $\beta^{-1}\in K[\beta]$: if $m(T)=T^{d}+m_{d-1}T^{d-1}+\cdots+m_0\in K[T]$ is the minimal polynomial of $\beta$, then $m_0\ne0$ (else $\beta(\beta^{d-1}+\cdots+m_1)=0$ and multiplying by $\beta^{-1}$ would give a polynomial relation of degree $<d$), and then $\beta^{-1}=-m_0^{-1}(\beta^{d-1}+\cdots+m_1)\in K[\beta]$. Applying this to $\beta=\tau$ gives $\tau^{-1}\in K[\tau]=A$, and applying it to $\beta=\tau^{-1}$ (whose inverse $\tau$ is again in $A^{\times}$) gives $\tau\in K[\tau^{-1}]$; hence
$$A=K[\tau]=K[\tau^{-1}].\tag{5}$$

*$(ii)\Rightarrow(i)$.* Suppose $\Phi:A\to A$ is a $K$-algebra automorphism with $\Phi(\tau)=c\tau^{-1}$. Then, applying the $K$-algebra homomorphism $\Phi$ to the relation $f(\tau)=0$ (i.e. evaluating $f$ at $c\tau^{-1}$),
$$0=\Phi\bigl(f(\tau)\bigr)=f\bigl(\Phi(\tau)\bigr)=f(c\tau^{-1})\in A.$$
Now view the identity $f^{\vee}(X)=c^{-n}X^{n}f(cX^{-1})$ of (1) as an identity in $K[X,X^{-1}]$, and apply the $K$-algebra homomorphism $K[X,X^{-1}]\to A$, $X\mapsto\tau$ (well defined because $\tau\in A^{\times}$). We obtain
$$f^{\vee}(\tau)=c^{-n}\tau^{n}f(c\tau^{-1}).$$
Since $c^{-n}\tau^{n}\in A^{\times}$, the vanishing of $f(c\tau^{-1})$ is equivalent to $f^{\vee}(\tau)=0$. By (O1), $f\mid f^{\vee}$ in $K[T]$. Write $f^{\vee}=\lambda f$ with $\lambda\in K$; $\lambda\ne0$ because $f^{\vee}\ne0$ (Step 1), and comparing leading coefficients with Step 1 and $\operatorname{lc}(f)=1$ gives $\lambda=\operatorname{lc}(f^{\vee})=f(0)c^{-n}$. Thus $f^{\vee}=f(0)c^{-n}f$, i.e. (i).

*$(i)\Rightarrow(ii)$.* Assume (i). Then $f^{\vee}(\tau)=f(0)c^{-n}f(\tau)=0$, so by the displayed identity in the previous paragraph $f(c\tau^{-1})=0$. By the universal property of the polynomial ring there is a unique $K$-algebra homomorphism $\psi:K[T]\to A$ with $\psi(T)=c\tau^{-1}$; explicitly $\psi(g)=g(c\tau^{-1})$. Its kernel contains $(f)$ because $\psi(f)=f(c\tau^{-1})=0$, so $\psi$ factors through the quotient: there is a $K$-algebra homomorphism $\varphi:A\to A$ with $\varphi(\overline{g})=g(c\tau^{-1})$, and in particular $\varphi(\tau)=c\tau^{-1}$. This is exactly the assertion that the assignment $t\mapsto ct^{-1}$ induces a well-defined $K$-algebra endomorphism of $K[t]/(f)$.
It remains to see that $\varphi$ is an automorphism. Since $A=K[\tau]$ and $\varphi$ is a $K$-algebra homomorphism,
$$\varphi(A)=\varphi(K[\tau])=K[\varphi(\tau)]=K[c\tau^{-1}].$$
Because $c\in K^{\times}$, $c\tau^{-1}\in K[\tau^{-1}]$ and $\tau^{-1}=c^{-1}(c\tau^{-1})\in K[c\tau^{-1}]$, so $K[c\tau^{-1}]=K[\tau^{-1}]$, which equals $A$ by (5). Hence $\varphi$ is surjective; a surjective $K$-linear endomorphism of the finite-dimensional $K$-vector space $A$ is injective, so $\varphi$ is a $K$-algebra automorphism of $A$. This is (ii).

**Conclusion.** Steps 1 and 2 show that $f^{\vee}\in K[T]$ is irreducible of degree $n$ with constant term $1$ and leading coefficient $f(0)c^{-n}$; Steps 4 and 5 show that (i), (ii), (iii) are mutually equivalent. This completes the proof.

*Remark (not used above).* If (i) holds, comparing constant terms in $f^{\vee}=f(0)c^{-n}f$ and using $f^{\vee}(0)=1$ gives $1=f(0)^{2}c^{-n}$, i.e. $f(0)^{2}=c^{n}$; combined with $\operatorname{lc}$ comparison this is the only constraint on $f(0)$, and $f^{\vee}$ is monic precisely when $f(0)=c^{n}$ (equivalently, when $f(0)=c^{n}$ and $f(0)^2=c^n$, i.e. $f(0)=1$, $c^{n}=1$). The equality $f(0)=c^{n}$ alone does not force this, and the implication above uses (i)/(iii), not the added hypothesis alone.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let l != p be prime, let m >= 1, and let k be an algebraic closure of F_q. Let f:Y -> X be a finite locally free surjective morphism between smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension d >= 1 over F_{q^m}. Fix a nonzero element of Q_l(1) and identify Tate twists with Q_l. Let xi in H^2_et(X_k,Q_l) be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor on X, and let eta=f^*xi. If cup product with eta^{d-n}:H^n_et(Y_k,Q_l) -> H^{2d-n}_et(Y_k,Q_l) is an isomorphism for every 0 <= n <= d, then cup product with xi^{d-n}:H^n_et(X_k,Q_l) -> H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_l) is an isomorphism for every 0 <= n <= d.
proof:
Write F := \mathbb F_{q^m} (a prime power, F=p^{am}), k:=\overline{\mathbb F}_q=\overline{F}, and fix a nonzero element u\in\mathbb Q_\ell(1); as instructed, we use u to identify every Tate twist \mathbb Q_\ell(n) with \mathbb Q_\ell (u^n\mapsto 1), and in particular we regard the Poincar\'e duality traces as maps to \mathbb Q_\ell.
