For a class \zeta\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) on a smooth projective F-scheme Z of pure dimension d we write L^\zeta_m:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{n+2m}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) for cup product with \zeta^{m}.

STEP 1 (the rank r of f is a positive integer equal to the function-field degree).
The F-scheme X is smooth over a field, hence regular, hence all its local rings are domains; it is geometrically connected, hence connected. A connected locally noetherian scheme all of whose local rings are domains is integral, so X is integral; the same argument shows Y is integral. Since f is finite locally free, f_*\mathcal O_Y is a locally free \mathcal O_X-module, so its rank is a locally constant function on the connected space X; say it is the constant r. As f is surjective, every fibre is non-empty, so r\ge 1. Let \eta_X (resp. \eta_Y) be the generic point of X (resp. Y). Since f is finite and surjective between integral schemes it is closed with finite fibres, and f^{-1}(\{\eta_X\})=\{\eta_Y\}; hence the generic fibre is \operatorname{Spec}\bigl((f_*\mathcal O_Y)_{\eta_X}\bigr)=\operatorname{Spec} k(Y), a one-point scheme. But (f_*\mathcal O_Y)_{\eta_X} is a finite-dimensional k(X)-algebra of dimension r. Thus k(Y) is a field extension of k(X) of degree r:
  r=[k(Y):k(X)]\ge 1.
In particular r is a positive integer, hence an invertible element of \mathbb Q_\ell.

STEP 2 (finite-dimensionality).
X and Y are proper over F. Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob (with the prime power F=p^{am} in the role of its \mathbb F_q, and with K=\mathbb Q_\ell the constant sheaf equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism) to X and to Y, we obtain that for every n\ge 0 the groups H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) are finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces.

STEP 3 (Poincar\'e duality pairings, and the dimension symmetry).
X and Y are smooth, projective, geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F. Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_77 to each of them (with \mathbb F_{q^m} in the role of that lemma's \mathbb F_{q^m}, m=1) we obtain, for Z\in\{X,Y\}, a trace isomorphism \operatorname{tr}_Z:H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathbb Q_\ell(-d), normalised by \operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):F] for closed points z of Z, such that for every 0\le n\le 2d the pairing
  \langle a,b\rangle_Z \;:=\; \operatorname{tr}_Z(a\cup b),\qquad a\in H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\ b\in H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),
viewed in \mathbb Q_\ell via the identification of Step 0, is PERFECT. Since all spaces involved are finite-dimensional (Step 2), perfectness gives a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism H^{2d-n}(Z_k)\simeq H^n(Z_k)^{\vee}, hence
  \dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell} H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=\dim_{\mathbb Q_\ell} H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\qquad\text{for all }0\le n\le 2d,\ Z\in\{X,Y\}.   (3.1)

STEP 4 (the Gysin/pushforward map for f, defined by adjunction).
Fix n with 0\le n\le d and let a\in H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). The map
  \lambda_a:H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow\mathbb Q_\ell,\qquad b\longmapsto \operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(a\cup f^*b\bigr),
is \mathbb Q_\ell-linear, because f^*, \cup and \operatorname{tr}_Y are \mathbb Q_\ell-linear. By perfectness of \langle\,,\rangle_X (Step 3) there is a UNIQUE element c\in H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) with \operatorname{tr}_X(c\cup b)=\lambda_a(b) for every b. We define f_*a:=c. The assignment a\mapsto f_*a is \mathbb Q_\ell-linear (uniqueness plus linearity of everything involved). Thus we have a well-defined \mathbb Q_\ell-linear homomorphism
  f_*:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)
satisfying, for all a\in H^n(Y_k) and all b\in H^{2d-n}(X_k),
  \operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(f_*a\cup b\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(a\cup f^*b\bigr).   (4.1)

STEP 5 (behaviour of the traces under f^*).
The morphism f is finite, hence proper; it is surjective by hypothesis; it is quasi-finite (finite fibres, since f is finite) and dominant, hence generically finite; and by Step 1 its degree [k(Y):k(X)] is r. Thus f:Y\to X satisfies the hypotheses of eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_top_trace_generically_finite (applied with \mathbb F_{q^m} in the role of that lemma's \mathbb F_q, with source Y, target X and D=d). Its conclusion, with the traces normalised exactly as in Step 3 (both are the Poincar\'e duality traces with \operatorname{tr}_Z(\mathrm{cl}(z))=[\kappa(z):F]), is that
  \operatorname{tr}_Y\circ f^*\circ\operatorname{tr}_X^{-1}
acts on \mathbb Q_\ell(-d) as multiplication by r; equivalently,
  \operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(f^*\omega\bigr)=r\,\operatorname{tr}_X(\omega)\qquad\text{for every }\omega\in H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).   (5.1)

STEP 6 (f_*\circ f^*=r\cdot\mathrm{id}).
Let x\in H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and b\in H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). Pullback on \mathrm{\acute et}ale cohomology is a homomorphism of graded \mathbb Q_\ell-algebras, so f^*(x\cup b)=f^*x\cup f^*b. Using (4.1) with a=f^*x, then (5.1) with \omega=x\cup b (note \deg(x\cup b)=2d), and finally \mathbb Q_\ell-linearity of \operatorname{tr}_X and of the cup product,
  \operatorname{tr}_X\bigl(f_*f^*x\cup b\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(f^*x\cup f^*b\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}_Y\bigl(f^*(x\cup b)\bigr)=r\,\operatorname{tr}_X(x\cup b)=\operatorname{tr}_X\bigl((r\,x)\cup b\bigr).
Since \langle\,,\rangle_X is perfect, the class in H^n(X_k) whose cup product with every b pairs as above is unique; hence f_*f^*x=r\,x. As this holds for all x,
  f_*\circ f^*=r\cdot\mathrm{id}_{H^n(X_k)}.   (6.1)

STEP 7 (f^* is injective).
Let x\in H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) with f^*x=0. Then by (6.1), r\,x=f_*f^*x=f_*0=0. Since r\ge 1 is a positive integer, r^{-1}\in\mathbb Q_\ell, so x=0. Hence f^* is injective in every degree.

STEP 8 (injectivity of cup product with \xi^{d-n} on X).
Fix n with 0\le n\le d and let x\in H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) satisfy x\cup\xi^{\,d-n}=0. Applying the ring homomorphism f^* and using \eta=f^*\xi together with functoriality of the cup product,
  0=f^*\bigl(x\cup\xi^{\,d-n}\bigr)=f^*x\cup (f^*\xi)^{d-n}=f^*x\cup\eta^{\,d-n}.
By hypothesis L^\eta_{d-n}:H^n(Y_k)\to H^{2d-n}(Y_k),\ u\mapsto u\cup\eta^{d-n}, is an isomorphism, hence injective; therefore f^*x=0, and Step 7 gives x=0. Thus L^\xi_{d-n} is injective.

STEP 9 (injective \Rightarrow isomorphism).
By (3.1) applied to Z=X, both H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) are finite-dimensional \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces of the same dimension. An injective \mathbb Q_\ell-linear map between finite-dimensional vector spaces of equal dimension is surjective, hence an isomorphism. Therefore
  L^\xi_{d-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\longrightarrow H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\quad x\longmapsto x\cup\xi^{\,d-n},
is an isomorphism.

STEP 10 (conclusion and edge cases).
Step 9 holds for each integer n with 0\le n\le d, which is exactly the required conclusion. The endpoint n=d is included (there L^\xi_0=\mathrm{id}, and the argument above applies verbatim since the hypothesis for n=d is that L^\eta_0=\mathrm{id} is an isomorphism); the case n=0 likewise needs no separate treatment, since injectivity of x\mapsto x\cup\xi^d was proved in Step 8 by the same argument. Note that the argument used only that \xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and that f is finite locally free surjective of positive rank; the very-ampleness and rationality of the divisor are more than needed. This completes the proof.

statement: Let S be a scheme, let E be a vector bundle on S, and let M be a line bundle on S. Write P_S(F) for the projective bundle of one-dimensional quotients of a vector bundle F, with projection pi_F:P_S(F)->S and tautological invertible sheaf O_{P_S(F)}(1). Tensoring a one-dimensional quotient q:E_T->Q of the pullback of E to an S-scheme T by M_T gives a one-dimensional quotient (E tensor M)_T->Q tensor M_T, and hence an S-morphism phi:P_S(E)->P_S(E tensor M). Then phi is an isomorphism and there is an isomorphism of invertible sheaves phi^* O_{P_S(E tensor M)}(1) isomorphic to O_{P_S(E)}(1) tensor pi_E^* M.
proof:
Proof.

Notation. Write Q := E ⊗_{O_S} M, P := P_S(E), P' := P_S(Q) = P_S(E ⊗ M), π := π_E : P → S and π' := π_Q : P' → S. For an S-scheme T with structure morphism p_T : T → S we write E_T := p_T^*E, M_T := p_T^*M, Q_T := p_T^*Q. Pullback of quasi-coherent sheaves is symmetric monoidal, so there is a canonical isomorphism of O_T-modules, natural (functorial) in T,
    θ_T : E_T ⊗_{O_T} M_T = p_T^*E ⊗_{O_T} p_T^*M  ⟶~  p_T^*(E ⊗_{O_S} M) = Q_T.
Let u : E_P ↠ O_P(1) and u' : Q_{P'} ↠ O_{P'}(1) be the universal (tautological) quotients.

Step 0 (universal property). This is the content of the phrase "the projective bundle of one-dimensional quotients": for every S-scheme T the map
    (UP_T)   Hom_S(T, P) ⟶ QuotInv(E_T),   f ↦ (f^*O_P(1), f^*u),
is a bijection, where QuotInv(F) denotes the set of isomorphism classes of pairs (L, q : F ↠ L) with L an invertible O_T-module and q surjective, and (L,q) ≅ (L_1,q_1) iff there is an O_T-linear isomorphism α : L → L_1 with α ∘ q = q_1. The analogous statement holds with P, E replaced by P', Q. Moreover the composite T → P → S (resp. T → P' → S) of the representing morphism with the projection is the structure morphism of T over S.

Step 1 (definition of φ on T-points). Define
    Φ_T : QuotInv(E_T) → QuotInv(Q_T),   Φ_T(L,q) := (L ⊗_{O_T} M_T, (q ⊗ id_{M_T}) ∘ θ_T^{-1}).
Well-definedness. The map q ⊗ id_{M_T} is surjective because tensoring a surjection of O_T-modules with the O_T-module M_T is right exact; L ⊗_{O_T} M_T is invertible because the tensor product of two invertible O_T-modules is invertible. If α : (L,q) → (L_1,q_1) is an isomorphism of quotients then α ⊗ id_{M_T} : L ⊗ M_T → L_1 ⊗ M_T satisfies (α ⊗ id) ∘ (q ⊗ id) = (q_1 ⊗ id), so Φ_T is well defined on isomorphism classes.
Functoriality. For a morphism g : T' → T over S, the identifications g^*E_T = E_{T'}, g^*M_T = M_{T'}, g^*Q_T = Q_{T'} make the square with θ_T and θ_{T'} commute, since θ is the canonical monoidal constraint for pullback and is natural in T. Hence g^*Φ_T(L,q) = Φ_{T'}(g^*L, g^*q). Thus the Φ_T assemble to a natural transformation of functors h_P → h_{P'} on Sch/S, and since Φ_T does not change the underlying T → S, it is a natural transformation over h_S. By the Yoneda lemma there is a unique S-morphism φ : P → P' with π' ∘ φ = π whose induced map on T-points is Φ_T; concretely, if f : T → P corresponds to (L,q), then φ ∘ f : T → P' corresponds to (L ⊗ M_T, (q ⊗ id) ∘ θ_T^{-1}). This φ is exactly the morphism obtained by tensoring quotients with M, as in the statement.

Step 2 (the candidate inverse on T-points). Let M_T^∨ := Hom_{O_T}(M_T, O_T). Since M_T is invertible, (M_T, M_T^∨) is a dual pair: with ev : M_T ⊗ M_T^∨ → O_T the evaluation and coev : O_T → M_T ⊗ M_T^∨ the canonical element (locally, for a local generator m of M_T and its dual functional μ with μ(m) = 1, one has coev(1) = m ⊗ μ), the triangle identities hold:
    (id_{M_T} ⊗ ev) ∘ (coev ⊗ id_{M_T}) = id_{M_T},      (ev ⊗ id_{M_T^∨}) ∘ (id_{M_T^∨} ⊗ coev) = id_{M_T^∨}.
Both are equalities of maps of invertible sheaves and are checked on an open cover trivialising M_T, where they read a ↦ a·μ(m) = a and b ↦ μ(m)·b = b.
Define κ_T : E_T → Q_T ⊗_{O_T} M_T^∨ as the composite
    E_T --id⊗coev--> E_T ⊗ M_T ⊗ M_T^∨ --θ_T⊗id--> Q_T ⊗ M_T^∨,
an isomorphism, with inverse (id ⊗ ev) ∘ θ_T^{-1} (using the evident identification Q_T ⊗ M_T^∨ ≅ E_T ⊗ M_T ⊗ M_T^∨). Define
    Ψ_T : QuotInv(Q_T) → QuotInv(E_T),   Ψ_T(L',q') := (L' ⊗_{O_T} M_T^∨, (q' ⊗ id_{M_T^∨}) ∘ κ_T).
This is well defined by the same right-exactness/invertibility argument and the same α ⊗ id argument as in Step 1 (κ_T is an isomorphism, so the composite is surjective), and it is functorial in T by the naturality of θ and of coev.

Step 3 (the composites are the identity). Equalities of O_T-module homomorphisms may be checked locally, so work over an open subset of T on which M_T is free of rank 1 with generator m and dual μ (μ(m) = 1); then coev(1) = m ⊗ μ and κ_T(e) = (e ⊗ m) ⊗ μ.
(a) Ψ_T(Φ_T(L,q)) = ((L ⊗ M_T) ⊗ M_T^∨, ((q ⊗ id_{M_T}) ∘ θ_T^{-1} ⊗ id_{M_T^∨}) ∘ κ_T). Compose the quotient map with the contraction isomorphism c_L : (L ⊗ M_T) ⊗ M_T^∨ → L, (l ⊗ m) ⊗ μ ↦ μ(m)·l. For a local section e of E_T,
    c_L( ((q ⊗ id) ∘ θ_T^{-1} ⊗ id)(κ_T(e)) ) = c_L( (q(e) ⊗ m) ⊗ μ ) = μ(m)·q(e) = q(e),
since θ_T^{-1}(e ⊗ m) = e ⊗ m. Hence the composite quotient is exactly q, and Ψ_T(Φ_T(L,q)) ≅ (L,q) via c_L; i.e. Ψ_T ∘ Φ_T = id. In basis-free form the composite is (q ⊗ id) ∘ (id ⊗ (ev ∘ (coev ⊗ id))) = q ⊗ id = q by the first triangle identity.
(b) Φ_T(Ψ_T(L',q')) = ((L' ⊗ M_T^∨) ⊗ M_T, ((q' ⊗ id_{M_T^∨}) ∘ κ_T ⊗ id_{M_T}) ∘ θ_T). Compose with the contraction c'_{L'} : (L' ⊗ M_T^∨) ⊗ M_T → L', (l ⊗ μ) ⊗ m ↦ μ(m)·l, and evaluate on the local generator e ⊗ m of Q_T = E_T ⊗ M_T. Since θ_T(e ⊗ m) = e ⊗ m,
    c'( ((q' ⊗ id) ∘ κ_T ⊗ id)(e ⊗ m) ) = c'( q''(e) ⊗ m ) where q''(e) = (q' ⊗ id)(κ_T(e)) = q'(e ⊗ m) ⊗ μ,
so the value is c'( (q'(e ⊗ m) ⊗ μ) ⊗ m ) = μ(m)·q'(e ⊗ m) = q'(e ⊗ m) = q'(x) for x = e ⊗ m. As such x generate Q_T, the composite quotient is q', whence Φ_T(Ψ_T(L',q')) ≅ (L',q'), i.e. Φ_T ∘ Ψ_T = id. Basis-free: the composite is q' ∘ (id ⊗ (ev ∘ (id ⊗ coev))) = q' by the second triangle identity.
Thus Φ_T and Ψ_T are mutually inverse bijections, natural in T.

Step 4 (φ is an isomorphism). The natural transformation Ψ : h_{P'} → h_P constructed in Step 2 is represented, again by Yoneda, by a unique S-morphism ψ : P' → P with π ∘ ψ = π'. The identities Ψ_T ∘ Φ_T = id and Φ_T ∘ Ψ_T = id proved in Step 3 say that ψ ∘ φ = id_P and φ ∘ ψ = id_{P'} (Yoneda is fully faithful, so equality of natural transformations is equality of morphisms). Hence φ is an isomorphism of S-schemes, with inverse ψ, and π' ∘ φ = π.

Step 5 (identification of the tautological bundle). Tensor the universal quotient u : E_P ↠ O_P(1) on P by the invertible sheaf π^*M. Using right exactness of ⊗ we get a surjection
    u ⊗ id_{π^*M} : E_P ⊗_{O_P} π^*M ↠ O_P(1) ⊗_{O_P} π^*M,
and the source is canonically E_P ⊗ π^*M = (E ⊗_{O_S} M) ⊗_{O_S} O_P = (E ⊗ M)_P = Q_P, where in the last equality we used that Q_P = p_P^*(E ⊗ M) for p_P = π, and also that Q_{P'} pulled back along φ equals (E ⊗ M) ⊗_{O_S} O_P because π' ∘ φ = π. Thus u ⊗ id_{π^*M} is an element of QuotInv(Q_P), i.e. an invertible quotient of Q_P.
By the definition of Φ_T in Step 1 applied to T = P and to the universal element (O_P(1), u) ∈ QuotInv(E_T) corresponding to id_P, this element is precisely Φ_P(O_P(1), u), hence by Step 1 it corresponds to the morphism φ ∘ id_P = φ : P → P'. On the other hand, by the universal property (UP_{P'}) the quotient of Q_P corresponding to φ is (φ^*O_{P'}(1), φ^*u'). Since both quotients represent the same element of QuotInv(Q_P), there exists an O_P-linear isomorphism
    φ^*O_{P'}(1)  ⟶~  O_P(1) ⊗_{O_P} π^*M
under which φ^*u' corresponds to u ⊗ id_{π^*M}. In other words,
    φ^* O_{P_S(E ⊗ M)}(1) ≅ O_{P_S(E)}(1) ⊗ π_E^* M
as invertible sheaves on P_S(E). This is the claimed relation, with the twist by π_E^*M (not by π_E^*M^∨), which is the correct direction for the quotient convention: tensoring a quotient E_T ↠ L with M raises the tautological quotient line bundle by M_T.

Step 6 (sanity check of the convention). Take S = Spec k, E = k^{⊕2}, M = k trivial. Then Q = E, φ = id_{P^1_k}, and the formula reads id^*O(1) ≅ O(1) ⊗ π^*k = O(1), which is correct. Equivalently, in the rank-1 case E = O_S^{⊕(r+1)} the universal quotient is O_P(1)^{⊕(r+1)} ↠ ... and twisting E by M replaces the universal quotient by its tensor with π^*M, again giving O_P(1) ⊗ π^*M.

This proves both assertions: φ is an isomorphism P_S(E) ⟶~ P_S(E ⊗ M) over S, and φ^*O_{P_S(E⊗M)}(1) ≅ O_{P_S(E)}(1) ⊗ π_E^*M. ∎

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(m\ge1\) and \(d\ge2\) be integers, and let \(X\subset\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb F_{q^m}}\) be a smooth geometrically connected closed subscheme of pure dimension \(d\). Then there exist an integer \(r\ge1\) divisible by \(m\) and hyperplanes \(H_1,\dots,H_{d-1}\subset\mathbb P^N_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}\) defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^r}\) such that, writing \(X_0=X_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}\) and \(X_j=X_{\mathbb F_{q^r}}\cap H_1\cap\cdots\cap H_j\) for \(1\le j\le d-1\), each \(X_j\) is smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-j\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^r}\); in particular \(X_{d-1}\) is a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over \(\mathbb F_{q^r}\).
proof:
We prove the lemma. All intersections of closed subschemes are scheme-theoretic.

Auxiliary Fact A. Let K'/K be an algebraic field extension and let Z be a scheme of finite type over K. Then: (a) if Z is smooth over K, then Z_K' is smooth over K'; (b) if Z is geometrically connected over K, then Z_K' is geometrically connected over K'; (c) if Z is pure of dimension e, then Z_K' is pure of dimension e; (d) Z is nonempty if and only if Z_K' is nonempty.

Proof of Fact A. Part (a) is stability of smoothness under base change. Part (d) follows because tensoring a nonzero K-vector space with a nonzero K-vector space is nonzero: if Spec A is a nonempty affine open of Z, then A is a nonzero K-vector space and A tensor_K K' is nonzero, since 1 tensor 1 is nonzero (for example, apply a K-linear map A -> K sending 1 to 1 and a K-linear map K' -> K sending 1 to 1 to their tensor). Thus Z_K' is nonempty.

For (b), choose an algebraic closure Omega of K containing K'. Then (Z_K')_Omega is canonically isomorphic to Z_Omega. If Z_K' were disconnected, it would have a nonempty proper open-and-closed subset U. Its complement would also be nonempty. By (d), both U_Omega and (Z_K' minus U)_Omega are nonempty, and they are open-and-closed in (Z_K')_Omega, contradicting connectedness of Z_Omega. Hence Z_K' is connected.

For (c), first assume Z=Spec A with A a finitely generated K-algebra. Put B=A tensor_K K'. Since K'/K is algebraic, B is integral over A: any element b in B is a finite sum of pure tensors, hence lies in A tensor_K L for the finite subextension L/K generated by the finitely many elements of K' appearing in the sum; A tensor_K L is finite free over A, hence integral over A.

We use the following elementary integrality fact. If A -> B is integral, q is a prime of B, and p=q cap A, then A_p -> B_q is integral. Indeed, for s in B not in q, the subalgebra C=A[s] is finite over A because s is integral over A. Let p_C=C cap q. Since s is not in q, s is not in p_C, so s is a unit in C_{p_C}. The ring C_{p_C} is finite over A_p (because C is finite over A and p_C cap A=p), so every element of C_{p_C}, in particular 1/s, is integral over A_p. Therefore every b/s in B_q is integral over A_p.

Now let q be a minimal prime of B and p=q cap A. Suppose p' is a prime of A properly contained in p. Localizing the integral extension A -> B at p and q gives an integral extension A_p -> B_q. The prime p'A_p of A_p has, by lying over for integral extensions, a prime Q of B_q lying over it. This Q corresponds to a prime q' of B with q' subset q and q' cap A=p'. Minimality of q forces q'=q, hence p'=p, contradiction. Thus p is minimal.

Then B/q is integral over A/p. The map A/p -> B/q is injective because q cap A=p. Let F=Frac(B/q). Since B/q is integral over A/p, every element of B/q is algebraic over Frac(A/p), so F is algebraic over Frac(A/p). By the standard dimension theorem for finitely generated domains over a field, dim R=trdeg_L Frac(R): if R is a finitely generated domain over L with trdeg_L Frac(R)=n, Noether normalization gives a finite injective map L[t_1,...,t_n] -> R; integral extensions preserve dimension, and dim L[t_1,...,t_n]=n. Applying this to the finitely generated K-domain A/p, whose dimension is e, gives trdeg_K Frac(A/p)=e. Since K'/K is algebraic, trdeg_{K'}F=trdeg_KF=e. Applying the same dimension theorem to the finitely generated K'-domain B/q gives dim B/q=e. Hence every irreducible component of Spec B has dimension e, so Spec B is pure of dimension e.

For a general finite type K-scheme Z, cover Z by affine opens. An irreducible component of an open subset of a finite type K-scheme is the intersection of that open subset with an irreducible component of Z. Also, every nonempty open subset of an irreducible finite type K-scheme has the same dimension as the whole irreducible scheme: reduce to affine opens, where a nonempty principal open has the same fraction field and hence the same transcendence degree, and therefore the same dimension by the dimension theorem above. Thus every nonempty affine open of Z is pure of dimension e. Applying the affine case to each affine open of Z_K' and using that every irreducible component of Z_K' meets some affine open and is an irreducible component of that affine open, we conclude that Z_K' is pure of dimension e. This proves Fact A.

Fact B. If Z is noetherian, then H^0_et(Z,Q_l) is the direct product of one copy of Q_l for each connected component of Z. Indeed, a noetherian scheme has finitely many connected components: it has finitely many irreducible components, and connected components are unions of irreducible components. These connected components are open and closed, and sections of the constant sheaf on a finite disjoint union of connected components are exactly locally constant Q_l-valued functions on the finite set of components.

Fact C. Let L be a field, let S be a smooth closed subscheme of P^N_L, pure of dimension e>=2, and let H be a hyperplane such that Y=S intersection H is smooth, nonempty, and pure of dimension e-1. Then Y is an effective ample Cartier divisor in S. Write H=V(ell) for a linear form ell, and let s be the restriction of ell to S. For x in S, the local ring O_{S,x} is regular local, hence a domain. If the germ s_x were zero, then s would vanish on an open neighborhood of x, hence on the irreducible component of S containing x; that component would be contained in Y, contradicting that Y has pure dimension e-1 while S is pure of dimension e. Thus s_x is a nonzero element of a domain, hence a nonzerodivisor. Therefore Y is an effective Cartier divisor. Its associated line bundle is O_S(1), which is ample because O(1) is ample on projective space and ampleness is preserved by restriction to closed subschemes. Hence Y is ample.

Main proof. Let k be an algebraic closure of F_q and choose a prime l not equal to p.

Case 1: d<N. Put K_0=F_{q^m}, r_0=m, and S_0=X_{K_0}. Then S_0 is a smooth projective geometrically connected closed subscheme of P^N_{K_0}, nonempty and pure of dimension d. We construct S_j and K_j=F_{q^{r_j}} for j=0,...,d-1 inductively. Suppose S_j is smooth projective geometrically connected nonempty pure of dimension e=d-j. Since 2<=e<=N-1, apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_581_bertini_hyperplane_section to S_j, using the prime power q^{r_j} in place of q. There exist an integer mu_j>=1 and a hyperplane H_{j+1} over K_{j+1}=F_{q^{r_j mu_j}} such that S_{j+1}=S_j times_{K_j} K_{j+1} intersection H_{j+1} is smooth, nonempty, and pure of dimension e-1. It is a closed subscheme of P^N_{K_{j+1}}, hence projective.

It remains to prove S_{j+1} geometrically connected. Let T_j=(S_j)_k and T_{j+1}=(S_{j+1})_k. By Fact A, T_j is smooth projective pure of dimension e and connected, and T_{j+1} is smooth nonempty pure of dimension e-1. By Fact C, T_{j+1} is an effective ample Cartier divisor in T_j. Since T_j is smooth, connected, and finite type over the algebraically closed field k, it is integral: regular local rings are domains, and if two irreducible components met, the local ring at a point of intersection would have zero divisors; connectedness then forces a single component. Therefore Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_420 applies to T_j and T_{j+1}. Taking cohomological degree 0, which is allowed because e>=2, lemma_420 gives an isomorphism H^0_et(T_j,Q_l) -> H^0_et(T_{j+1},Q_l). By Fact B, connectedness of T_j implies H^0_et(T_j,Q_l) is one-dimensional over Q_l; hence H^0_et(T_{j+1},Q_l) is one-dimensional, so T_{j+1} is connected. Thus S_{j+1} is geometrically connected over K_{j+1}. This completes Case 1.

Case 2: d=N. Since X is smooth, it is reduced. The scheme P^N is integral. A proper closed subscheme of P^N has all irreducible components of dimension strictly less than N: this is the standard dimension theorem for projective space, obtained by covering by affine spaces and applying Krull's principal ideal theorem on affine charts. Hence a reduced closed subscheme of pure dimension N must be all of P^N. Thus X=P^N. Choose an F_{q^m}-rational hyperplane H_1, for example X_0=0. Put K_1=F_{q^m}, r_1=m, and S_1=P^{N-1}_{K_1}. This is smooth projective geometrically connected nonempty pure of dimension N-1. If N=2, this is already the desired curve. If N>=3, repeat the inductive step of Case 1 for j=1,...,N-2: at step j, e=N-j satisfies 2<=e<=N-1, apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_581_bertini_hyperplane_section to S_j to obtain K_{j+1}=F_{q^{r_j mu_j}}, a hyperplane H_{j+1} over K_{j+1}, and S_{j+1}=S_j times_{K_j}K_{j+1} intersection H_{j+1}; prove geometric connectedness exactly as in Case 1 using Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_420.

Final assembly. Let r=r_{d-1}. In both cases the integers r_j form a divisibility chain starting from r_0=m (in Case 2 one may also set S_0=X_{F_{q^m}} and r_0=m), so r is divisible by m and every K_j is contained in K_r=F_{q^r}. Define X_j=(S_j)_{K_r} for 0<=j<=d-1. Since base change commutes with scheme-theoretic intersections and each H_i is defined over K_i subset K_r, we have X_j=X_{K_r} intersection H_1 intersection ... intersection H_j. By Fact A, each X_j is smooth, geometrically connected, and pure of dimension d-j over K_r. In particular X_{d-1} is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension 1, i.e. a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over F_{q^r}. This proves the lemma.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be smooth projective geometrically connected varieties of pure dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), and let \(F_X\), \(F_Y\) be the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius automorphisms on their \(\ell\)-adic cohomology. Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Let \(\Gamma\in H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k\times Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the cycle class of a codimension-\(d\) algebraic cycle on \(X\times Y\) defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\). For \(n\ge0\), let \(L_\Gamma:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the map obtained by pullback to \(X_k\times Y_k\), cup product with \(\Gamma\), and Gysin pushforward along the projection to \(Y_k\). Suppose \(L_\Gamma\circ F_X=F_Y\circ L_\Gamma\), \(L_\Gamma\) is injective, and \(F_Y\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\). Then \(F_X\) is semisimple on \(H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
proof:
Write K = Q_\ell and \bar K = \overline{Q}_\ell. Set
  V := H^n_{\acute et}(X_k, Q_\ell),  W := H^n_{\acute et}(Y_k, Q_\ell),  T := F_X|_V,  S := F_Y|_W,  L := L_\Gamma : V \to W.
The only properties of the geometric construction of L_\Gamma (pullback to X_k \times Y_k, cup product with the cycle class \Gamma, Gysin pushforward along the second projection) that we use are the three hypotheses stated: L is a K-linear map, it satisfies L\circ T = S\circ L, it is injective, and S is semisimple. The proof is therefore a statement about linear operators, plus the finiteness needed to speak about eigenvalues.

STEP 0 (finite-dimensionality, and invertibility of the Frobenius operators).
Both X and Y are proper over \mathbb F_{q^m}. View X (resp. Y) as a proper variety over the finite field \mathbb F_{q^m}; the constant sheaf Q_\ell on X_k (resp. Y_k) is lisse of rank 1 on the Noetherian scheme X_k (resp. Y_k), hence is an object of D^b_c(X_k, Q_\ell) (resp. D^b_c(Y_k, Q_\ell)), and it carries its natural arithmetic-Frobenius isomorphism \psi: F^*Q_\ell \xrightarrow{\sim} Q_\ell. Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob with the prime power q^m in the role of q (and with K = Q_\ell, \phi = \psi) gives that H^n_{\acute et}(X_k, Q_\ell) and H^n_{\acute et}(Y_k, Q_\ell) are finite-dimensional K-vector spaces. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a (again with \mathbb F_{q^m} in the role of \mathbb F_q), the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius pullback is a K-linear automorphism of each of these spaces; this agrees with the statement's description of F_X, F_Y as automorphisms. In particular T \in GL_K(V) and S \in GL_K(W), and both V and W are finite-dimensional.
(Edge case: if V = 0 there is nothing to prove, since the zero operator on the zero space is semisimple; the argument below covers this case as well, with all sums indexed by the empty set.)

STEP 1 (the image of L is S-stable, and L conjugates T to S|_{\operatorname{im} L}).
Let w \in \operatorname{im} L, say w = L(v) with v \in V. Then, using the intertwining hypothesis,
  S(w) = S(L(v)) = (L\circ T)(v) = L(Tv) \in \operatorname{im} L.
Hence U_0 := \operatorname{im} L \subseteq W is an S-stable K-linear subspace. Since L is injective, L: V \xrightarrow{\sim} U_0 is a K-linear isomorphism, and the relation L\circ T = S\circ L says precisely that
  L \circ T \circ L^{-1} = S|_{U_0},
so T and S|_{U_0} are conjugate K-linear operators.

STEP 2 (base change to \bar K).
Tensoring with \bar K over K is exact (\bar K is a flat, indeed free, K-module), so the \bar K-linear map
  L_{\bar K} := L \otimes_K \mathrm{id}_{\bar K} : V_{\bar K} := V\otimes_K \bar K \longrightarrow W_{\bar K} := W\otimes_K \bar K
is still injective; it is the operator obtained by extending scalars from L. Likewise T_{\bar K} := T\otimes 1 and S_{\bar K} := S\otimes 1 satisfy
  L_{\bar K}\circ T_{\bar K} = S_{\bar K}\circ L_{\bar K}
(both sides are \bar K-linear and agree on the spanning set v\otimes 1, since they agree there because L\circ T = S\circ L). Put U := \operatorname{im} L_{\bar K} \subseteq W_{\bar K}. Repeating the computation of Step 1 over \bar K, for u = L_{\bar K}(\xi) \in U one has S_{\bar K}(u) = L_{\bar K}(T_{\bar K}\xi) \in U, so U is S_{\bar K}-stable, and
  L_{\bar K}: V_{\bar K} \xrightarrow{\sim} U, \qquad L_{\bar K}\circ T_{\bar K}\circ L_{\bar K}^{-1} = S_{\bar K}|_U .   (1)
Thus T_{\bar K} is conjugate over \bar K to the restriction of S_{\bar K} to the stable subspace U.

STEP 3 (S_{\bar K} is diagonalisable, with a finite eigenvalue decomposition).
By hypothesis S is semisimple on W, and by Step 0 W is finite-dimensional over K = Q_\ell. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5 (applied to W and S), S is semisimple on W if and only if S_{\bar K} is diagonalisable on W_{\bar K}; hence S_{\bar K} is diagonalisable. Since W_{\bar K} is finite-dimensional, S_{\bar K} has only finitely many distinct eigenvalues; list them \alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r \in \bar K (r = 0 exactly when W_{\bar K} = 0). Diagonalisability means that the characteristic (equivalently minimal) polynomial of S_{\bar K} splits over \bar K as \prod_{j=1}^r (t-\alpha_j) with each root simple, and therefore
  W_{\bar K} = \bigoplus_{j=1}^{r} E_j, \qquad E_j := \ker(S_{\bar K}-\alpha_j),
the eigenspace decomposition. (Explicitly: the polynomials \prod_{i\ne j}(t-\alpha_i) annihilate E_j and the Chinese remainder theorem in \bar K[t] applied to \bar K[t]/(\prod_i(t-\alpha_i)) \cong \prod_j \bar K gives the decomposition into the kernels; and every vector of E_j is an eigenvector by definition.)

STEP 4 (U is the direct sum of its intersections with the eigenspaces).
For 1 \le j \le r define the Lagrange interpolation polynomial
  p_j(t) := \prod_{1\le i\le r,\, i\ne j} \frac{t-\alpha_i}{\alpha_j-\alpha_i} \;\in\; \bar K[t],
which is well defined because the \alpha_i are pairwise distinct (so \alpha_j-\alpha_i \ne 0); it satisfies p_j(\alpha_i) = \delta_{ij}. The operator P_j := p_j(S_{\bar K}) is the projection of W_{\bar K} onto E_j along \bigoplus_{i\ne j} E_i: indeed, under the isomorphism \bar K[t]/(\prod_i(t-\alpha_i)) \cong \prod_i \bar K, the class of p_j maps to the tuple (\delta_{ij})_i, so P_j acts as the identity on E_j and as 0 on E_i for i\ne j.

Now U is S_{\bar K}-stable by Step 2, hence U is stable under every polynomial in S_{\bar K}, in particular under each P_j. For an arbitrary u \in U we have
  u = \mathrm{id}(u) = \Big(\textstyle\sum_{j=1}^r P_j\Big)(u) = \sum_{j=1}^r P_j u,
since \sum_j p_j(t) - 1 vanishes at each of the r distinct roots \alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r of the minimal polynomial of S_{\bar K}, hence is divisible by that minimal polynomial and \sum_j P_j = \mathrm{id}. Each P_j u lies in U (stability) and in E_j (image of P_j). Therefore
  U = \sum_{j=1}^r (U\cap E_j),
and the sum is direct because the sum \sum_j E_j inside W_{\bar K} is direct. (When U = 0 the right-hand side is the empty/zero sum, and the equality still holds.)

STEP 5 (S_{\bar K}|_U is diagonalisable).
Choose for each j a \bar K-basis B_j of U\cap E_j. By Step 4, B := \bigsqcup_j B_j is a \bar K-basis of U, and every element of B is an eigenvector of S_{\bar K} (with eigenvalue \alpha_j). Hence the matrix of S_{\bar K}|_U in the basis B is diagonal, i.e. S_{\bar K}|_U is diagonalisable.

STEP 6 (descent of diagonalisability along the conjugacy (1)).
We spell out the conjugation explicitly rather than quoting it. For each b \in B, injectivity of L_{\bar K} gives a unique \tilde b \in V_{\bar K} with L_{\bar K}(\tilde b) = b. Since b \in E_j, S_{\bar K} b = \alpha_j b, and by the intertwining relation
  L_{\bar K}(T_{\bar K}\tilde b) = S_{\bar K}(L_{\bar K}\tilde b) = S_{\bar K} b = \alpha_j b = L_{\bar K}(\alpha_j\tilde b).
Injectivity of L_{\bar K} yields T_{\bar K}\tilde b = \alpha_j\tilde b, so each \tilde b is an eigenvector of T_{\bar K}. Moreover B spans U and L_{\bar K} is surjective onto U, so every \xi \in V_{\bar K} satisfies L_{\bar K}\xi = \sum_b \lambda_b b = L_{\bar K}\big(\sum_b\lambda_b\tilde b\big), whence \xi = \sum_b \lambda_b\tilde b by injectivity; and the \tilde b are linearly independent because L_{\bar K} is injective. Thus \{\tilde b\}_{b\in B} is a \bar K-basis of V_{\bar K} consisting of eigenvectors of T_{\bar K}, i.e. T_{\bar K} is diagonalisable on V_{\bar K}.

STEP 7 (conclusion).
V is finite-dimensional over K = Q_\ell (Step 0) and T_{\bar K} = T\otimes_K \bar K is diagonalisable on V\otimes_K\bar K (Step 6). Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5 in the reverse direction, T = F_X is semisimple on H^n_{\acute et}(X_k, Q_\ell). This is exactly the desired conclusion, for the given n.

The argument used no property of n and no property of the cycle \Gamma beyond the stated hypotheses on L_\Gamma, so it holds for every n \ge 0 (including n > 2d, where both groups vanish by finiteness/vanishing and the claim is vacuous, and including n = 0). This completes the proof.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power and \(\ell\neq p\) a prime, let \(Y\) be a smooth projective variety of pure dimension \(d\ge0\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(N\) be a vector bundle of rank \(r\ge1\) on \(Y\) defined over \(\mathbb F_q\), let \(B=\mathbb P_Y(N\oplus\mathcal O_Y)\) be the projective bundle of one-dimensional quotients, let \(Z_0\subset B\) be the section induced by the surjection \(N\oplus\mathcal O_Y\to\mathcal O_Y\), let \(j:V:=B\setminus Z_0\hookrightarrow B\) be the complementary open immersion, and let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Then for every integer \(n\ge0\) there is an exact sequence of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces \[ 0\to H^{n-2r}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)(-r)\longrightarrow H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(B_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\;j^*\;} H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to 0, \] with the convention that \(H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)=0\) for \(m<0\).
proof:
PROOF. Throughout, $H^m(Z_k)$ abbreviates $H^m_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Z_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)$, and $H^m(Z_k):=0$ for $m<0$. Fix once and for all a nonzero element of $\mathbb Q_\ell(1)$; this is the convention under which the first Chern class of a line bundle is viewed as a class in $H^2(-,\mathbb Q_\ell)$ in the cited projective-bundle lemma, and all twists will be re-inserted only at the very end (Step 7).

NOTATION. Let $\pi:B=\mathbb P_Y(N\oplus\mathcal O_Y)\to Y$ be the structural morphism (quotient convention), $\mathcal O_B(1)$ the universal quotient of $\pi^*(N\oplus\mathcal O_Y)$, and $\xi:=c_1(\mathcal O_B(1))\in H^2(B_k)$. Let $S:=\mathbb P_Y(N)$, with projection $\rho:S\to Y$, universal quotient line bundle $\mathcal O_S(1)$ of $\rho^*N$, and $\eta:=c_1(\mathcal O_S(1))\in H^2(S_k)$. Let $i_\infty:S\hookrightarrow B$ be the closed immersion classifying the quotient $N\oplus\mathcal O_Y\twoheadrightarrow N$, and $Z_0\subset B$ the closed subscheme (a section of $\pi$) classifying the quotient $N\oplus\mathcal O_Y\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal O_Y$; this is exactly the $Z_0$ of the statement, since a quotient by a line bundle is the same as a section of the quotient-convention projective bundle.

STEP 1 (the complement is a line bundle over $\mathbb P_Y(N)$). Apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_complement_of_section_is_tautological_line_bundle with its base scheme $S$ equal to our $Y$ and its bundle $N$ equal to our $N$ (its rank $c$ is our $r\ge1$, so the hypothesis $c\ge1$ holds). It yields an isomorphism of $Y$-schemes
$$\Theta:V=B\setminus Z_0\;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\;\mathrm{Tot}_S(\mathcal O_S(1)),$$
which on $T$-points sends a quotient $q:N_T\oplus\mathcal O_{Y,T}\twoheadrightarrow L$ (with $L$ invertible) to the pair consisting of the $T$-point $q|_{N_T}\in\mathbb P_Y(N)(T)=S(T)$ and the section $q(0,1)\in\Gamma(T,L)$ of the pullback of $\mathcal O_S(1)$. (In particular $q|_{N_T}$ is surjective for every $T$-point of $V$: at geometric points this is because a nonzero map to a $1$-dimensional space is surjective, and the condition is open; the lemma asserts the displayed formula defines a morphism into $\mathrm{Tot}_S(\mathcal O_S(1))$, whose $T$-points are by definition pairs $(s:T\to S,\sigma\in\Gamma(T,s^*\mathcal O_S(1)))$, so $q|_{N_T}$ must be a quotient.) Let $\mathrm{pr}:V\to S$ be the induced projection. The construction is functorial in the base and all input data ($N$, $N\oplus\mathcal O_Y$, the two quotient maps) are defined over $\mathbb F_q$; hence $\Theta$ and $\mathrm{pr}$ are defined over $\mathbb F_q$, and after base change to $k$ we have $V_k\simeq\mathrm{Tot}_{S_k}(\mathcal O_{S_k}(1))$ with $\mathrm{pr}_k$ the projection. Note that this total space uses exactly the convention $\mathrm{Tot}(\mathcal L)=\underline{\mathrm{Spec}}_{\mathcal O}\bigoplus_{m\ge0}\mathrm{Sym}^m\mathcal L^\vee$ of the homotopy-invariance lemma quoted in Step 3, since for that scheme $\mathrm{Hom}_S(T,\mathrm{Tot}(\mathcal L))=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal O_T\text{-alg}}(\mathrm{Sym}(s^*\mathcal L^\vee),\mathcal O_T)=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal O_T}(s^*\mathcal L^\vee,\mathcal O_T)=\Gamma(T,s^*\mathcal L)$.
Because $\Theta$ is an isomorphism of $Y$-schemes, $\pi\circ j=\rho\circ\mathrm{pr}$ as morphisms $V\to Y$.

STEP 2 (compatibility of hyperplane classes). We claim $j^*\mathcal O_B(1)\simeq\mathrm{pr}^*\mathcal O_S(1)$ and hence $j^*\xi=\mathrm{pr}^*\eta$. For any $Y$-scheme $T$ and any $T$-point $q:N_T\oplus\mathcal O_T\twoheadrightarrow L$ of $V$, the pullback of $\mathcal O_B(1)$ is $L$ together with the quotient $q$, while the pullback of $\mathrm{pr}^*\mathcal O_S(1)$ is $L$ together with the quotient $q|_{N_T}$ (by the description of $\mathrm{pr}$ in Step 1 and the universal property of $\mathcal O_S(1)$). The identity of $L$ is therefore an isomorphism of the two pulled-back line bundles, compatible with the two quotient maps. By the universal property of $\mathcal O_B(1)$ and $\mathcal O_S(1)$ these fiberwise identifications come from a unique $\mathcal O_V$-linear map $\alpha:j^*\mathcal O_B(1)\to\mathrm{pr}^*\mathcal O_S(1)$; on every geometric fiber $\alpha$ is the identity of the $1$-dimensional vector space $L$, so $\alpha$ is an isomorphism (a map of line bundles which is an isomorphism on all geometric fibers is an isomorphism). Functoriality of $c_1$ for isomorphic line bundles and its compatibility with pullback give $j^*\xi=c_1(j^*\mathcal O_B(1))=c_1(\mathrm{pr}^*\mathcal O_S(1))=\mathrm{pr}^*\eta$. Combining with $\pi j=\rho\,\mathrm{pr}$, for all $a\ge0$ and all $x\in H^*(Y_k)$,
$$j^*\big(\pi^*x\smile\xi^a\big)=\mathrm{pr}^*\big(\rho^*x\smile\eta^a\big).\tag{1}$$

STEP 3 (bases). $Y$ is smooth projective over $\mathbb F_q$; $N\oplus\mathcal O_Y$ has rank $r+1$ and $N$ has rank $r$. The projective bundle theorem eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_110 (which assumes only smooth projectivity of the base, not geometric connectedness) gives, for every $n$, $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphisms
$$\Phi_{B,n}:\bigoplus_{a=0}^{r}H^{n-2a}(Y_k)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^n(B_k),\quad (x_a)\mapsto\textstyle\sum_{a}\pi^*x_a\smile\xi^a,$$
$$\Phi_{S,n}:\bigoplus_{a=0}^{r-1}H^{n-2a}(Y_k)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^n(S_k),\quad (y_a)\mapsto\textstyle\sum_{a}\rho^*y_a\smile\eta^a.$$
$S$ is smooth projective of pure dimension $d+r-1\ge0$ over $\mathbb F_q$ (projective bundle over $Y$; $N$ is defined over $\mathbb F_q$), and $\mathcal O_S(1)$ is defined over $\mathbb F_q$. Apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_homotopy_invariance_pure_dimension with its base $Y$ equal to our $S$ (its $m=1$) and its bundle $E$ equal to $\mathcal O_S(1)$ (rank $1\ge1$): for every $n$, $\mathrm{pr}_k^*:H^n(S_k)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^n(V_k)$ is an isomorphism. (That lemma requires no geometric connectedness of the base, so no reduction step is needed.) Set $\Psi_n:=\mathrm{pr}_k^*\circ\Phi_{S,n}:\bigoplus_{a=0}^{r-1}H^{n-2a}(Y_k)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^n(V_k)$.

STEP 4 (the relation for $\eta$). Since $\Phi_{S,2r}$ is an isomorphism, there are unique $u_b\in H^{2r-2b}(Y_k)$, $0\le b\le r-1$, with
$$\eta^r=\textstyle\sum_{b=0}^{r-1}\rho^*u_b\smile\eta^b.\tag{2}$$
More generally, for each $a\ge0$, since $\Phi_{S,2a}$ is an isomorphism, there are unique $v_{a,b}\in H^{2a-2b}(Y_k)$ ($0\le b\le r-1$; automatically $v_{a,b}=0$ for $b>a$) with
$$\eta^a=\textstyle\sum_{b=0}^{r-1}\rho^*v_{a,b}\smile\eta^b.\tag{3}$$
Taking $a=b$ and comparing with the manifest expansion $\eta^b=\rho^*(1)\smile\eta^b$, uniqueness gives $v_{b,b}=1$ and $v_{b,c}=0$ for $c<b$; also $v_{0,0}=1$, $v_{0,c}=0$ for $c>0$, and $v_{r,b}=u_b$. Since $\rho^*$ is a graded ring homomorphism and all $\eta^b$ have even degree (so no Koszul signs occur), (3) implies for every $x\in H^m(Y_k)$
$$\rho^*x\smile\eta^a=\textstyle\sum_{b=0}^{r-1}\rho^*(x\smile v_{a,b})\smile\eta^b,\tag{4}$$
for the right side equals $\rho^*x\smile\big(\sum_b\rho^*v_{a,b}\eta^b\big)=\rho^*x\smile\eta^a$ and the expansion in the basis $\{\eta^0,\dots,\eta^{r-1}\}$ over $\rho^*H^*(Y_k)$ is unique.

STEP 5 (the matrix of the map). Put $A_a:=H^{n-2a}(Y_k)$ for $0\le a\le r$, $E_n:=\bigoplus_{a=0}^{r}A_a$, $F_n:=\bigoplus_{b=0}^{r-1}A_b$, and
$$f_n:=\Psi_n^{-1}\circ j^*\circ\Phi_{B,n}:E_n\longrightarrow F_n,$$
a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear map. For $x=(x_0,\dots,x_r)\in E_n$, using (1) and then (4) (and $v_{a,b}=0$ for $b>a$, $v_{b,b}=1$),
$$j^*\Phi_{B,n}(x)=\mathrm{pr}^*\Big(\sum_{a=0}^{r}\rho^*x_a\smile\eta^a\Big)=\mathrm{pr}^*\Big(\sum_{b=0}^{r-1}\rho^*\Big(x_b+\sum_{a=b+1}^{r}x_a\smile v_{a,b}\Big)\smile\eta^b\Big).$$
The products $x_a\smile v_{a,b}$ land in $H^{(n-2a)+(2a-2b)}(Y_k)=H^{n-2b}(Y_k)=A_b$, so the expression is well defined. Since $\Psi_n=\mathrm{pr}_k^*\circ\Phi_{S,n}$ is an isomorphism, comparing $\eta$-coefficients yields
$$f_n(x)_b=x_b+\sum_{a=b+1}^{r}x_a\smile v_{a,b},\qquad 0\le b\le r-1.\tag{5}$$

STEP 6 (surjectivity and kernel of $f_n$). For $m\le r-1$ put $W_m:=\bigoplus_{a=0}^{m}A_a\subseteq E_n$; note $F_n=W_{r-1}$. Define $T:W_{r-1}\to W_{r-1}$ by $T(x)_b=\sum_{a=b+1}^{r-1}x_a\smile v_{a,b}$. Then $T(W_m)\subseteq W_{m-1}$ for all $m$ (the term $x_a$ with $a\ge b+1$ has $a\le m$), so $T^r=0$, and $\mathrm{id}+T$ is an automorphism of $W_{r-1}$ with inverse $\sum_{k=0}^{r-1}(-T)^k$.

Surjectivity. Given $y\in F_n=W_{r-1}$, choose $x_{<r}\in W_{r-1}$ with $(\mathrm{id}+T)x_{<r}=y$ and set $x_a=0$ for $a\ge r$. Then (5) gives $f_n(x)=y$.

Kernel. Set $\zeta:=\xi^r-\sum_{b=0}^{r-1}\pi^*u_b\smile\xi^b\in H^{2r}(B_k)$ and define $\kappa:A_r\to E_n$ by $\kappa(x):=\Phi_{B,n}^{-1}(\pi^*x\smile\zeta)$.
(i) $p_r\circ\kappa=\mathrm{id}_{A_r}$, where $p_r:E_n\to A_r$ is the projection to the last factor: indeed $\pi^*x\smile\zeta=\pi^*x\smile\xi^r+\sum_{b<r}\pi^*(-x\smile u_b)\smile\xi^b$ (using $\pi^*x\smile\pi^*u_b=\pi^*(x\smile u_b)$) is an expansion in the basis of $\Phi_{B,n}$, whose coefficients are unique because $\Phi_{B,n}$ is an isomorphism; the coefficient of $\xi^r$ is $x$. Hence $\kappa$ is injective.
(ii) $\mathrm{im}\,\kappa\subseteq\ker f_n$: by (1) applied with $a=r$ and with $a=b$, together with (2),
$$j^*(\pi^*x\smile\zeta)=\mathrm{pr}^*\Big(\rho^*x\smile\Big(\eta^r-\sum_{b=0}^{r-1}\rho^*u_b\smile\eta^b\Big)\Big)=\mathrm{pr}^*(\rho^*x\smile 0)=0,$$
so $f_n\kappa(x)=\Psi_n^{-1}(0)=0$.
(iii) $p_r|_{\ker f_n}$ is injective: if $x\in\ker f_n$ with $x_r=0$, then $x\in W_{r-1}$ and $0=f_n(x)=(\mathrm{id}+T)x$, so $x=0$.
From (i)--(iii), $\ker f_n=\mathrm{im}\,\kappa$ and $p_r:\ker f_n\xrightarrow{\sim}A_r$ is an isomorphism with inverse $\kappa$. Translating by the isomorphism $\Phi_{B,n}$,
$$\ker j^*=\{\,\pi^*x\smile\zeta\ :\ x\in H^{n-2r}(Y_k)\,\},\qquad x\longmapsto\pi^*x\smile\zeta\ \text{is a bijection }H^{n-2r}(Y_k)\xrightarrow{\sim}\ker j^*.\tag{6}$$

STEP 7 (the exact sequence). Since $f_n$ is surjective and $\Phi_{B,n},\Psi_n$ are isomorphisms, $j^*=\Psi_n\circ f_n\circ\Phi_{B,n}^{-1}$ is surjective: exactness at $H^n(V_k)$. Exactness at $H^n(B_k)$ is precisely (6). Exactness at $0\to$ the left term is the injectivity of $\iota$ constructed next.

It remains to produce the injection out of the Tate-twisted group. By (6), $\theta:H^{n-2r}(Y_k)\xrightarrow{\sim}\ker j^*$, $\theta(x)=\pi^*x\smile\zeta$, is a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism. The space $\mathbb Q_\ell(-r)$ is $1$-dimensional over $\mathbb Q_\ell$; choose a $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear isomorphism $\lambda:\mathbb Q_\ell(-r)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbb Q_\ell$ and define
$$\iota:H^{n-2r}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)(-r)\longrightarrow H^n(B_k,\mathbb Q_\ell),\qquad \iota(x\otimes t):=\lambda(t)\,\big(\pi^*x\smile\zeta\big).$$
This is $\mathbb Q_\ell$-linear and equals $\theta\circ(\mathrm{id}\otimes\lambda)$, hence is an isomorphism onto $\ker j^*$. (Only existence of such an $\iota$ is asserted, so the choice of $\lambda$ is immaterial; no Frobenius equivariance is claimed.)

Edge cases. If $n<2r$, then $n-2r<0$, so $H^{n-2r}(Y_k)=0$ by the convention of the statement; then $A_r=0$, (6) gives $\ker j^*=0$, and $j^*$ is an isomorphism, so $0\to 0\to H^n(B_k)\xrightarrow{j^*}H^n(V_k)\to0$ is exact, which is the asserted sequence. If $n\ge2r$, the sequence $0\to H^{n-2r}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)(-r)\xrightarrow{\iota}H^n(B_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{j^*}H^n(V_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to0$ is exact by the preceding paragraph. (Consistently, in degree $n<2r$ the map $f_n$ is an isomorphism: all summands $A_a$ with $2a>n$ vanish and (5) is 'identity plus strictly upper triangular' on the surviving range.)

This establishes the claimed short exact sequence for every $n\ge0$. $\blacksquare$

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let l != p be prime, let m >= 1, and put k = overline(F_q). Let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d >= 1 over F_{q^m}. Suppose there exist an integer m' >= 1 divisible by m, smooth projective geometrically connected curves C_1,...,C_r over F_{q^{m'}}, and a proper surjective generically finite morphism C_1 x_{F_{q^{m'}}} ... x_{F_{q^{m'}}} C_r -> X_{F_{q^{m'}}}. Then the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (id x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k,Q_l) for every n >= 0.
proof: Let K=F_{q^{m'}} and put Y=C_1 x_K ... x_K C_r. First verify that Y is a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d over K. Each C_i is smooth, projective and geometrically connected over K. Finite products preserve smoothness and projectivity (Segre embedding for projectivity). To check geometric connectedness, base change to k. Each (C_i)_k is proper, reduced and connected, so its global functions form a finite-dimensional reduced k-algebra with no nontrivial idempotents; since k is algebraically closed, this algebra is k. For a product of projective schemes over k, repeated application of the projection formula gives H^0(Y_k,O_{Y_k}) = tensor_k H^0((C_i)_k,O_{(C_i)_k}) = k. Since Y_k is proper and reduced, a nontrivial clopen decomposition would give a nontrivial idempotent in H^0(Y_k,O_{Y_k}); hence Y_k is connected. Thus Y is geometrically connected over K. Each C_i has pure dimension 1, so Y has pure dimension r. The given morphism f:Y -> X_K is proper, surjective and generically finite. The variety X is smooth, projective and geometrically connected over F_{q^m}, hence irreducible: smooth over a field is regular, regular local rings are domains, so irreducible components are open and closed, and connectedness forces a single component. A generically finite surjective morphism to an irreducible variety is finite over a dense open subset, so dim Y = dim X = d. Therefore r=d and Y has pure dimension d. Now set Q=q^{m'}. Since Q is a prime power and the C_i are smooth projective geometrically connected curves over F_Q, lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_382_product_of_curves_semisimplicity applies to Y=C_1 x_F_Q ... x_F_Q C_r. It gives semisimplicity of the Q-power arithmetic Frobenius on H^n_et(Y_{k'},Q_l) for every n>=0, where k' is an algebraic closure of K. Since k is also an algebraic closure of K, we may take k'=k. Thus the q^{m'}-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^n_et(Y_k,Q_l) for every n>=0. Finally apply lemma Spark/9827c89e17d0e461/707a9f with the given m' (which is divisible by m), the variety Y, and the morphism f. All hypotheses are satisfied: X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d>=1 over F_{q^m}, Y is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d over F_{q^{m'}}, f is proper surjective generically finite, and the q^{m'}-power arithmetic Frobenius is semisimple on H^n_et(Y_k,Q_l) for all n. The lemma yields that the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (id x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k,Q_l) for every n>=0. This proves the target statement.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let l\neq p be prime, let m\ge 1, and let k be an algebraic closure of \mathbb F_q. Let X be a smooth projective variety over \mathbb F_{q^m}, and fix a nonzero element of \mathbb Q_l(1), used to identify \mathbb Q_l(j) with \mathbb Q_l. Let \sigma_m:k\to k, \sigma_m(u)=u^{q^m}, let \tau=\mathrm{id}_{X_k}\times\operatorname{Spec}\sigma_m, and let F=\tau^* on H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_l). For a codimension-j cycle z on X_k defined over some finite extension of \mathbb F_{q^m}, let c_z\in H^{2j}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_l) denote the class of z under the chosen identification. Then for every j\ge 0 and every such z there exists \lambda\in\mathbb Q_l^{\times} with F(c_z)=\lambda\, c_{\tau^{-1}z}, where \tau^{-1}z is the inverse-image cycle.
proof: Let k=overline(F_q). Fix a nonzero element e in Q_l(1). For each j>=0 let cl_j(z) denote the l-adic cycle class of a codimension-j cycle z in H^{2j}_{et}(X_k,Q_l(j)), and let c_z be the unique vector in H^{2j}_{et}(X_k,Q_l) such that cl_j(z)=c_z tensor e^{tensor j}. Put sigma_m(u)=u^{q^m}, tau=id_{X_k} x Spec sigma_m, and F=tau^* on H^{2j}_{et}(X_k,Q_l). If X is empty, all cycles and cohomology groups are zero, and lambda=1 works. Hence assume X is nonempty. If necessary, decompose X into irreducible components; the cycle class map and F are additive, and tau permutes components, so the argument is componentwise. Thus we may assume X is smooth projective of pure dimension. By lemma_6a, applied with the prime power q^m in place of q, F is a Q_l-linear automorphism. We prove the statement for every codimension-j cycle z on X_k; the hypothesis that z is defined over a finite extension of F_{q^m} is then a special case. The morphism tau is an automorphism of the scheme X_k over F_{q^m}, with inverse id_{X_k} x Spec sigma_m^{-1}. Hence tau is flat of relative dimension 0. The l-adic cycle class maps are functorial for flat pullback in codimension 0: if f:Y->X is flat of relative dimension 0, then f^*(cl_j(z))=cl_j(f^{-1}z). This is the standard flat-pullback compatibility of cycle classes; it can be checked on integral closed subschemes by writing cl_j(Z)=i_!(1) for the Gysin map of i:Z->X and using flat base change for the cartesian square defining f^{-1}Z, then extending by linearity from the generators of the Chow group. Applying this to f=tau gives tau^*(cl_j(z))=cl_j(tau^{-1}z), where tau^* on the left is the pullback on twisted cohomology H^{2j}_{et}(X_k,Q_l(j)). Here tau^* on the Tate twist sheaf means the usual pullback of mu_{l^n}^{-j}, using the canonical identification of tau^{-1}mu_{l^n} with mu_{l^n} induced by the q^m-power map on roots of unity. It remains to compare this twisted pullback with F under the chosen trivialization. The sheaf Q_l(j) is the l-adic Tate twist. By lemma_78, for the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius, viewing X as a smooth projective variety over F_{q^m}, the induced pullback on the coefficient module Q_l(j) is multiplication by a nonzero scalar; in the convention of lemma_78 this scalar is (q^m)^{-j}, while the opposite convention would give its inverse. The only property needed is that there is an element delta_j in Q_l^x such that for every v in H^{2j}_{et}(X_k,Q_l), tau^*(v tensor e^{tensor j}) = F(v) tensor delta_j e^{tensor j}. Indeed, on the untwisted Q_l factor the pullback is exactly F, and on the Tate twist factor it is the arithmetic Frobenius action on Q_l(j), which lemma_78 identifies with a power of q^m. Since l != p, q is invertible in Q_l, so this scalar is nonzero. Now use cl_j(z)=c_z tensor e^{tensor j}. The previous displayed formula gives tau^*(cl_j(z)) = F(c_z) tensor delta_j e^{tensor j} = delta_j F(c_z) tensor e^{tensor j}. On the other hand, by flat-pullback compatibility and the definition of c_{tau^{-1}z}, tau^*(cl_j(z)) = cl_j(tau^{-1}z) = c_{tau^{-1}z} tensor e^{tensor j}. Comparing the two expressions and applying the isomorphism H^{2j}_{et}(X_k,Q_l) tensor Q_l(j) -> H^{2j}_{et}(X_k,Q_l(j)) that sends v tensor e^{tensor j} to v, we obtain c_{tau^{-1}z} = delta_j F(c_z). Since delta_j is nonzero, lambda=delta_j^{-1} belongs to Q_l^x and satisfies F(c_z)=lambda c_{tau^{-1}z}. The degenerate cases are included. If j=0, lemma_78 gives delta_0=1, so lambda=1. If X is empty, all cycles and cohomology groups are zero and lambda=1 works. If z=0, or more generally if c_z=0, then the displayed equality gives c_{tau^{-1}z}=0, so the same lambda works. If c_z is nonzero, lemma_6a implies F(c_z) is nonzero, and the equality shows c_{tau^{-1}z} is nonzero. This proves the lemma.

statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(C\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(\mathcal A\) be an ample line bundle on \(C\), and fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) identifying Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Then cup product with the cycle class \(\operatorname{cl}(\mathcal A)\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism \(H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(C_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\)-vector spaces.
proof:
Set Q=q^m, so Q is a prime power and k=overline{F}_Q=overline{F}_q. We first choose a very ample divisor on C over F_Q whose associated line bundle is a positive tensor power of A.

1. Existence of the divisor. By the standard theorem on ample line bundles on projective schemes over a field, there exists an integer N>=1 such that L=A^N (tensor power) is very ample over F_Q. For completeness, one may argue as follows: ampleness of A implies, by Serre vanishing, that for all sufficiently large N the line bundle A^N separates closed points and tangent vectors; the corresponding base-point-free linear system then gives a closed immersion into projective space with pullback O(1)=A^N, i.e. A^N is very ample.

Since L is very ample, H^0(C,L) contains a nonzero section s defined over F_Q. Let H=Z(s) be its zero scheme. Because C is a smooth curve and s is nonzero, H is an effective Cartier divisor defined over F_Q, and O_C(H) is isomorphic to L. If H were empty, then s would be nowhere zero and would trivialise L, so L would be isomorphic to O_C. This cannot happen, because O_C is not ample on a positive-dimensional connected projective scheme. Indeed, C is nonempty, so choose a closed point x. If O_C were ample, the ideal sheaf I_x of x would be globally generated. Since C is proper and geometrically connected, H^0(C,O_C)=F_Q (it is a finite extension of F_Q whose base change to k is k); hence H^0(C,I_x)=0, because any global function vanishing at x is a constant in F_Q whose image in kappa(x) is zero. But smoothness of C at x gives m_x/m_x^2 nonzero, so I_x cannot be globally generated. Thus H is nonempty. Its associated line bundle O_C(H)=L is very ample, so H is a very ample divisor on C over F_Q.

2. Apply the curve hard Lefschetz lemma. Apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_hard_lefschetz_curve with the base field F_Q in place of F_q. Its hypotheses are satisfied: C is smooth projective geometrically connected of dimension 1 over F_Q, k=overline{F}_Q, ell!=p, and H is a very ample divisor defined over F_Q. Let xi_H=cl(H) in H^2_et(C_k,Q_ell) be the cycle class obtained from the fixed nonzero element of Q_ell(1). The lemma says that L_H:H^0_et(C_k,Q_ell)->H^2_et(C_k,Q_ell), u |-> u cup xi_H, is a Q_ell-linear isomorphism.

3. Compare xi_H with cl(A). Under the fixed identification Q_ell(1)=Q_ell, the cycle class of a Cartier divisor D is c_1(O_C(D)), and the cycle class of a line bundle M is c_1(M). The first Chern class is additive under tensor products: c_1(M tensor N)=c_1(M)+c_1(N). Therefore xi_H=c_1(O_C(H))=c_1(A^N)=N c_1(A)=N cl(A). (This additivity is the standard group-homomorphism property of the cycle class map on Cartier divisors: the divisor of a product of local equations is the sum of the divisors, and O(D+E)=O(D) tensor O(E).)

Consequently, for every u in H^0_et(C_k,Q_ell), u cup xi_H = u cup (N cl(A)) = N (u cup cl(A)). Thus L_H = N L_A as linear maps, where L_A is cup product with cl(A). Since N is a positive integer, its image in Q_ell is nonzero and invertible. Hence L_A = N^{-1} L_H is an isomorphism. This proves the claim.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let ell != p be prime, let m>=1, and put k=overline(F_q). Let f:Y -> X be a surjective morphism of smooth projective geometrically connected varieties over F_{q^m}, and let n>=0. If the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (id_{Y_k} x Spec sigma)^*, sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, is semisimple on H^n_et(Y_k,Q_ell), then (id_{X_k} x Spec sigma)^* is semisimple on H^n_et(X_k,Q_ell).
proof:
Write Q := q^m = p^{am}, which is again a prime power, and let sigma: k -> k, sigma(c) = c^{Q} = c^{q^m}, be the Q-power automorphism of k = overline{F}_q. Put
  V := H^n_et(Y_k, Q_ell),  W := H^n_et(X_k, Q_ell),
and denote by T_Y := (id_{Y_k} x Spec sigma)^* and T_X := (id_{X_k} x Spec sigma)^* the corresponding Q-power arithmetic Frobenius operators.

Step 1 (finite-dimensionality). X and Y are projective, hence proper, over F_{q^m} = F_Q. Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob with the prime power Q, with K = Q_ell the constant sheaf on Z_k equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism psi: F_Z^* Q_ell -> Q_ell, for Z = X and for Z = Y. It gives that H^n_et(Z_k, Q_ell) is finite-dimensional over Q_ell. Thus V and W are finite-dimensional Q_ell-vector spaces.

Step 2 (invertibility of the Frobenius operators). Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a to the F_Q-schemes X and Y (its hypothesis "scheme over F_q" is used with the base field F_Q and its Q-power automorphism sigma). It says that (id_Z x Spec sigma)^* and (id_Z x Spec sigma^{-1})^* are mutually inverse Q_ell-linear automorphisms of H^n_et(Z_k, Q_ell). Hence T_X in GL_{Q_ell}(W) and T_Y in GL_{Q_ell}(V).

Step 3 (injectivity of f^*). The morphism f: Y -> X is a surjective morphism of smooth projective geometrically connected varieties over F_Q. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_375 (applied with the prime power Q in place of its q), the pullback
  f^* : W = H^n_et(X_k, Q_ell) -> V = H^n_et(Y_k, Q_ell)
is injective for every n >= 0.

Step 4 (Frobenius compatibility). Because f is defined over F_{q^m} = F_Q, its base change f_k: Y_k -> X_k to k satisfies, for every k-point, the commutativity of
  Y_k --id x Spec sigma--> Y_k
   |f_k                 |f_k
   v                    v
  X_k --id x Spec sigma--> X_k :
indeed both composites are the morphism induced on the fibre product Y x_{F_Q} Spec k by the pair (f, sigma), using that f commutes with the F_Q-structure maps (f is F_Q-linear) and that sigma is a field automorphism fixing F_Q. Passing to contravariant pullback on etale cohomology gives
  T_Y o f^* = f^* o T_X.   (*)

Step 5 (the image is T_Y-stable, and T_Y acts invertibly on it). Set U := f^*(W) subset V, a Q_ell-linear subspace of the finite-dimensional space V, hence finite-dimensional. If u = f^*(w) in U then by (*) T_Y(u) = f^*(T_X(w)) in U, so U is T_Y-stable; write S := T_Y|_U in End_{Q_ell}(U). Since T_Y is an automorphism of V, S is injective; an injective endomorphism of the finite-dimensional space U is bijective, so S in GL_{Q_ell}(U).

Step 6 (restriction of a semisimple operator to a stable subspace is semisimple). Assume T_Y is semisimple on V (this is the hypothesis of the lemma). By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5, the base change T_V := T_Y tensor id on V_bar := V tensor_{Q_ell} Q_ell_bar is diagonalizable. The subspace U_bar := U tensor_{Q_ell} Q_ell_bar is T_V-stable (T_Y-stability of U is preserved by extension of scalars), and T_V is diagonalizable, so its minimal polynomial mu(t) in Q_ell_bar[t] is a product of distinct linear factors: indeed, writing V_bar = (+)_{lambda in spec T_V} ker(T_V - lambda) we get Q_ell_bar[t]/(mu) acting faithfully on V_bar and mu = prod_{lambda in spec T_V}(t - lambda), which is squarefree (conversely, a squarefree split mu gives diagonalizability by the Chinese remainder theorem applied to Q_ell_bar[t]/(mu) = prod_lambda Q_ell_bar and the resulting decomposition into eigenspaces).
Let nu(t) be the minimal polynomial of the restriction T_V|_{U_bar}. Since mu(T_V) = 0 on V_bar, its restriction mu(T_V)|_{U_bar} = 0, so nu divides mu in Q_ell_bar[t]. A divisor of a squarefree polynomial is squarefree, so nu is a product of distinct linear factors over Q_ell_bar; by the criterion recalled above, T_V|_{U_bar} is diagonalizable. But T_V|_{U_bar} = S tensor id. Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_5 in the reverse direction to S on U, we conclude that S = T_Y|_U is semisimple on U.

Step 7 (transport along f^*). The map f^*: W -> U is Q_ell-linear, surjective by the definition of U, and injective by Step 3; hence it is an isomorphism. By (*) it intertwines T_X and S:
  f^* o T_X = S o f^*.
The spaces W and U are finite-dimensional over Q_ell and the operators T_X and S are invertible (Steps 2 and 5). Therefore eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_8 applies to alpha = f^*: W -> U, T_V = T_X and T_W = S, and yields: T_X is semisimple on W if and only if S is semisimple on U.

Step 8 (conclusion). By Step 6, S is semisimple on U; by Step 7, T_X is semisimple on W = H^n_et(X_k, Q_ell). This is exactly the required conclusion.

All cases are covered: n >= 0 was arbitrary, and no hypothesis beyond those stated (surjectivity of f, smooth projective geometrically connected over F_{q^m}, ell != p) was used. Note that f was not required to be generically finite, and no top-degree trace statement was invoked; the only input beyond formal linear algebra is the injectivity of f^* from eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_375.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, let beta:V x V -> K be a perfect bilinear form, let epsilon in {1,-1} satisfy beta(y,x)=epsilon beta(x,y), let c in K^*, and let T in GL_K(V) satisfy beta(Tx,Ty)=c beta(x,y) for all x,y in V. Let Kbar be an algebraic closure of K and let E_alpha be the alpha-eigenspace of T on V tensor_K Kbar. Then T is semisimple on V if and only if, for every eigenvalue alpha of T, the induced Kbar-bilinear pairing E_alpha x E_{c/alpha} -> Kbar is perfect.
proof:
We prove the statement by pure linear algebra. All the hypotheses (characteristic 0, perfectness, $\varepsilon$-symmetry, the similitude relation) are preserved by arbitrary field extension, so we work over $\overline K$ from the start, after one preliminary reduction.

=== Step 0. Reduction to the split case. ===
Put $\bar V:=V\otimes_K\overline K$ and let $\bar T:=T\otimes\mathrm{id}$. Extend $\beta$ $\overline K$-bilinearly by $\beta(v\otimes\lambda,w\otimes\mu):=\lambda\mu\,\beta(v,w)$; in any $K$-basis of $V$ the matrix of $\beta$ on $\bar V$ is the same matrix as on $V$, hence is invertible, so $\beta$ is still perfect on $\bar V$; $\varepsilon$-symmetry and $\beta(\bar Tx,\bar Ty)=c\,\beta(x,y)$ (with $c\in K^{\times}\subset\overline K^{\times}$) are immediate from the definitions.

We record the base-change fact for semisimplicity: $T$ is semisimple on $V$ if and only if $\bar T$ is diagonalisable on $\bar V$. Indeed, by the structure theorem for $K[t]$-modules, $V\cong\bigoplus_j K[t]/(p_j^{e_j})$ with the $p_j$ irreducible and $e_j\ge1$, and $T$ is semisimple iff all $e_j=1$. The minimal polynomial $\mu_T\in K[t]$ is unchanged by the extension $\overline K/K$ (both are the monic generators of the same principal ideal $\{f\in K[t]:f(T)=0\}$ after extension), and $\bar T$ is diagonalisable iff $\mu_T$ splits over $\overline K$ with simple roots, i.e. iff $\mu_T$ is square-free, i.e. (as $\mu_T=\mathrm{lcm}_j p_j^{e_j}$) iff all $e_j=1$. This proves the equivalence.

Henceforth we write $V$ for $\bar V$, $T$ for $\bar T$, and $K$ for $\overline K$; $K$ is algebraically closed of characteristic $0$. All eigenvalues below lie in $K$, and all are non-zero because $T\in\mathrm{GL}(V)$.

=== Step 1. The adjoint of $T$. ===
Since $\beta$ is perfect, for every $A\in\mathrm{End}_K(V)$ there is a unique $A^{\dagger}\in\mathrm{End}_K(V)$ with
$$\beta(Ax,y)=\beta(x,A^{\dagger}y)\qquad\forall x,y\in V.$$
The map $A\mapsto A^{\dagger}$ is $K$-linear and an anti-involution: $\beta(ABx,y)=\beta(Bx,A^{\dagger}y)=\beta(x,B^{\dagger}A^{\dagger}y)$, so $(AB)^{\dagger}=B^{\dagger}A^{\dagger}$, and $(\lambda A)^{\dagger}=\lambda A^{\dagger}$.
Applying this to $A=T$: for all $x,y$, $\beta(x,T^{\dagger}Ty)=\beta(Tx,Ty)=c\,\beta(x,y)=\beta(x,cy)$; perfectness gives $T^{\dagger}T=c\,\mathrm{id}$, hence
$$T^{\dagger}=c\,T^{-1},\qquad (T^{-1})^{\dagger}=(T^{\dagger})^{-1}=c^{-1}T. \tag{1}$$
Equivalently, $\beta(Tx,y)=\beta(x,cT^{-1}y)$ and $\beta(x,T^{-1}y)=c^{-1}\beta(Tx,y)$ for all $x,y$.

=== Step 2. Generalised eigenspaces are mutually orthogonal away from $\gamma=c/\alpha$. ===
For an eigenvalue $\alpha$ let $G_\alpha:=\ker(T-\alpha)^{m_\alpha}$ be the generalised eigenspace, with $m_\alpha$ the nilpotency index of $T-\alpha$ on $G_\alpha$. Each $G_\alpha$ is stable by $T$ and by $T^{-1}$, hence by every polynomial in $T,T^{-1}$.

Claim: if $\alpha\gamma\ne c$ then $\beta(G_\alpha,G_\gamma)=0$.
Proof: let $v\in G_\alpha$, $w\in G_\gamma$, $m:=m_\gamma$. On $G_\alpha$ write $T=\alpha+N$ with $N$ nilpotent; then $T^{-1}=\alpha^{-1}\sum_{k\ge0}(-N/\alpha)^{k}$ (finite sum), so $cT^{-1}-\gamma=(c/\alpha-\gamma)\cdot u$ where $u$ is a polynomial in $N$ with constant term $1$, hence invertible on $G_\alpha$. Since $\alpha\gamma\ne c$ and $\alpha\ne0$, the scalar $c/\alpha-\gamma$ is non-zero, so $A:=(cT^{-1}-\gamma)^{m}$ is an automorphism of $G_\alpha$. Choose $v'\in G_\alpha$ with $Av=v$. Using (1), $A^{\dagger}=(T-\gamma)^{m}$. Therefore
$$\beta(v,w)=\beta(Av',w)=\beta(v',A^{\dagger}w)=\beta\bigl(v',(T-\gamma)^{m}w\bigr)=\beta(v',0)=0.\quad\blacksquare$$
In particular, taking $v,w$ eigenvectors gives the sharper relation
$$(\alpha\gamma-c)\,\beta(v,w)=\beta(Tv,Tw)-c\beta(v,w)=0 \tag{2}$$\nfor $v\in E_\alpha,\ w\in E_\gamma$.

=== Step 3. The pairing $G_\alpha\times G_{c/\alpha}\to K$ is perfect. ===
Since $K$ is algebraically closed, $V=\bigoplus_{\gamma}G_\gamma$. Fix $\alpha$ and put $\delta:=c/\alpha$. By Step 2, $G_\alpha\perp G_\gamma$ for every $\gamma\ne\delta$. If $0\ne v\in G_\alpha$, perfectness of $\beta$ gives $u\in V$ with $\beta(v,u)\ne0$; writing $u=\sum_\gamma u_\gamma$ with $u_\gamma\in G_\gamma$, all terms with $\gamma\ne\delta$ vanish by Step 2, so $\beta(v,u_\delta)\ne0$ with $u_\delta\in G_\delta$. Thus $G_\alpha\to G_\delta^{\vee}$ is injective; the same argument with the roles of $\alpha,\delta$ interchanged (note $c/\delta=\alpha$) shows $G_\delta\to G_\alpha^{\vee}$ is injective. Hence $\dim G_\alpha=\dim G_\delta$ and both maps are isomorphisms, i.e. $\beta|_{G_\alpha\times G_\delta}$ is perfect.

=== Step 4. Proof of ($\Rightarrow$). ===
Assume $T$ semisimple, so $V=\bigoplus_\gamma E_\gamma$ with $E_\gamma=\ker(T-\gamma)$ and $G_\gamma=E_\gamma$. Fix an eigenvalue $\alpha$, put $\delta=c/\alpha$, and consider $\beta|_{E_\alpha\times E_\delta}$.
(a) If $0\ne v\in E_\alpha$, write $u=\sum_\gamma u_\gamma$ with $\beta(v,u)\ne0$; by (2), $\beta(v,u_\gamma)=0$ unless $\gamma=c/\alpha=\delta$, so $\beta(v,u_\delta)\ne0$. Thus $E_\alpha\to E_\delta^{\vee}$ is injective; in particular $E_\delta\ne0$.
(b) Interchanging $\alpha$ and $\delta$ (valid since $\delta$ is now known to be an eigenvalue and $c/\delta=\alpha$) gives an injection $E_\delta\to E_\alpha^{\vee}$.
So $\dim E_\alpha=\dim E_\delta$ and both maps are isomorphisms: $\beta|_{E_\alpha\times E_{c/\alpha}}$ is perfect. Since $\alpha$ was arbitrary, this proves ($\Rightarrow$).

=== Step 5. Proof of ($\Leftarrow$). ===
Assume that for every eigenvalue $\alpha$ the pairing $E_\alpha\times E_{c/\alpha}\to K$ is perfect. Fix an eigenvalue $\alpha$, put $\delta:=c/\alpha$, and write
$$G:=G_\alpha,\quad H:=G_\delta,\quad N:=(T-\alpha)|_{G},\quad M:=(T-\delta)|_{H}.$$
Both $N$ and $M$ are nilpotent, $E_\alpha=\ker N$ (indeed $\ker(T-\alpha)=\bigoplus_\gamma(E_\alpha\cap G_\gamma)$ and $E_\alpha\cap G_\gamma=0$ for $\gamma\ne\alpha$ because $T|_{G_\gamma}$ has the single eigenvalue $\gamma$), and similarly $E_\delta=\ker M$.

By Step 3, $\beta|_{G\times H}$ is perfect. For $y\in H$ the functional $x\mapsto\beta(Nx,y)$ on $G$ is therefore represented by a unique element of $H$; call it $N^{*}y$, so that
$$\beta(Nx,y)=\beta(x,N^{*}y)\qquad(x\in G,\ y\in H).$$
We compute $N^{*}$. For $x\in G,\ y\in H$, using Step 1,
$$\beta(Nx,y)=\beta(Tx,y)-\alpha\beta(x,y)=\beta(x,cT^{-1}y)-\beta(x,\alpha y)=\beta\bigl(x,(cT^{-1}-\alpha)y\bigr).$$
The operator $cT^{-1}-\alpha$ preserves $H$ (as a rational function of $T$), and on $H$ we have the identity
$$cT^{-1}-\alpha=-\alpha\,T^{-1}(T-\delta),\qquad\text{since }-\alpha T^{-1}(T-\delta)=-\alpha\,\mathrm{id}+\alpha\delta T^{-1}=-\alpha+cT^{-1}$$\nusing $\alpha\delta=c$. Uniqueness in the definition of $N^{*}$ therefore gives
$$N^{*}=-\alpha\,T^{-1}M\ \ \text{on } H.$$
Consequently
$$\bigl(\mathrm{im}\,N\bigr)^{\perp}\cap H=\{y\in H:\beta(Nx,y)=0\ \forall x\in G\}=\ker N^{*}=\ker\bigl(T^{-1}M|_{H}\bigr)=\ker M=E_\delta, \tag{3}$$\nwhere we used $T^{-1}$ invertible on $H$ and $\alpha\ne0$.

Now suppose, for a contradiction, that $N\ne0$. Let $k\ge1$ be minimal with $N^{k}=0$; then $k\ge2$ and $N^{k-1}\ne0$. Pick $x\in G$ with $v:=N^{k-1}x\ne0$. Then $Nv=0$ and $v\in\mathrm{im}\,N$, so
$$0\ne v\in E_\alpha\cap\mathrm{im}\,N.$$
By hypothesis the pairing $E_\alpha\times E_\delta\to K$ is perfect; its left non-degeneracy applied to the non-zero $v\in E_\alpha$ yields $w\in E_\delta$ with $\beta(v,w)\ne0$. But $v\in\mathrm{im}\,N$ and $w\in E_\delta=(\mathrm{im}\,N)^{\perp}\cap H$ by (3), so $\beta(v,w)=0$, a contradiction.

Hence $N=0$, i.e. $T|_{G_\alpha}=\alpha\,\mathrm{id}_{G_\alpha}$: $T$ acts as a scalar on each generalised eigenspace. As this holds for every eigenvalue $\alpha$ and $V=\bigoplus_\alpha G_\alpha$, $T$ is diagonalisable over $K=\overline K$. By Step 0, $T$ is semisimple on $V$ over the original field.

=== Conclusion. ===
Steps 4 and 5 give the equivalence: $T$ is semisimple on $V$ if and only if for every eigenvalue $\alpha$ the induced $\overline K$-bilinear pairing $E_\alpha\times E_{c/\alpha}\to\overline K$ is perfect. (The empty case $V=0$ is trivial: there are no eigenvalues and the zero operator is semisimple.) This completes the proof.

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let \(\bar K\) be an algebraic closure of K, let V be a finite-dimensional K-vector space, and let \(T\in\operatorname{GL}_K(V)\) be an operator whose base change to \(V\otimes_K\bar K\) is diagonalizable. Then for every integer \(k\ge1\) the automorphism induced by T on the k-th exterior power \({\textstyle\bigwedge}^k_K V\) has diagonalizable base change to \(({\textstyle\bigwedge}^k_K V)\otimes_K\bar K\).
proof:
We prove the statement by a direct linear-algebra argument; no external results are needed.

**Setup and notation.** Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $0$, $\bar K$ an algebraic closure, $V$ a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space with $\dim_K V=n$, and $T\in\operatorname{GL}_K(V)$ an operator such that its base change
$$T_{\bar K}:=T\otimes_K\mathrm{id}_{\bar K}\in\operatorname{GL}_{\bar K}(V_{\bar K}),\qquad V_{\bar K}:=V\otimes_K\bar K,$$
is diagonalizable. Fix an integer $k\ge 1$. Write $\textstyle\bigwedge^k_KV$ for the $k$-th exterior power and $\textstyle\bigwedge^kT$ for the $\bar K$-... rather, the $K$-linear automorphism it induces:
$$\textstyle\bigwedge^kT:\ \bigwedge^k_KV\longrightarrow\bigwedge^k_KV,\qquad v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_k\longmapsto Tv_1\wedge\cdots\wedge Tv_k.$$
This is well defined because the map $(v_1,\dots,v_k)\mapsto Tv_1\wedge\cdots\wedge Tv_k$ is $K$-multilinear and alternating (swapping $v_i,v_{i+1}$ swaps two factors in the wedge, and $T$ being a function makes repeated arguments give a wedge with a repeated factor, hence $0$), so the universal property of $\bigwedge^k_KV$ yields a unique $K$-linear map $\bigwedge^kT$. Functoriality gives $\bigwedge^k(S\circ S')=(\bigwedge^kS)\circ(\bigwedge^kS')$ and $\bigwedge^k\mathrm{id}=\mathrm{id}$; applying this to $S=T$, $S'=T^{-1}$ shows $\bigwedge^kT\in\operatorname{GL}_K(\bigwedge^k_KV)$, as the statement asserts.

**Step 1: exterior powers commute with the scalar extension.** We claim there is a canonical $\bar K$-linear isomorphism
$$\Phi:\Bigl(\textstyle\bigwedge^k_KV\Bigr)\otimes_K\bar K\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \textstyle\bigwedge^k_{\bar K}\bigl(V_{\bar K}\bigr),\qquad (v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_k)\otimes\lambda\ \longmapsto\ \lambda\,(v_1\otimes 1)\wedge\cdots\wedge(v_k\otimes 1).$$
Existence: the right-hand side is $\bar K$-multilinear and alternating in $(v_1,\dots,v_k)$ (the map $v\mapsto v\otimes1$ is $K$-linear, and the wedge on the right is $\bar K$-multilinear and alternating), so by the universal property there is a unique $K$-multilinear... precisely, a unique $K$-linear map $\bigwedge^k_KV\to\bigwedge^k_{\bar K}(V_{\bar K})$ as displayed, and hence by the universal property of the tensor product a unique $\bar K$-linear map $\Phi$ as displayed.

That $\Phi$ is an isomorphism is checked on a basis. Choose a $K$-basis $e_1,\dots,e_n$ of $V$. Recall the standard fact (proved below) that $\{e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_k}:1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n\}$ is a $K$-basis of $\bigwedge^k_KV$. Then $\{(e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_k})\otimes1\}$ is a $\bar K$-basis of the left-hand side. Since $e_1\otimes1,\dots,e_n\otimes1$ is a $\bar K$-basis of $V_{\bar K}$, the same standard fact gives that $\{(e_{i_1}\otimes1)\wedge\cdots\wedge(e_{i_k}\otimes1)\}$ is a $\bar K$-basis of the right-hand side. By construction $\Phi$ sends the first basis bijectively onto the second, so $\Phi$ is a $\bar K$-linear isomorphism.

*Proof of the standard fact.* Spanning: expand each $v_j=\sum_a c_{ja}e_a$; by multilinearilty $v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_k=\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k}c_{1a_1}\cdots c_{ka_k}\,e_{a_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{a_k}$; terms with a repeated index vanish (alternating, and $\operatorname{char}K=0\ne2$ so $x\wedge x=-\,x\wedge x$ forces $x\wedge x=0$), and the remaining terms are $\pm$ a basis wedge with strictly increasing indices. Linear independence: for each increasing $k$-tuple $I=(i_1<\cdots<i_k)$ define the $K$-multilinear alternating map $\det_I:(V)^k\to K$ by $\det_I(w_1,\dots,w_k)=\det\bigl(c_{a\,i_b}\bigr)_{1\le a,b\le k}$, where $w_b=\sum_a c_{ab}e_a$. By the universal property it factors through a linear functional $\delta_I:\bigwedge^k_KV\to K$, and $\delta_I(e_{j_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{j_k})$ is the determinant of the $k\times k$ matrix with $(a,b)$-entry $\delta_{i_a,j_b}$, which is $1$ if $I=J$ and $0$ otherwise. Hence any linear relation among the basis wedges vanishes against each $\delta_I$, so they are independent. (This also covers $k>n$, where the index set is empty and $\bigwedge^k_KV=0$.)

**Step 2: $\Phi$ identifies the two operators.** Let $F$ denote the $\bar K$-linear automorphism of $(\bigwedge^k_KV)\otimes_K\bar K$ induced by $\bigwedge^kT$, i.e. $F=(\bigwedge^kT)\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\bar K}$, and let $G:=\bigwedge^k_{\bar K}(T_{\bar K})$ be the automorphism of $\bigwedge^k_{\bar K}(V_{\bar K})$ induced by $T_{\bar K}$. We claim $\Phi\circ F=G\circ\Phi$. Both are $\bar K$-linear, and the elements $(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_k)\otimes\lambda$ span the source, so it suffices on those:
$$\Phi\bigl(F((v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_k)\otimes\lambda)\bigr)=\Phi\bigl((Tv_1\wedge\cdots\wedge Tv_k)\otimes\lambda\bigr)=\lambda\,(Tv_1\otimes1)\wedge\cdots\wedge(Tv_k\otimes1),$$
while
$$G\bigl(\Phi((v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_k)\otimes\lambda)\bigr)=\lambda\,T_{\bar K}(v_1\otimes1)\wedge\cdots\wedge T_{\bar K}(v_k\otimes1)=\lambda\,(Tv_1\otimes1)\wedge\cdots\wedge(Tv_k\otimes1),$$
since $T_{\bar K}(v\otimes\mu)=Tv\otimes\mu$ by definition of the base-changed operator. Thus the diagram commutes, so $F$ and $G$ are conjugate operators; in particular $F$ is diagonalizable if and only if $G$ is.

**Step 3: $G=\bigwedge^k_{\bar K}(T_{\bar K})$ is diagonalizable.** By hypothesis $T_{\bar K}$ is diagonalizable, so there is a $\bar K$-basis $\mathcal B=\{f_1,\dots,f_n\}$ of $V_{\bar K}$ consisting of eigenvectors of $T_{\bar K}$; write $T_{\bar K}f_j=\alpha_jf_j$ with $\alpha_j\in\bar K^{\times}$ (nonzero because $T_{\bar K}$ is invertible). By the standard fact of Step 1 applied to the $\bar K$-basis $\mathcal B$, the elements
$$f_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge f_{i_k},\qquad 1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n,$$
